about: Predict the change (docs/anp-spec.md section 8.2). Each scenario states a perturbation; the learner predicts up, down or none for each variable, then sees its causal chain. Levels: 1 one step in one system, 2 several steps in one system, 3 across systems, 4 a time course answered in two stages (the immediate change, then after compensation). A variable's chain lists keys of its stage's steps, in causal order from the stage's start; shared steps merge into one diagram. Item ids: predict:<scenario>:<variable>, with -<stage> added for level 4. Checked by scripts/lib/anp-tool-checks/predict.mjs.

levels.4: Time course: the change, then compensation

scenarios.title: A tube narrows
scenarios.misconception: halving the radius halves the flow
scenarios.setup: Water flows through a rubber tube from a tank. The pressures at the two ends of the tube are held constant. You squeeze the tube until its radius is half what it was.
scenarios.start: Tube radius halves

steps.p: Pressures at both ends held fixed

variables.name: Resistance of the tube
variables.why: Resistance depends on the fourth power of the radius. Half the radius gives 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 16 times the resistance.

variables.name: Flow through the tube
variables.why: Flow equals the pressure gradient divided by resistance. The gradient has not changed and resistance is about 16 times higher, so flow falls to about one sixteenth, far more than half.

variables.name: Pressure gradient between the two ends
variables.why: The gradient is the difference between the pressures at the two ends, and both are held fixed. Squeezing the tube changes resistance, not the pressure difference that drives flow.

scenarios.title: Solute added to one side
scenarios.theme: add solute to one side of a membrane, predict water movement
scenarios.misconception: the solute moves to even out the concentrations
scenarios.setup: Two compartments of equal volume are separated by a membrane that lets water through but not glucose. Both start as pure water. You dissolve glucose in side A.
scenarios.start: Glucose dissolved in side A

steps.wa: Membrane holds glucose back on side A
steps.os: Water streams from B into A (osmosis)
steps.sa: Side A holds solute that cannot cross

variables.name: Net movement of water from side B into side A
variables.why: The membrane holds the glucose back on side A. That held-back solute lowers the water pressure in the membrane's pores on side A, so water streams through them from B into A. That net movement of water is osmosis: water follows solute.

variables.name: Volume of side A
variables.why: Water arrives on side A and the glucose cannot leave, so the volume of side A grows.

variables.name: Volume of side B
variables.why: The water that moves into A comes from B, so side B loses volume.

variables.name: Amount of glucose on side B
variables.why: The membrane does not let glucose through, so none reaches side B. Water moves instead, which is why the volumes change.

variables.name: Osmotic pressure of the solution on side A
variables.why: Osmotic pressure depends on the concentration of solute that cannot cross the membrane. Side A went from none to some, so its osmotic pressure rose, and that is what pulls water in.

scenarios.title: Acid added with and without a buffer
scenarios.theme: add acid to a buffered vs unbuffered solution
scenarios.misconception: a buffer keeps pH exactly constant
scenarios.setup: Two beakers hold the same salt solution at pH 7.4. Beaker 2 also contains bicarbonate, the base half of the carbonic acid–bicarbonate buffer. You add the same small amount of a strong acid to each beaker.
scenarios.start: Strong acid added to both beakers

steps.nob: Beaker 1: nothing takes up the H+
steps.bind: Beaker 2: bicarbonate binds most of the H+
steps.few: Beaker 2: a little H+ stays free

variables.name: Hydrogen ion concentration in beaker 1
variables.why: A strong acid releases all its hydrogen ions in water. With no buffer to take them up, every one of them stays free.

variables.name: pH of beaker 1
variables.why: pH falls as hydrogen ion concentration rises. Without a buffer, even a small amount of strong acid can drop the pH by several units.

variables.name: Bicarbonate in beaker 2
variables.why: Bicarbonate combines with the added hydrogen ions, so some of it is used up. That is the buffer doing its job.

variables.name: Carbonic acid in beaker 2
variables.why: Each hydrogen ion that bicarbonate takes up becomes part of a carbonic acid molecule. Carbonic acid is a weak acid, so it holds on to most of that hydrogen.

variables.name: pH of beaker 2
variables.why: A buffer limits a pH change; it does not prevent one. A small share of the hydrogen ions stays free, so the pH falls a little, far less than in beaker 1.

scenarios.title: A red blood cell in a hypertonic solution
scenarios.theme: a red blood cell placed in a hypertonic solution
scenarios.misconception: salt moves into the cell to balance the concentrations
scenarios.setup: A red blood cell is moved from plasma into a salt solution much more concentrated than the fluid inside the cell. Water crosses the membrane freely; the salt, in effect, does not.
scenarios.start: Cell placed in a hypertonic solution

steps.wi: More held-back solute outside the cell
steps.out: Water leaves the cell by osmosis
steps.stay: Solutes stay on their own side

variables.name: Net movement of water out of the cell
variables.why: The solution outside holds more solute that cannot cross. Water follows solute, so it flows out of the cell through the membrane and its water channels, toward the more concentrated side. That is osmosis.

variables.name: Cell volume
variables.why: Water leaves and nothing replaces it, so the cell shrinks and its membrane crinkles. That is crenation.

variables.name: Solute concentration inside the cell
variables.why: The solute particles stay inside while water leaves, so the same amount of solute sits in a smaller volume.

variables.name: Number of solute particles inside the cell
variables.why: Only water crossed the membrane. The number of particles inside is the same; their concentration rose because the water around them left.

scenarios.title: More glucose, busy carriers
scenarios.misconception: a steeper gradient always speeds transport
scenarios.setup: Glucose enters a cell by facilitated diffusion through carrier proteins. The glucose concentration outside is already so high that every carrier is busy all the time. The outside concentration now doubles.
scenarios.start: Outside glucose doubles

steps.max: Entry stays at the transport maximum
steps.none: Nothing signals the cell to add carriers

variables.name: Glucose concentration gradient across the membrane
variables.why: The inside concentration has not changed and the outside has doubled, so the difference between them is larger.

variables.name: Rate of glucose entry into the cell
variables.why: Facilitated diffusion depends on a limited number of carriers. Once every carrier is busy (saturation), a steeper gradient cannot speed entry: the rate stays at its maximum.

variables.name: Number of glucose carriers in the membrane
variables.why: The glucose level outside does not change how many carrier proteins the cell has in its membrane in this moment, so the ceiling on the rate stays where it was.

scenarios.title: The sodium–potassium pump is poisoned
scenarios.misconception: the gradients vanish instantly when the pump stops
scenarios.setup: A poison binds the sodium–potassium pumps of a cell and stops them. The cell keeps making ATP. Predict the changes over the next hour.
scenarios.start: Sodium–potassium pumps stop

steps.naout: Pump no longer moves Na+ out
steps.kin: Pump no longer moves K+ in
steps.atp: ATP use by the pumps falls
steps.co: Less energy to drive glucose in with Na+

variables.name: Sodium concentration inside the cell
variables.why: Sodium leaks in down its gradient all the time, and normally the pump throws it back out. With the pump stopped, the leak continues and sodium accumulates inside.

variables.name: Potassium concentration inside the cell
variables.why: Potassium leaks out down its gradient. The pump normally brings it back in; now nothing replaces what leaks out.

variables.name: Cell volume
variables.why: The pump moves three sodium ions out for every two potassium ions in, so it constantly removes solute from the cell. Without it, sodium and the ions that follow it build up inside, water follows by osmosis, and the cell swells.

variables.name: ATP used by the sodium–potassium pumps
variables.why: The pump is an enzyme that splits ATP to power each cycle. A blocked pump does not cycle, so it uses no ATP, even though ATP is still available.

variables.name: Glucose uptake that is coupled to sodium entry
variables.why: This is secondary active transport: sodium moving down its gradient drags glucose in with it. As sodium builds up inside, the gradient shrinks and has less energy to give, so glucose uptake slows.

scenarios.title: A cell’s oxygen supply is cut off
scenarios.theme: oxygen supply to a cell is cut off
scenarios.misconception: without oxygen a cell makes no ATP at all
scenarios.setup: A blood vessel supplying a small patch of tissue is blocked, so its cells receive no oxygen. Predict the changes inside one cell over the next few minutes.
scenarios.start: No oxygen reaches the cell

steps.pyr: Pyruvate cannot be broken down aerobically
steps.two: Glycolysis yields only 2 ATP per glucose

variables.name: ATP made by aerobic respiration
variables.why: Oxygen is the final electron acceptor of the electron transport chain. Without it the chain stops, and so does the ATP it would have made.

variables.name: Lactate production
variables.why: Pyruvate from glycolysis can no longer be broken down in the mitochondria. The cell converts it to lactate, which frees up the electron carrier glycolysis needs to keep running.

variables.name: Rate of glycolysis
variables.why: As ATP falls and ADP rises, the enzymes of glycolysis are stimulated. The cell breaks down glucose faster to make up part of the shortfall.

variables.name: Total ATP produced per minute
variables.why: Glycolysis alone yields 2 ATP per glucose, against roughly 30 when aerobic respiration runs as well. Even with faster glycolysis, total ATP production falls.

variables.name: Carbon dioxide produced by the cell
variables.why: Most of the CO2 a cell makes is released in the citric acid cycle, which stops when the electron transport chain stops. Converting pyruvate to lactate releases no CO2.

scenarios.title: Body temperature rises above its set point
scenarios.theme: a regulated variable rises above its set point
scenarios.misconception: exercise raises the temperature set point
scenarios.setup: You run hard on a warm day, and your body temperature climbs above its set point. Predict how your temperature loop responds.
scenarios.start: Body temperature above the set point

variables.name: Signals from warm-sensitive sensory receptors
variables.why: Warm-sensitive nerve endings in the skin, and temperature-sensitive neurons in the brain, fire faster as they warm.

variables.name: Diameter of blood vessels in the skin
variables.why: The control center relaxes the smooth muscle of skin blood vessels. The vessels widen and carry more warm blood close to the surface.

variables.name: Sweat released onto the skin
variables.why: The control center signals the sweat glands to release sweat. As sweat evaporates, it carries heat away.

variables.name: Heat lost from the skin
variables.why: More warm blood at the surface and more sweat evaporating both move heat out of the body. The response opposes the rise: negative feedback.

variables.name: The temperature set point
variables.why: Exercise raises your temperature, not your target. The control center compares the higher temperature with an unchanged set point and responds to the difference. (A fever is different: there the set point itself moves up.)

scenarios.title: Blood pressure dips for a moment
scenarios.misconception: the loop lowers pressure further because negative feedback means lowering
scenarios.setup: You stand up quickly and your blood pressure dips for a moment. Predict how the blood pressure loop responds over the next few seconds.
scenarios.start: Blood pressure dips

steps.cc: Control center in the brain responds
steps.bp: Blood pressure rises back toward the set point

variables.name: Signals from stretch-sensitive sensory receptors in large arteries
variables.why: Lower pressure stretches the artery walls less, so the stretch-sensitive nerve endings in them fire less often. That drop is how the change is detected.

variables.name: Heart rate
variables.why: The control center in the brain reads the drop in signals as low pressure and sends commands that speed up the heart.

variables.name: Diameter of small arteries
variables.why: The same commands contract the smooth muscle in the walls of small arteries. The narrower vessels raise resistance to flow.

variables.name: Blood pressure a few seconds later, compared with the dip
variables.why: A faster heart and narrower small arteries push pressure back up. The response opposes the original fall, which is what negative feedback means.

scenarios.title: Potassium outside the cell doubles
scenarios.theme: extracellular potassium rises, predict resting potential
scenarios.misconception: a rise in outside potassium makes the inside more negative
scenarios.setup: The potassium concentration in the fluid around a cell rises from 4 to 8 mmol/L (hyperkalemia). The concentration inside the cell stays the same. For voltages, "increases" means the number goes up: −70 mV becoming −60 mV is an increase.
scenarios.start: Potassium outside doubles

steps.eq: Less voltage needed to balance it
steps.ek: K+ equilibrium potential becomes less negative

variables.name: Potassium concentration gradient across the membrane
variables.why: Inside is unchanged and outside has risen, so the difference between them is smaller.

variables.name: Net outward leak of potassium, at the moment the outside level rises
variables.why: The concentration gradient is what pushes potassium out through leak channels. A smaller gradient pushes less potassium out at the same voltage.

variables.name: Potassium equilibrium potential (as a number in mV)
variables.why: The equilibrium potential is the voltage that exactly balances the concentration gradient. A smaller gradient is balanced by a smaller voltage, so it moves from about −95 mV to about −77 mV.

variables.name: Resting membrane potential (as a number in mV)
variables.why: The resting membrane is far more permeable to potassium than to anything else, so the resting potential sits close to the potassium equilibrium potential and moves with it. The cell depolarizes, for example from −70 toward −60 mV.

scenarios.title: A toxin blocks voltage-gated sodium channels
scenarios.theme: sodium channels are blocked, predict the action potential
scenarios.misconception: blocking sodium channels abolishes the resting potential
scenarios.setup: A toxin blocks the voltage-gated sodium channels of a neuron. Its leak channels and sodium–potassium pumps still work. A stimulus arrives that would normally bring the membrane to threshold.
scenarios.start: Voltage-gated Na+ channels blocked

steps.leak: Leak channels and pump still work
steps.stim: Stimulus still opens its own channels

variables.name: Resting membrane potential
variables.why: The resting potential is set by leak channels and the sodium–potassium pump. Voltage-gated sodium channels are closed at rest anyway, so blocking them does not change it.

variables.name: Size of the graded potential the stimulus produces
variables.why: A graded potential comes from ligand-gated or mechanically gated channels at the site of the stimulus. Those still open, so the graded potential is normal.

variables.name: Number of action potentials fired
variables.why: An action potential needs voltage-gated sodium channels to open at threshold and let sodium rush in. With them blocked, the membrane can reach threshold but nothing follows.

variables.name: Signals carried along the axon to its far end
variables.why: Propagation is each patch of membrane firing an action potential that triggers the next. With no action potential at the start, nothing travels along the axon.

scenarios.title: A stronger stimulus
scenarios.misconception: a stronger stimulus makes bigger action potentials
scenarios.setup: A neuron is stimulated just above threshold and fires action potentials. The stimulus is then made twice as strong.
scenarios.start: Stimulus twice as strong

steps.thr: Threshold is reached sooner after each refractory period
steps.aon: All-or-none: each action potential is full size
steps.amp: Height of each action potential unchanged

variables.name: Size of the graded potential at the stimulus site
variables.why: Graded potentials vary with the strength of the stimulus: a stronger stimulus opens more channels and moves the membrane further.

variables.name: Height of each action potential
variables.why: An action potential is all-or-none. Once threshold is reached, the voltage-gated channels produce the same full-size spike whatever the stimulus strength.

variables.name: Number of action potentials per second
variables.why: A stronger stimulus drives the membrane back to threshold sooner after each refractory period, so spikes come closer together. Neurons signal strength by frequency, not by spike size.

scenarios.title: A drug occupies a hormone’s receptor proteins
scenarios.misconception: blocking the receptor protein lowers the hormone level
scenarios.setup: A drug binds the receptor proteins that a hormone acts on. It fits the binding site but does not activate the receptor protein. The hormone level in the blood stays the same.
scenarios.start: Drug occupies the binding sites

steps.free: Fewer binding sites free for the hormone

variables.name: Hormone concentration in the blood
variables.why: The drug acts on the target cells, not on the cells that release the hormone. The same amount of hormone is released and carried in the blood.

variables.name: Receptor proteins activated by the hormone
variables.why: Each binding site holds one molecule at a time. Sites taken by the drug cannot bind the hormone, so fewer receptor proteins are activated.

variables.name: Response of the target cells
variables.why: A target cell responds in proportion to how many of its receptor proteins are activated. With fewer activated, the response is smaller even though the hormone is all there.

scenarios.title: Weeks of a high hormone level
scenarios.misconception: more hormone always means more effect
scenarios.setup: A person’s blood level of a hormone stays abnormally high for several weeks. Then the level suddenly returns to normal.
scenarios.start: Hormone level high for weeks

steps.wane: Response to the high level wanes over the weeks
steps.norm: Normal level binds fewer receptor proteins
steps.under: Response falls below the old normal

variables.name: Number of receptor proteins for that hormone on each target cell
variables.why: Constant heavy stimulation leads target cells to take receptor proteins out of the membrane and make fewer. That is down-regulation.

variables.name: Target cell response to the still-high level, week 4 compared with week 1
variables.why: The hormone level has not changed, but each cell has fewer receptor proteins to bind it, so the same level produces a smaller effect.

variables.name: Response right after the level returns to normal, compared with before the weeks of high levels
variables.why: The cells are still down-regulated. A normal hormone level now activates fewer receptor proteins than it used to, so the response is below the old normal until the cells make more.

scenarios.title: The pacemaker potential slows
scenarios.misconception: a slower heart is a weaker heart
scenarios.setup: A drug reduces the funny current in the SA node’s pacemaker cells, so each pacemaker potential rises toward threshold more slowly. The drug has no other action.
scenarios.start: Less funny current in the SA node

steps.con: Force at the same filling unchanged

variables.name: Slope of the pacemaker potential
variables.why: The funny current is the slow inward current that drives the pacemaker potential upward. Less of it makes the voltage climb more slowly.

variables.name: Time between one SA node action potential and the next
variables.why: The membrane starts from the same low point and rises to the same threshold, just more slowly, so each cycle takes longer.

variables.name: Heart rate
variables.why: The SA node sets the heart rate. Longer cycles mean fewer beats per minute.

variables.name: Force of each ventricular contraction, at the same filling
variables.why: The drug acts only on the pacemaker current, which contractile cells do not use to contract. At the same filling, each contraction is as forceful as before. (With more time between beats, the ventricles fill a little more, and a later topic shows how extra filling changes the force.)

scenarios.title: The AV node conducts more slowly
scenarios.misconception: slow AV conduction slows the heart rate
scenarios.setup: Conduction through the AV node slows, so each impulse takes longer to cross it. Every impulse still gets through (first-degree heart block).
scenarios.start: Slower conduction through the AV node

steps.delay: Longer delay between atria and ventricles
steps.fast: Bundle branches and Purkinje fibers conduct normally
steps.sa: SA node still sets the pace
steps.all: Every impulse still reaches the ventricles

variables.name: PR interval
variables.why: The PR interval runs from the start of atrial depolarization to the start of ventricular depolarization, and most of it is the AV nodal delay. A slower AV node lengthens it.

variables.name: Width of the QRS complex
variables.why: The QRS complex shows the ventricles depolarizing. Once an impulse leaves the AV node, it spreads through the bundle branches and Purkinje fibers at normal speed.

variables.name: Heart rate
variables.why: The SA node still fires at its usual rate, and every impulse still reaches the ventricles, only later. Each beat is delayed by the same amount, so the rate does not change.

scenarios.title: L-type calcium channels are partly blocked
scenarios.misconception: cardiac contraction uses only calcium from outside the cell
scenarios.setup: A drug partly blocks the L-type calcium channels of ventricular contractile cells.
scenarios.start: Fewer L-type channels open

steps.in: Less Ca2+ enters during the plateau
steps.trig: Weaker trigger for calcium-induced calcium release
steps.sr: Less Ca2+ released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum
steps.leak: Resting potential set by K+ leak

variables.name: Calcium entering the cell during the plateau
variables.why: The plateau is held up by calcium flowing in through L-type channels. With fewer channels open, less calcium enters.

variables.name: Calcium released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum
variables.why: The calcium that enters is mainly a trigger: it opens release channels in the sarcoplasmic reticulum, which supplies most of the calcium for contraction. A smaller trigger releases less.

variables.name: Force of each contraction
variables.why: Less calcium in the cytoplasm means fewer binding sites uncovered on the thin filaments, so fewer cross-bridges form and contraction is weaker.

variables.name: Resting membrane potential
variables.why: L-type channels are closed at rest. The resting potential depends on potassium leak channels and the pump, which the drug does not touch.

scenarios.title: A stiff, narrow aortic valve
scenarios.misconception: the ventricle ejects the same way through any valve opening
scenarios.setup: Over many years, the aortic valve has become stiff and narrow (aortic stenosis). It still opens, but its opening is much smaller than normal. Compare each heartbeat with a heart that has a normal valve.
scenarios.start: Aortic valve opening much smaller

steps.lvp: Left ventricle must generate higher pressure to eject
steps.dp: Large pressure difference across the valve
steps.jet: Blood speeds through the narrow opening
steps.mur: Turbulent jet: a murmur in systole
steps.work: Heavier pressure load on every beat

variables.name: Peak pressure in the left ventricle during ejection
variables.why: The narrow valve resists outflow. To push blood through it, the ventricle has to reach a much higher pressure than the aorta.

variables.name: Pressure difference between the left ventricle and the aorta during ejection
variables.why: With a normal valve, ventricular and aortic pressures are almost equal during ejection. A narrow valve absorbs a large share of the pressure, so a big difference opens up across it.

variables.name: Speed of blood through the valve opening
variables.why: The same volume has to pass through a smaller opening in the same time, so it moves much faster. The fast, turbulent jet is what you hear as a murmur during systole.

variables.name: Thickness of the left ventricular wall, over the years
variables.why: Generating high pressure on every beat is a sustained load. Cardiac muscle cells respond by adding contractile proteins and growing thicker, and the wall thickens.

scenarios.title: A torn chord: the mitral valve leaks
scenarios.misconception: a leaky valve only matters when the valve is supposed to be open
scenarios.setup: One of the chordae tendineae holding the mitral valve tears. From the next beat on, the valve cannot close fully, and during ventricular systole some blood leaks back into the left atrium.
scenarios.start: Mitral valve cannot close fully

steps.back: Blood flows back into the left atrium in systole
steps.pv: Pressure backs up into the pulmonary veins
steps.split: Part of each ejection goes backward
steps.fwd: Less blood ejected into the aorta
steps.ret: The leaked blood returns to the ventricle in diastole

variables.name: Left atrial pressure during ventricular systole
variables.why: Normally the closed mitral valve shields the atrium from ventricular pressure. Now high-pressure blood jets back into the atrium with every contraction.

variables.name: Volume ejected into the aorta per beat
variables.why: When the ventricle contracts, blood leaves by two routes: forward through the aortic valve and backward through the leak. What goes backward does not reach the body.

variables.name: Left ventricular end-diastolic volume
variables.why: The blood that leaked into the atrium comes back into the ventricle during filling, on top of the normal return from the lungs.

variables.name: Pressure in the pulmonary veins
variables.why: The pulmonary veins open into the left atrium with no valves between them. A pressure rise in the atrium passes straight back into them.

scenarios.title: Venous return rises
scenarios.theme: increased venous return, predict EDV, SV, CO
scenarios.misconception: the Frank–Starling mechanism is a rise in contractility
scenarios.setup: You lie down and raise your legs, and more blood returns to your heart. Assume heart rate and sympathetic activity stay the same.
scenarios.start: Venous return rises

steps.str: Muscle fibers stretched closer to their best length
steps.nos: No change in sympathetic signals to the heart

variables.name: End-diastolic volume
variables.why: More blood arriving during diastole fills the ventricles further before they contract.

variables.name: Stroke volume
variables.why: More filling stretches the muscle fibers toward the length where they generate the most force, so the ventricle contracts harder and ejects more. That is the Frank–Starling mechanism.

variables.name: Cardiac output
variables.why: Cardiac output equals heart rate times stroke volume. Heart rate is unchanged and stroke volume is up.

variables.name: Contractility
variables.why: Contractility is how strongly the muscle contracts at a given length, and it changes with sympathetic signals or drugs. Here the extra force comes from extra stretch, not from a change in contractility.

scenarios.title: A beta blocker
scenarios.theme: a beta blocker, predict heart rate, contractility, cardiac output
scenarios.misconception: a beta blocker stops the heart’s own pacemaker
scenarios.setup: A person at rest takes a beta blocker, a drug that blocks beta-1 receptors on the heart so norepinephrine and epinephrine cannot act there.
scenarios.start: Beta-1 receptors blocked

steps.sa: Less sympathetic effect on the SA node
steps.ven: Less sympathetic effect on ventricular muscle

variables.name: Heart rate
variables.why: Norepinephrine on beta-1 receptors speeds the pacemaker potential. With those receptor proteins blocked, the SA node fires at a slower rate, set by its own cells and the vagus.

variables.name: Filling time of the ventricles
variables.why: A slower heart rate lengthens each cardiac cycle, and most of the extra time is added to diastole, when the ventricles fill.

variables.name: Contractility
variables.why: Beta-1 stimulation of ventricular muscle raises the calcium available for each contraction. Blocking it lowers contractility.

variables.name: Cardiac output
variables.why: Heart rate falls and contractility falls. Longer filling helps stroke volume a little, but not enough to offset the slower rate, so cardiac output falls.

scenarios.title: Aortic pressure suddenly rises
scenarios.misconception: a higher afterload permanently lowers stroke volume
scenarios.setup: A drug suddenly constricts the arterioles and aortic pressure jumps. Venous return and contractility stay the same. Follow the left ventricle over the next several beats.

stages.label: The first beat
stages.prompt: The first beat after the rise, compared with the beat before it.
stages.start: Aortic pressure jumps

steps.open: More pressure needed to open the aortic valve
steps.less: Less time and pressure left for ejection
steps.esv: More blood left behind: ESV rises
steps.filled: This beat filled before the change

variables.name: Afterload
variables.why: Afterload is the pressure the ventricle must overcome to eject. The aortic valve opens only when ventricular pressure exceeds aortic pressure, and aortic pressure is now higher.

variables.name: Stroke volume
variables.why: More of the contraction is spent building pressure before the valve opens, so the ventricle ejects less before it relaxes.

variables.name: End-systolic volume
variables.why: The ventricle started with the usual volume and ejected less of it, so more is left at the end of systole.

variables.name: End-diastolic volume
variables.why: This beat filled before the pressure rose, from the normal venous return, so it starts from the usual volume.

stages.label: A few beats later
stages.prompt: A few beats later, compared with that first beat. Venous return and contractility are still unchanged.
stages.start: Extra blood left in the ventricle

steps.add: Normal venous return adds to the leftover blood

variables.name: End-diastolic volume
variables.why: The blood left behind after the first beat stays in the ventricle, and the normal venous return is added on top of it.

variables.name: Stretch of ventricular muscle fibers before contraction
variables.why: A fuller ventricle stretches its muscle fibers further before each contraction.

variables.name: Stroke volume
variables.why: More stretch gives a stronger contraction, so the ventricle can eject against the higher pressure. Within a few beats, output again matches venous return. That is the Frank–Starling mechanism at work.

variables.name: Contractility
variables.why: Nothing has changed the sympathetic input or the muscle’s calcium handling. The recovery comes from stretch, not from a change in contractility.

scenarios.title: Arterioles dilate throughout the body
scenarios.misconception: wider vessels raise blood pressure because more blood fits in them
scenarios.setup: A drug relaxes the smooth muscle of arterioles throughout the body. Consider the first few seconds, before any reflex responds, while the heart keeps pumping the same volume each minute.
scenarios.start: Arteriole smooth muscle relaxes

steps.res: Resistance falls steeply (fourth power of the radius)
steps.run: Blood runs off from the arteries faster

variables.name: Radius of arterioles
variables.why: Relaxed smooth muscle lets the arteriole wall widen under the pressure inside it.

variables.name: Total peripheral resistance
variables.why: Resistance depends on the fourth power of the radius, and the arterioles are where most systemic resistance sits. Wider arterioles lower total peripheral resistance sharply.

variables.name: Mean arterial pressure
variables.why: With the same flow from the heart passing through lower resistance, less pressure is needed to drive it. Blood runs off from the arteries faster, so arterial pressure falls.

variables.name: Diastolic pressure
variables.why: Between beats, the arteries empty through the arterioles. With less resistance they empty faster, so pressure sinks lower before the next beat.

scenarios.title: The arterioles to one organ constrict
scenarios.misconception: flow falls only when the pressure gradient falls
scenarios.setup: The arterioles supplying one small organ constrict to half their radius. Mean arterial pressure and the rest of the circulation stay the same.
scenarios.start: That organ’s arterioles halve their radius

steps.res: Resistance of that organ’s vessels rises steeply
steps.flow: Blood flow to the organ falls
steps.drop: More pressure lost across the narrowed arterioles
steps.grad: Pressure gradient across the organ unchanged

variables.name: Resistance of that organ’s vessels
variables.why: Resistance rises with the fourth power of a falling radius, and the arterioles are the main resistance in any organ. Halving their radius raises it roughly 16-fold at that level.

variables.name: Blood flow to that organ
variables.why: Flow equals pressure gradient divided by resistance. The gradient is the same and resistance is much higher, so flow falls.

variables.name: Blood pressure in the vessels downstream of the constricted arterioles
variables.why: Pressure is used up overcoming resistance. The narrowed arterioles consume more of it, so less is left for the vessels beyond them.

variables.name: Pressure gradient from the aorta to the organ’s veins
variables.why: Mean arterial pressure and venous pressure are both unchanged, so the overall gradient across the organ is the same. Flow fell because resistance rose.

scenarios.title: Sympathetic output to the heart and vessels rises
scenarios.misconception: sympathetic stimulation raises pressure only by speeding the heart
scenarios.setup: Sympathetic nerve signals to the heart, arterioles and veins increase sharply, as in a moment of sudden fright.
scenarios.start: Sympathetic output rises

steps.b1sa: Norepinephrine on beta-1 receptors of the SA node
steps.b1v: Norepinephrine on beta-1 receptors of ventricular muscle
steps.a1: Norepinephrine on alpha-1 receptors of arterioles

variables.name: Heart rate
variables.why: Norepinephrine acting on beta-1 receptors speeds the pacemaker potential, so the SA node reaches threshold sooner.

variables.name: Contractility
variables.why: Beta-1 stimulation of ventricular muscle raises the calcium available for each contraction, so each beat is more forceful at the same filling.

variables.name: Venous return
variables.why: Sympathetic signals constrict the veins, squeezing blood out of the venous reservoir toward the heart.

variables.name: Stroke volume
variables.why: Stronger contractions eject more of the blood in the ventricle, and the extra venous return fills it further as well.

variables.name: Total peripheral resistance
variables.why: Norepinephrine on alpha-1 receptors contracts arteriole smooth muscle in the skin, gut and kidneys. Narrower arterioles raise resistance.

variables.name: Mean arterial pressure
variables.why: MAP = heart rate × stroke volume × TPR, and all three have risen.

scenarios.title: The vagus nerves are stimulated
scenarios.misconception: parasympathetic signals relax the arterioles and weaken the ventricles
scenarios.setup: Parasympathetic output to the heart through the vagus nerves rises. Sympathetic output does not change.
scenarios.start: Vagal output rises

steps.ach: More acetylcholine at the SA and AV nodes
steps.sparse: Few vagal fibers reach ventricular muscle
steps.noart: Most arterioles have no parasympathetic nerves

variables.name: Heart rate
variables.why: Acetylcholine on muscarinic receptors of the SA node makes the pacemaker potential start lower and rise more slowly, so the node fires less often.

variables.name: PR interval
variables.why: Vagal fibers also supply the AV node. Acetylcholine slows conduction through it, lengthening the delay between atrial and ventricular depolarization.

variables.name: Contractility of the ventricles
variables.why: Vagal fibers end mainly on the SA node, the AV node and the atria. Ventricular muscle has little parasympathetic innervation, so its contractility barely changes.

variables.name: Total peripheral resistance
variables.why: Most arterioles receive sympathetic fibers only. Raising vagal output does not reach them, so resistance stays the same.

variables.name: Cardiac output
variables.why: Cardiac output is heart rate times stroke volume, and heart rate has fallen.

variables.name: Mean arterial pressure
variables.why: MAP = CO × TPR. Cardiac output fell and TPR stayed the same, so MAP falls.

scenarios.title: Pressure on a carotid sinus
scenarios.misconception: the baroreceptors measure pressure, so pushing on them cannot fool the reflex
scenarios.setup: A clinician presses firmly on one carotid sinus through the skin of the neck.
scenarios.start: Carotid sinus wall stretched from outside

variables.name: Baroreceptor firing
variables.why: Baroreceptors respond to stretch of the artery wall. Pressing on the sinus stretches it, so they fire as if blood pressure had risen.

variables.name: Vagal (parasympathetic) output to the heart
variables.why: More baroreceptor input tells the cardiovascular center that pressure is high, and it responds by boosting vagal output.

variables.name: Sympathetic output to the heart and arterioles
variables.why: The same input holds back the sympathetic side of the cardiovascular center.

variables.name: Heart rate
variables.why: More vagal and less sympathetic signal at the SA node slow the heart, often within a beat or two.

variables.name: Mean arterial pressure
variables.why: A slower heart and relaxed arterioles lower cardiac output and TPR. The reflex is correcting a pressure rise that never happened, so pressure falls below normal.

scenarios.title: Standing up quickly
scenarios.misconception: blood pressure is corrected by the heart alone
scenarios.setup: You have been lying down and stand up quickly. Gravity pulls about half a liter of blood into the veins of your legs and abdomen. Predict what happens over the next 10 to 20 seconds as your reflexes respond.
scenarios.start: Blood pools in the leg veins

steps.baro: Baroreceptors stretch less and fire less
steps.cvc: Cardiovascular center: sympathetic up, vagal down

variables.name: Venous return
variables.why: Blood held in the stretched leg veins is not returning to the heart, so less arrives each second.

variables.name: End-diastolic volume
variables.why: Less blood arriving means the ventricles fill less before each contraction.

variables.name: Stroke volume
variables.why: Less filling stretches the ventricular muscle less, so it contracts less forcefully and ejects less.

variables.name: Baroreceptor firing
variables.why: Lower stroke volume lowers cardiac output and pressure, most of all in the arteries of the head. The carotid sinuses and aortic arch stretch less and their baroreceptors fire less.

variables.name: Heart rate
variables.why: Less baroreceptor input lets the cardiovascular center raise sympathetic and cut vagal output to the SA node. Heart rate typically rises 10 to 20 beats per minute.

variables.name: Total peripheral resistance
variables.why: The same sympathetic rise constricts arterioles in the skin, gut, kidneys and resting muscle, raising resistance and helping pressure recover.

scenarios.title: Starting a hard run
scenarios.misconception: blood pressure rises in exercise because resistance rises
scenarios.setup: A healthy 30-year-old goes from standing still to a steady hard run. Predict the state a few minutes in, compared with rest.
scenarios.start: Hard exercise begins

steps.brain: Motor areas and muscle sensors signal the cardiovascular center
steps.sym: Vagal output falls, sympathetic output rises
steps.pump: Muscle pump and deeper breathing push blood back to the heart
steps.mf: Blood flow to working muscle rises
steps.vc: Arterioles of gut and kidneys constrict
steps.gut: Blood flow to gut and kidneys falls
steps.map: MAP rises modestly (CO rises more than TPR falls)
steps.pp: Systolic rises a lot; pulse pressure widens

variables.name: Heart rate
variables.why: Signals from the brain’s motor areas and from sensors in working muscle reach the cardiovascular center, which cuts vagal and raises sympathetic output to the SA node.

variables.name: Stroke volume
variables.why: The skeletal muscle pump and deeper breathing return more blood, raising end-diastolic volume, and sympathetic signals raise contractility. Both increase stroke volume.

variables.name: Cardiac output
variables.why: Heart rate and stroke volume both rise, so cardiac output climbs from about 5 to as much as 20 L/min.

variables.name: Blood flow to the working muscles
variables.why: Active muscle releases CO2, H+, K+ and adenosine and uses up oxygen. These relax its arterioles (local control), overriding sympathetic constriction there.

variables.name: Total peripheral resistance
variables.why: Skeletal muscle is a large share of the body. When its arterioles dilate, the fall in resistance outweighs the constriction elsewhere.

variables.name: Blood flow to the gut and kidneys
variables.why: Sympathetic signals constrict the arterioles of the gut and kidneys, which have no local metabolite build-up to override it. Their share of the output shrinks.

variables.name: Mean arterial pressure
variables.why: MAP = CO × TPR. Cardiac output rises about four-fold while TPR falls to about 30 percent of its resting value, so their product, and MAP, rises by only about 20 percent (4 × 0.3 = 1.2).

variables.name: Pulse pressure
variables.why: A larger, more forceful stroke volume raises systolic pressure a lot, while low resistance keeps diastolic pressure about the same. The gap between them widens.

scenarios.title: A narrowed coronary artery on the stairs
scenarios.misconception: a narrowed artery always causes symptoms at rest
scenarios.setup: A plaque narrows one coronary artery to half its normal radius. At rest, the heart muscle it supplies still gets enough blood, because the arterioles downstream have dilated to make up for the narrowing. Then the person climbs several flights of stairs.
scenarios.start: Coronary artery radius halved by plaque

steps.res: Resistance of the narrowed segment rises steeply
steps.comp: Downstream arterioles already dilated at rest
steps.room: Little room left for further dilation
steps.sym: Climbing raises heart rate and contractility
steps.cap: Flow cannot rise enough to match
steps.gap: Oxygen supply falls short of demand (ischemia)

variables.name: Resistance of the narrowed segment
variables.why: Resistance depends on the fourth power of the radius, so a segment at half its radius has about 16 times the resistance of a normal segment of the same length.

variables.name: Room left for the downstream arterioles to dilate further
variables.why: To keep resting flow normal, the downstream arterioles have already used up much of their ability to widen. When demand rises, there is less dilation left to call on.

variables.name: Oxygen use by that heart muscle during the climb, compared with rest
variables.why: Climbing raises sympathetic output, so heart rate and contractility rise. The heart muscle does more work and uses more oxygen.

variables.name: Gap between oxygen supply and oxygen demand in that muscle during the climb
variables.why: Demand rises but flow through the narrowed artery cannot rise enough, so supply falls short. That ischemia is what causes chest pain on exertion (angina), which fades with rest.

scenarios.title: Damaged kidneys leak albumin
scenarios.misconception: edema always comes from too much pressure in the vessels
scenarios.setup: Damaged kidneys leak large amounts of albumin into the urine for weeks, and the liver cannot make enough to replace it. Predict the Starling forces in a typical capillary in the legs.
scenarios.start: Plasma albumin falls

steps.filt: Filtration out of capillaries speeds up

variables.name: Blood colloid osmotic pressure
variables.why: Albumin supplies most of the colloid osmotic pressure of plasma. Less albumin means less inward pull.

variables.name: Capillary hydrostatic pressure
variables.why: Nothing in this change alters arterial pressure, arteriole tone or venous pressure, so the pressure of blood in the capillaries is the same.

variables.name: Net filtration pressure
variables.why: NFP = (CHP + IFCOP) − (BCOP + IFHP). BCOP has fallen and the others are about the same, so NFP rises.

variables.name: Rate of filtration out of the capillaries
variables.why: A larger net filtration pressure drives fluid out faster, along the whole length of the capillary.

variables.name: Volume of interstitial fluid in the legs
variables.why: When fluid filters out faster than it drains away, it collects between cells. The swelling shows first in the feet and ankles when you are upright.

scenarios.title: Standing still for hours
scenarios.misconception: swollen ankles after standing mean the heart is failing
scenarios.setup: You stand still at a counter for two hours, barely moving your legs.
scenarios.start: Standing still, legs not moving

steps.col: Weight of the blood column adds to venous pressure
steps.nopump: No muscle pump to empty the leg veins
steps.vp: Venous pressure at the ankles rises
steps.chp: Pressure passes back into the capillaries

variables.name: Venous pressure at the ankles
variables.why: Gravity adds the weight of the column of blood above your ankles, and with your legs still, the skeletal muscle pump is not emptying the veins. Ankle venous pressure can reach about 90 mm Hg.

variables.name: Capillary hydrostatic pressure in the feet
variables.why: No high resistance sits between the capillaries and the veins, so a rise in venous pressure passes back into the capillaries almost fully.

variables.name: Filtration out of the capillaries in the feet
variables.why: Higher capillary hydrostatic pressure pushes fluid out faster.

variables.name: Interstitial fluid around the ankles
variables.why: Fluid filters out faster than it drains away, so it collects in the tissue. Your shoes feel tight. Walking brings it back down.

variables.name: Blood colloid osmotic pressure
variables.why: Standing does not change how much protein is in your plasma, so the inward pull is the same. The swelling comes from the push, not the pull.

scenarios.title: An insect sting
scenarios.misconception: swelling after an injury is blood leaking from broken vessels
scenarios.setup: An insect sting in the skin releases histamine. Histamine widens the gaps between endothelial cells of nearby capillaries and relaxes the local arterioles.
scenarios.start: Histamine released in the skin

steps.diff: Oncotic difference across the wall shrinks
steps.small: Leak is tiny compared with total plasma

variables.name: Protein in the interstitial fluid at the sting
variables.why: Wider gaps let plasma proteins, normally held back, escape into the tissue.

variables.name: Capillary hydrostatic pressure at the sting
variables.why: Relaxed arterioles lose less pressure, so more of the arterial pressure reaches the capillaries beyond them.

variables.name: Filtration out of the local capillaries
variables.why: Two changes add up: more protein outside weakens the oncotic pull holding fluid in, and higher capillary pressure pushes more out.

variables.name: Swelling at the sting
variables.why: Fluid filters out faster than it drains away, so the area swells within minutes. The fluid is plasma that crossed intact walls, not blood from broken vessels.

variables.name: Blood colloid osmotic pressure in the rest of the body
variables.why: The protein lost at one small sting is a tiny fraction of the protein in all your plasma, so the body-wide value does not measurably change.

scenarios.title: Hemorrhage: the loss, then compensation
scenarios.misconception: hematocrit falls the moment you bleed
scenarios.setup: A 25-year-old loses about 1 liter of blood from a deep cut in the thigh over ten minutes. The bleeding is then stopped. No fluid or blood has been given yet.

stages.label: The immediate change
stages.prompt: The direct effect of the lost volume, before any reflex or hormone has acted. Compare with before the bleed.
stages.start: 1 liter of whole blood lost

steps.baro: Baroreceptors stretch less and fire less
steps.noref: No reflex has reached the SA node yet
steps.whole: Cells and plasma lost in the same proportion

variables.name: Blood volume
variables.why: A liter of blood has left the vessels, about a fifth of an adult’s total.

variables.name: Venous return
variables.why: Most of your blood sits in the veins. Losing volume empties them first, so less blood returns to the heart.

variables.name: Stroke volume
variables.why: Less venous return means less filling, and a less-stretched ventricle ejects less.

variables.name: Mean arterial pressure
variables.why: Lower stroke volume lowers cardiac output, and MAP = CO × TPR.

variables.name: Baroreceptor firing
variables.why: Lower arterial pressure stretches the carotid sinuses and aortic arch less, so their baroreceptors fire less. This is the signal that starts the compensation.

variables.name: Heart rate
variables.why: Nothing about losing volume acts directly on the SA node. The fast heart rate of a bleeding patient is the reflex response, which is the next stage, not a direct effect.

variables.name: Hematocrit
variables.why: Whole blood was lost, red cells and plasma together, so the fraction of blood that is red cells is the same. It falls later, when fluid moves in and dilutes the cells that remain.

stages.label: After compensation
stages.prompt: The baroreceptor reflex acts within seconds; hormones and water drawn back into the blood from the tissues follow over the next few hours. Compare with the moment just after the bleed.
stages.start: Baroreceptors firing less

steps.cvc: Cardiovascular center: sympathetic up, vagal down
steps.in: Brief inflow, then less filtration while drainage continues
steps.urine: Kidneys keep water and sodium: less urine

variables.name: Heart rate
variables.why: Less baroreceptor input lets the cardiovascular center raise sympathetic and cut vagal output to the SA node.

variables.name: Total peripheral resistance
variables.why: Sympathetic signals constrict arterioles in the skin, gut, kidneys and resting muscle. Blood flow to the brain and heart is protected.

variables.name: Mean arterial pressure
variables.why: Faster heart rate, stronger contractions, constricted veins and higher TPR push pressure back toward its set point. After a liter, it usually ends up close to normal, though the volume is still missing.

variables.name: Capillary hydrostatic pressure in skin and gut
variables.why: Constricted arterioles use up more of the pressure, and arterial pressure was already low, so less reaches the capillaries beyond them.

variables.name: Plasma volume
variables.why: Capillary pressure drops below the inward oncotic pull, so for a few minutes fluid moves from the tissues into the plasma. After that, the capillaries keep filtering less than before while the separate drainage route keeps returning fluid at its old rate, so the plasma keeps gaining fluid for hours. ADH and aldosterone add to it by keeping water and sodium in the body.

variables.name: Hematocrit
variables.why: The fluid that moves in has no red cells, so it dilutes those that remain. New red cells take days, so hematocrit falls in the hours after a bleed.

variables.name: ADH secretion
variables.why: Low pressure and low volume, sensed by the baroreceptors and by stretch-sensitive sensory receptors in the atria, make the hypothalamus raise ADH release from the posterior pituitary.

variables.name: Aldosterone secretion
variables.why: Lower pressure in the kidney’s vessels and sympathetic signals make the kidneys release renin. Renin leads to angiotensin II, which makes the adrenal cortex release aldosterone.

variables.name: Urine output
variables.why: ADH makes the kidney tubules reabsorb more water, and aldosterone more sodium. Less of the remaining fluid is lost as urine.

scenarios.title: Left-sided heart failure
scenarios.misconception: the body’s responses to heart failure all help
scenarios.setup: After a large heart attack, the left ventricle’s contractility is permanently reduced. Predict the state weeks later, compared with before the heart attack.
scenarios.start: Left ventricular contractility reduced

steps.ej: Ventricle ejects a smaller share of its blood
steps.left: More blood left behind each beat
steps.back: Pressure backs up into the left atrium and pulmonary veins
steps.lung: Fluid filters into the lung tissue
steps.low: Cardiac output falls; pressure tends to fall
steps.vol: Kidneys keep sodium and water: blood volume rises

variables.name: Ejection fraction
variables.why: Weaker contractions eject a smaller fraction of the blood in the ventricle.

variables.name: Left ventricular end-diastolic volume
variables.why: Blood left behind each beat adds to what returns from the lungs, and the retained fluid adds more, so the ventricle stays fuller and dilates.

variables.name: Capillary hydrostatic pressure in the lungs
variables.why: A full, weak left ventricle raises pressure in the left atrium. That pressure passes back through the valveless pulmonary veins into the lung capillaries.

variables.name: Fluid in the lung tissue
variables.why: Higher capillary pressure speeds filtration, and fluid collects in the lungs faster than it drains. This is why breathlessness is a key symptom.

variables.name: Resting heart rate
variables.why: Low cardiac output lowers pressure at the baroreceptors, and the reflex raises sympathetic output to the SA node.

variables.name: Aldosterone secretion
variables.why: Low flow and pressure in the kidneys’ vessels, plus sympathetic signals, trigger renin release, angiotensin II and aldosterone.

variables.name: Blood volume
variables.why: The kidneys respond as if the body had lost volume and retain sodium and water. That raises filling, but it also worsens the congestion: the loop is correcting the wrong problem.

scenarios.title: Right-sided heart failure
scenarios.misconception: a failing right ventricle floods the lungs
scenarios.setup: The right ventricle can no longer pump out all the blood returning to it. The left ventricle is healthy.
scenarios.start: Right ventricle pumps out less

steps.ra: Blood backs up into the right atrium
steps.sv: Pressure in the systemic veins rises
steps.chp: Capillary pressure in the legs rises
steps.lung: Less blood sent through the lungs
steps.la: Less blood reaches the left ventricle

variables.name: Pressure in the systemic veins
variables.why: Blood that the right ventricle does not pump on backs up into the right atrium and the venae cavae, raising pressure throughout the systemic veins. The neck veins may bulge.

variables.name: Interstitial fluid in the legs and ankles
variables.why: Higher venous pressure passes back into the capillaries, raising filtration. Fluid collects in the lowest parts of the body.

variables.name: Blood flow through the pulmonary circuit
variables.why: The right ventricle is the pump for the pulmonary circuit. When it ejects less, less blood flows through the lungs.

variables.name: Left ventricular end-diastolic volume
variables.why: The left heart can only pump what reaches it from the lungs. Less arrives, so it fills less.

scenarios.title: Fluid fills the pericardial sac
scenarios.misconception: fluid around the heart weakens its contractions
scenarios.setup: Fluid builds up quickly in the pericardial sac (cardiac tamponade). The fibrous pericardium cannot stretch fast enough to make room.
scenarios.start: Fluid accumulates in the pericardial sac

steps.squeeze: Ventricles cannot expand fully in diastole

variables.name: End-diastolic volume
variables.why: The fluid presses on the heart from outside. The ventricles cannot expand against it, so they fill less.

variables.name: Stroke volume
variables.why: Less filling means less stretch and less blood to eject.

variables.name: Contractility
variables.why: The heart muscle is not damaged. The problem is filling, not the strength of each contraction at a given stretch.

variables.name: Mean arterial pressure
variables.why: Lower stroke volume lowers cardiac output, and pressure falls with it.

variables.name: Heart rate
variables.why: Falling pressure reduces baroreceptor firing, and the reflex speeds the heart. The fast rate cannot fix a filling problem, which is why the fluid must be drained.

scenarios.title: Dehydration on a hot hike
scenarios.misconception: dehydration makes the plasma more dilute
scenarios.setup: A hiker loses 3 liters of sweat over a hot day and drinks nothing. Sweat contains less salt than plasma does.
scenarios.start: Water lost in excess of salt

steps.kid: Lower volume and sympathetic signals reach the kidneys

variables.name: Plasma volume
variables.why: Sweat is made from plasma fluid, so losing 3 liters without drinking shrinks the plasma (and, as water shifts, the other body fluids).

variables.name: Plasma osmolarity
variables.why: Sweat carries away proportionally more water than solute, so the solutes left behind are more concentrated.

variables.name: ADH release
variables.why: Osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus shrink as plasma osmolarity rises and excite the ADH-making neurons of the hypothalamus, whose endings in the posterior pituitary release more ADH. Low volume adds to the signal.

variables.name: Thirst
variables.why: The same osmoreceptors drive the thirst center. Drinking is the only way to replace the water.

variables.name: Urine volume
variables.why: ADH makes the kidney tubules reabsorb more water, so less, more concentrated urine is produced.

variables.name: Renin release
variables.why: Lower blood volume and pressure in the kidney’s vessels, and sympathetic signals, make the kidneys release more renin.

scenarios.title: Two liters of IV saline
scenarios.misconception: any IV fluid changes plasma osmolarity
scenarios.setup: A patient with a normal blood volume is given 2 liters of isotonic saline by IV over 30 minutes. Predict the next hour.
scenarios.start: 2 L of isotonic saline infused

steps.kid: Higher pressure and less sympathetic signal at the kidneys
steps.urine: Kidneys excrete more sodium and water
steps.iso: Saline has the same osmolarity as plasma

variables.name: Blood volume
variables.why: The saline enters the veins and adds to the plasma (and, within minutes, some of it filters out into the interstitial fluid).

variables.name: ANP release
variables.why: More venous return stretches the atrial walls, and stretched atrial muscle cells release atrial natriuretic peptide.

variables.name: Renin release
variables.why: Higher pressure in the kidney’s vessels and less sympathetic signal reduce renin release, so angiotensin II and aldosterone fall too.

variables.name: ADH release
variables.why: Stretch-sensitive sensory receptors in the atria and large veins signal the hypothalamus that volume is high, and ADH release falls.

variables.name: Urine output
variables.why: More ANP and less aldosterone and ADH make the kidneys excrete more sodium and water, removing the excess.

variables.name: Plasma osmolarity
variables.why: Isotonic saline has the same osmolarity as plasma, so adding it expands volume without changing concentration. That is why the osmoreceptors stay quiet.

variables.name: Blood colloid osmotic pressure
variables.why: Saline contains no protein, so it dilutes the plasma proteins, lowering their oncotic pull.

scenarios.title: An ACE inhibitor
scenarios.misconception: blocking the pathway also lowers renin
scenarios.setup: A person whose blood pressure runs too high starts taking an ACE inhibitor, a drug that blocks angiotensin-converting enzyme. Predict the state after several weeks.
scenarios.start: ACE blocked

steps.ang: Less angiotensin I converted to angiotensin II
steps.na: Kidneys keep less sodium and water
steps.brake: Angiotensin II no longer holds back renin release

variables.name: Angiotensin II
variables.why: ACE converts angiotensin I into angiotensin II. Blocking it cuts production of angiotensin II.

variables.name: Aldosterone
variables.why: Angiotensin II is a main stimulus for aldosterone release by the adrenal cortex. Less of it means less aldosterone.

variables.name: Total peripheral resistance
variables.why: Angiotensin II is a powerful constrictor of arterioles. With less of it, arterioles relax and resistance falls.

variables.name: Mean arterial pressure
variables.why: Lower TPR and a slightly smaller blood volume both lower MAP. That is why the drug is used.

variables.name: Renin release
variables.why: Angiotensin II normally feeds back to hold renin release down. Without that brake, and with lower pressure at the kidneys, renin release rises, but ACE is blocked so it cannot produce much angiotensin II.

variables.name: Blood potassium
variables.why: Aldosterone makes the kidneys secrete potassium as they reabsorb sodium. Less aldosterone means less potassium excreted, so blood potassium can rise.

scenarios.title: Breathing through your mouth on a cold, dusty day
scenarios.misconception: air breathed through the mouth reaches the alveoli cold and dry
scenarios.setup: Your nose is blocked by a cold, so you spend a winter afternoon clearing a dusty garage while breathing through your mouth. Compare with breathing the same air through your nose.
scenarios.start: Air enters through the mouth instead of the nose

steps.skip: Air bypasses the nasal cavity and joins the route at the oropharynx
steps.heat: No warming from the blood vessels under the nasal mucosa
steps.water: No humidifying from the mucus of the nasal cavity
steps.filter: No nasal hairs, and no swirling past the conchae to throw particles onto mucus
steps.lower: The pharynx, trachea and the air tubes of the lungs must do more of the warming and humidifying
steps.dry: Water evaporates faster from their lining, drying it
steps.deep: The air is still at body temperature before it reaches the alveoli

variables.name: Temperature of the air reaching the pharynx
variables.why: Through the nose, heat passes from warm blood in the thin-walled vessels under the mucosa into the air. Through the mouth that step is skipped, so colder air reaches the pharynx.

variables.name: Water vapor in the air reaching the pharynx
variables.why: Water evaporating from the mucus of the nasal cavity normally moistens the air before it reaches the pharynx. The mouth route skips that surface.

variables.name: Dust trapped before the air reaches the pharynx
variables.why: In the nose, hairs catch large particles and the conchae break the airstream into narrow, turbulent channels, so heavier particles hit the sticky mucus. The mouth has neither, so more dust travels deeper, where the mucociliary escalator must carry it back up.

variables.name: Dryness of the throat and airway lining
variables.why: The air still has to be humidified, so the lining further down gives up more water to it. Hours of mouth breathing dry the throat, and drier mucus is harder for the cilia to move.

variables.name: Temperature of the air when it reaches the alveoli
variables.why: The rest of the conducting zone is also lined by warm, moist mucosa, so it finishes the job the nose skipped. The cost is paid by the airway lining, not by the alveoli.

scenarios.title: An airway narrows to half its radius
scenarios.misconception: halving an airway’s radius halves the airflow through it
scenarios.setup: The smooth muscle around one bronchiole contracts, and its radius falls to half. The pressure difference along the airway stays the same.
scenarios.start: Airway smooth muscle contracts

steps.res: Resistance rises 16-fold (radius to the fourth power)
steps.flow: Airflow falls to one sixteenth at the same pressure difference
steps.press: A 16 times larger pressure difference is needed for the old flow

variables.name: Radius of the airway
variables.why: Contracting smooth muscle squeezes the airway, and a bronchiole has no cartilage to hold it open, so its radius shrinks.

variables.name: Resistance of the airway
variables.why: Resistance depends on 1 ÷ radius to the fourth power. Half the radius gives 2⁴ = 16 times the resistance, not twice.

variables.name: Airflow through it at the same pressure difference
variables.why: Flow = ΔP ÷ R. With ΔP unchanged and R 16 times larger, flow falls to one sixteenth of what it was.

variables.name: Pressure difference needed to keep the old airflow
variables.why: To push the same flow through 16 times the resistance, ΔP must be 16 times larger, so the breathing muscles must work much harder.

scenarios.title: Air enters one pleural cavity
scenarios.misconception: a hole in one side of the chest collapses both lungs
scenarios.setup: A stab wound opens a hole through the right chest wall into the right pleural cavity. Predict what happens on each side over the next minute, compared with before the injury.
scenarios.start: Air enters the right pleural cavity

steps.film: The pleural fluid seal on the right is broken
steps.ipp: Right intrapleural pressure rises toward atmospheric (0)
steps.recoil: The right lung recoils toward its hilum
steps.air: The right lung no longer follows the chest wall
steps.wall: The right chest wall springs slightly outward
steps.sep: The left lung has its own pleural cavity

variables.name: Right intrapleural pressure
variables.why: Air at atmospheric pressure fills the gap between the pleural layers, so the pressure there, about 4 mm Hg below atmospheric before, rises toward 0.

variables.name: Right transpulmonary pressure
variables.why: Transpulmonary pressure is alveolar minus intrapleural pressure. Alveolar pressure is still about 0, and intrapleural pressure has risen to about 0, so the difference that held the lung open falls toward 0.

variables.name: Volume of the right lung
variables.why: With nothing holding it open, the elastic fibers and surface tension of the lung pull it inward, and it collapses toward the hilum.

variables.name: Air moved in and out of the right lung with each breath
variables.why: The broken seal means the lung surface no longer follows the chest wall, so moving the chest wall barely changes that lung’s volume or alveolar pressure, and little air flows.

variables.name: How far out the right chest wall sits
variables.why: At rest the chest wall tends to spring outward, and the lung’s pull held it in. Once the seal breaks, that pull is gone and the wall moves slightly out.

variables.name: Volume of the left lung
variables.why: Each lung has its own pleural cavity, so the left pleural seal is intact and the left lung stays inflated. Only a tension pneumothorax, which pushes the mediastinum across, threatens the other side.

scenarios.title: An asthma attack
scenarios.misconception: in asthma, breathing in is harder than breathing out
scenarios.setup: A person with allergic asthma strokes a cat, and within minutes an attack begins. Predict the changes compared with before the attack.
scenarios.start: Allergen binds IgE on mast cells in the airway wall

steps.mast: Mast cells release histamine and leukotrienes
steps.swell: The airway wall swells and thick mucus plugs the lumen
steps.flow: Less air flows for the same pressure difference
steps.work: Breathing muscles, including accessory muscles, work harder
steps.exp: Narrowed airways close early as the lungs shrink during breath out
steps.trap: Air is trapped in the alveoli

variables.name: Radius of the bronchi and bronchioles
variables.why: Three changes act at once: smooth muscle contracts, the inflamed wall thickens, and mucus fills the lumen. All three shrink the space air can pass through.

variables.name: Airway resistance
variables.why: Resistance rises with 1 ÷ radius⁴, so a modest narrowing produces a large rise in resistance.

variables.name: Airflow at the usual breathing effort
variables.why: Flow = ΔP ÷ R. The usual pressure difference now moves much less air.

variables.name: Use of the accessory breathing muscles
variables.why: To move enough air through high resistance, the person must create larger pressure differences, so the neck and other accessory muscles join in.

variables.name: Air left in the alveoli after a breath out
variables.why: During expiration the shrinking lungs stop pulling the airways open, and in forced expiration the pressure around them squeezes them. Already narrowed airways close early, so breathing out suffers most and air is trapped behind them.

scenarios.title: A baby born too early to make surfactant
scenarios.misconception: surfactant is needed only to open the lungs at the first breath
scenarios.setup: A baby is born at 28 weeks of pregnancy, before the type II alveolar cells make enough surfactant. Compare the baby’s lungs with those of a baby born at full term.
scenarios.start: Too little surfactant lines the alveoli

steps.st: Surface tension of the alveolar fluid stays high
steps.comp: Lung compliance falls: the lungs are stiff
steps.work: Each breath needs a larger pressure change and more muscle work
steps.coll: Small alveoli collapse at the end of each breath out
steps.fluid: More fluid is pulled from the capillaries into the alveoli

variables.name: Surface tension of the fluid lining the alveoli
variables.why: Surfactant phospholipids push between water molecules at the air-water surface and weaken their pull on each other. Without enough of them, the surface pulls hard.

variables.name: Lung compliance
variables.why: Surface tension accounts for more than half of the lungs’ resistance to stretch. More of it means less volume change for each unit of pressure: lower compliance.

variables.name: Pressure change needed to take in the same volume of air
variables.why: Compliance = ΔV ÷ ΔP, so with lower compliance a larger ΔP is needed for the same ΔV. The baby pulls so hard that the soft tissue between the ribs is sucked inward.

variables.name: Alveoli still open at the end of a breath out
variables.why: Surfactant normally protects small alveoli most, because its film packs tighter as they shrink. Without it, small alveoli collapse at the end of every breath out and must be reopened with the next.

variables.name: Fluid drawn into the alveoli
variables.why: Strong surface tension pulls fluid out of the capillaries into the alveolar space as well as collapsing the alveoli.

scenarios.title: Fast, shallow breathing after broken ribs
scenarios.misconception: a normal minute ventilation means normal fresh air to the alveoli
scenarios.setup: Because deep breaths hurt, a patient with broken ribs takes 30 breaths a minute of 200 mL each, instead of his usual 12 breaths of 500 mL. His dead space is 150 mL. Compare with his usual breathing.
scenarios.start: Breaths become fast and shallow

steps.ds: Dead space is still 150 mL on every breath
steps.fresh: Fresh air per breath: 200 − 150 = 50 mL instead of 350 mL
steps.o2: Oxygen in the alveolar air falls
steps.co2: Carbon dioxide builds up in the alveolar air

variables.name: Minute ventilation
variables.why: Minute ventilation is tidal volume × rate: 500 × 12 = 6,000 before and 200 × 30 = 6,000 now. The total air moved looks normal.

variables.name: Anatomical dead space
variables.why: Anatomical dead space is the volume of the conducting zone, set by the size of the airways, so it stays about 150 mL whatever the breath size.

variables.name: Fresh air reaching the alveoli with each breath
variables.why: The last 150 mL of every breath stops in the conducting zone. A 200 mL breath leaves only 50 mL of fresh air for the alveoli.

variables.name: Alveolar ventilation
variables.why: Alveolar ventilation = (tidal volume − dead space) × rate. Dead space is a fixed cost paid on every breath, and shallow breaths pay it more often for less fresh air.

variables.name: Oxygen in the alveolar air
variables.why: Blood keeps taking oxygen out of the alveoli, but far less fresh air arrives to replace it.

variables.name: Carbon dioxide in the alveolar air
variables.why: Blood keeps adding carbon dioxide to the alveoli, and too little fresh air washes it out.

scenarios.title: The air on a high summit
scenarios.misconception: the air high on a mountain holds a smaller percentage of oxygen
scenarios.setup: You travel from sea level, where total air pressure is 760 mm Hg, to a summit 4,300 m up, where it is about 455 mm Hg. Compare the air there with the air at sea level.
scenarios.start: Total air pressure falls

steps.frac: Oxygen is still 20.9% of dry air
steps.water: Water vapor in the warm, moist airways stays at 47 mm Hg
steps.dry: The dry gases share less pressure: 455 − 47 = 408 mm Hg
steps.po2: PO2 of breathed-in air falls from about 150 to 85 mm Hg
steps.grad: A smaller PO2 gradient pushes oxygen into the blood

variables.name: Percentage of oxygen in dry air
variables.why: Air is about 21% oxygen at every altitude people climb to. What changes is the total pressure the gases share.

variables.name: Partial pressure of water vapor in the airways
variables.why: Water vapor in air saturated at body temperature always has a partial pressure of 47 mm Hg, whatever the total pressure.

variables.name: PO2 of breathed-in air once warmed and moistened
variables.why: Partial pressure = the pressure the dry gases share × the oxygen fraction: 408 × 0.209 = 85 mm Hg, against 713 × 0.209 = 150 mm Hg at sea level.

variables.name: Alveolar PO2
variables.why: The alveoli are refilled with air whose PO2 is lower, while blood keeps removing oxygen, so the alveolar value settles lower too.

variables.name: PO2 gradient from alveolar air to the blood arriving in the lungs
variables.why: Oxygen diffuses down its partial pressure gradient. A lower alveolar PO2 means a smaller difference from the blood arriving in the pulmonary capillaries, so oxygen crosses more slowly.

scenarios.title: A clot blocks a pulmonary artery branch
scenarios.misconception: every alveolus that gets air takes part in gas exchange
scenarios.setup: A blood clot lodges in a branch of the right pulmonary artery (a pulmonary embolism). The alveoli it supplied still receive air with every breath. Predict for those alveoli, and for the rest of the lung.
scenarios.start: Blood flow to a group of alveoli stops

steps.q: Air still arrives but no blood flows past
steps.vq: V/Q in that region rises very high
steps.ds: Their air becomes alveolar dead space
steps.gas: Their air stays like breathed-in air
steps.divert: The heart’s output goes to the rest of the lung
steps.restq: Blood flow through the other alveoli rises

variables.name: Ventilation–perfusion ratio in the blocked region
variables.why: V/Q compares airflow with blood flow. Ventilation continues while blood flow falls toward zero, so the ratio rises toward infinity.

variables.name: Alveolar dead space
variables.why: Alveolar dead space is alveoli that receive air but little or no blood, so no gas exchange can happen in them.

variables.name: PCO2 of the air in the blocked alveoli
variables.why: Carbon dioxide reaches the alveoli only in blood. With no blood passing, none is added, and the air there stays near the 0.3 mm Hg of breathed-in air.

variables.name: PO2 of the air in the blocked alveoli
variables.why: No blood is taking oxygen out, so the alveolar PO2 rises from about 100 toward the 150 mm Hg of breathed-in air.

variables.name: Blood flow through the rest of the lung
variables.why: The right ventricle still pumps its whole output into the pulmonary arteries, so the blood that cannot pass the clot flows through the open branches instead.

scenarios.title: Hemoglobin in warm, working muscle
scenarios.misconception: a right shift means hemoglobin carries more oxygen
scenarios.setup: During a hard run, the leg muscles become warmer and more acidic, with more carbon dioxide. Keep tissue PO2 at 40 mm Hg for this question. Compare hemoglobin in their capillaries with hemoglobin in resting muscle at the same PO2.
scenarios.start: Temperature, carbon dioxide and H+ rise in the muscle

steps.shape: Hemoglobin is held in its tense, low-affinity shape
steps.sat: Saturation at PO2 40 falls from about 75% to about 53%
steps.rel: More oxygen is released to the muscle

variables.name: Hemoglobin’s affinity for oxygen
variables.why: Carbon dioxide and H+ bind the globin chains and hold the tense shape, and heat weakens the bond between oxygen and heme. Each lowers affinity.

variables.name: P50
variables.why: With lower affinity, a higher PO2 is needed to half-fill hemoglobin, so the curve slides right and P50 rises.

variables.name: Saturation at a PO2 of 40 mm Hg
variables.why: On a right-shifted curve every PO2 gives a lower saturation: about 53% instead of 75% at 40 mm Hg.

variables.name: Oxygen released per 100 mL of blood
variables.why: Blood arrives about 98% saturated either way. Leaving at 53% instead of 75% releases nearly twice as much oxygen, from about 4.6 to about 9 mL per 100 mL.

scenarios.title: Carbon monoxide poisoning
scenarios.misconception: a normal pulse oximeter reading rules out an oxygen problem
scenarios.setup: A family sleeps in a house with a cracked furnace flue. By morning about 30% of their hemoglobin carries carbon monoxide. Their lungs are healthy. Compare with their normal state.
scenarios.start: Carbon monoxide binds heme iron about 200 to 250 times more tightly than oxygen

steps.sites: Sites holding carbon monoxide cannot carry oxygen
steps.content: Oxygen content of arterial blood falls
steps.diss: Oxygen still dissolves in plasma as usual
steps.ox: A standard oximeter reads carboxyhemoglobin as oxyhemoglobin
steps.left: The remaining hemoglobin is held in its relaxed shape: left shift
steps.rel: Less of the remaining oxygen is released in the tissues
steps.mito: Carbon monoxide also binds the last enzyme of the electron transport chain
steps.atp: Aerobic ATP production in tissue cells falls

variables.name: Oxygen content of arterial blood
variables.why: Nearly all oxygen travels on hemoglobin, and every site carbon monoxide occupies is lost to oxygen. With 30% of sites taken, content falls by about a third.

variables.name: Arterial PO2
variables.why: PO2 measures only the oxygen dissolved in plasma. Healthy lungs load plasma normally, and carbon monoxide does not change how much oxygen dissolves.

variables.name: SpO2 on a standard pulse oximeter
variables.why: Carboxyhemoglobin is bright red and absorbs light like oxyhemoglobin, so a two-light oximeter counts it as loaded. The reading stays near normal and hides the problem.

variables.name: P50 of the remaining hemoglobin
