variables.why: Carbon monoxide on one site holds the whole molecule in its relaxed, high-affinity shape, so the curve shifts left and P50 falls.

variables.name: Oxygen released to the tissues at their usual PO2
variables.why: There is less oxygen on hemoglobin to begin with, and the left shift makes hemoglobin hold on to what it has.

variables.name: Aerobic ATP production in tissue cells
variables.why: Less oxygen reaches the mitochondria, and carbon monoxide also blocks the enzyme that hands electrons to oxygen, so the electron transport chain slows. Brain and heart, which depend most on aerobic respiration, show it first.

scenarios.title: Anemia with healthy lungs
scenarios.misconception: saturation tells you how much oxygen the blood carries
scenarios.setup: A woman has lost blood slowly for months, and her hemoglobin has fallen from 14 to 8 g per 100 mL. Her lungs are healthy. Compare her arterial blood with before.
scenarios.start: Hemoglobin concentration falls

steps.dis: The lungs load plasma with oxygen as usual
steps.sat: Each hemoglobin molecule still loads fully
steps.cont: Less hemoglobin carries less oxygen per 100 mL
steps.bpg: Red blood cells make more 2,3-BPG over days
steps.right: The curve shifts right, so a larger share is released

variables.name: Arterial PO2
variables.why: PO2 depends on the lungs, which are healthy. Oxygen dissolves in her plasma to the same partial pressure as before.

variables.name: Arterial saturation (SaO2)
variables.why: Saturation is the percentage of hemoglobin’s sites that are loaded. At a normal PO2, the hemoglobin she has is as fully loaded as ever, about 97%.

variables.name: Oxygen content of arterial blood
variables.why: Content ≈ 1.34 × hemoglobin × saturation. With 8 instead of 14 g per 100 mL, she carries about 10.4 instead of 18.2 mL of oxygen per 100 mL.

variables.name: 2,3-BPG in her red blood cells
variables.why: When the oxygen supply to red blood cells stays low for days, they make more 2,3-BPG from a side branch of glycolysis.

variables.name: Share of the arriving oxygen released in the tissues
variables.why: 2,3-BPG holds hemoglobin in its tense shape and shifts the curve right, so at tissue PO2 a larger share of the oxygen comes off. It partly offsets the smaller amount carried.

scenarios.title: Holding your breath
scenarios.misconception: blood pH falls during a breath-hold because oxygen runs out
scenarios.setup: A swimmer holds her breath underwater for 40 seconds. Compare her arterial blood at the end with before she went under.
scenarios.start: No air moves in or out of the lungs

steps.right: CO2 + H2O → H2CO3 → H+ + HCO3− runs to the right
steps.h: Hydrogen ions rise (buffers bind most, not all)

variables.name: Arterial PCO2
variables.why: Carbon dioxide leaves the body only through the lungs. Production goes on while removal stops, so it builds up in the blood.

variables.name: Hydrogen ion concentration
variables.why: More carbon dioxide pushes the reaction to the right, speeded by carbonic anhydrase in red blood cells, and more carbonic acid splits into H+ and bicarbonate.

variables.name: Blood pH
variables.why: pH measures free hydrogen ions. Hemoglobin and other buffers bind most of the new ones, but the few left free lower the pH. The cause is the carbon dioxide, not the falling oxygen.

variables.name: Bicarbonate in the plasma
variables.why: Each carbonic acid that splits gives one bicarbonate as well as one H+. The bicarbonate leaves the red blood cells through band 3, so plasma bicarbonate rises a little.

scenarios.title: Hyperventilating during a panic attack
scenarios.misconception: hyperventilation loads the blood with extra oxygen
scenarios.setup: During a panic attack, a man breathes fast and deep for several minutes, far more than his carbon dioxide production requires. Compare with his calm state.
scenarios.start: Alveolar ventilation far exceeds carbon dioxide production

steps.pco2: Arterial PCO2 falls below 35 mm Hg (hypocapnia)
steps.ph: Fewer H+ ions: blood pH rises
steps.ca: More calcium binds plasma proteins, so free calcium falls
steps.exc: Nerves and muscles become more excitable
steps.brain: Low carbon dioxide constricts arterioles in the brain
steps.flow: Blood flow to the brain falls: lightheadedness
steps.hb: Hemoglobin was already almost fully saturated

variables.name: Arterial PCO2
variables.why: He blows off carbon dioxide faster than his cells make it, so arterial PCO2 falls. That, not the breathing rate, is what defines hyperventilation.

variables.name: Blood pH
variables.why: Less carbon dioxide pulls CO2 + H2O ⇌ H+ + HCO3− to the left, using up hydrogen ions, so pH rises toward alkalosis.

variables.name: Free calcium in the plasma
variables.why: In alkalosis, plasma proteins such as albumin release H+ and bind more calcium in its place, so less calcium is free.

variables.name: Excitability of nerves and muscles
variables.why: Low free calcium makes nerves and muscles fire more easily, causing tingling around the mouth and cramping spasms of the hands.

variables.name: Blood flow to the brain
variables.why: Carbon dioxide dilates brain arterioles, so a low PCO2 lets them constrict. Less blood reaches the brain, and he feels lightheaded.

variables.name: Arterial oxygen saturation
variables.why: At a normal PO2 hemoglobin is already about 97 to 98% saturated, on the flat top of the dissociation curve. Extra breathing adds almost nothing to it.

scenarios.title: An opioid overdose slows breathing
scenarios.misconception: hypoventilation means a slow breathing rate
scenarios.setup: A man takes an overdose of an opioid painkiller, which depresses the respiratory centers in his brainstem. He breathes slowly and shallowly. Compare with before.
scenarios.start: The respiratory centers are depressed

steps.fire: Fewer, weaker bursts reach the phrenic and intercostal nerves
steps.va: Alveolar ventilation falls below carbon dioxide production
steps.pco2: Arterial PCO2 rises above 45 mm Hg (hypercapnia)
steps.po2: Less fresh air: alveolar and arterial PO2 fall
steps.drowsy: High carbon dioxide deepens drowsiness and confusion

variables.name: Alveolar ventilation
variables.why: Weaker signals reach the diaphragm and intercostals, so breaths are fewer and smaller, and more of each small breath is dead space.

variables.name: Arterial PCO2
variables.why: With carbon dioxide production steady, PCO2 is inversely proportional to alveolar ventilation: halve the ventilation and PCO2 doubles. A high PCO2 is what defines hypoventilation.

variables.name: Blood pH
variables.why: More carbon dioxide pushes the reaction toward carbonic acid, releasing hydrogen ions.

variables.name: Arterial PO2
variables.why: Blood keeps removing oxygen from the alveoli while too little fresh air replaces it, so alveolar and then arterial PO2 fall.

variables.name: Alertness
variables.why: A high PCO2 causes headache, drowsiness and confusion, which adds to the drug’s own sedation. A depressed drive plus drowsiness can spiral toward unconsciousness.

scenarios.title: Going up to 4,300 m: the first hours and three weeks later
scenarios.theme: high altitude, first hours and after acclimatization
scenarios.misconception: breathing rises as much as it can within the first hours at altitude
scenarios.setup: A climber flies from sea level to a town at 4,300 m, where arterial PO2 falls to about 50 mm Hg, and stays there for three weeks.

stages.label: The first hours
stages.prompt: The first few hours at altitude, compared with sea level.
stages.start: Arterial PO2 falls to about 50 mm Hg

steps.cb: Carotid bodies fire strongly (PO2 below 60 mm Hg)
steps.blow: The extra ventilation blows off carbon dioxide
steps.csf: Carbon dioxide leaves the brain’s fluid, and its pH rises
steps.brake: Central chemoreceptors cut their drive: a brake

variables.name: Ventilation
variables.why: Below a PO2 of about 60 mm Hg, carotid body firing rises steeply, and the respiratory centers drive deeper, faster breathing.

variables.name: Arterial PCO2
variables.why: Carbon dioxide production has not changed, but more of it is breathed out, so PCO2 falls.

variables.name: Blood pH
variables.why: Less carbon dioxide means fewer hydrogen ions, so the blood becomes alkaline.

variables.name: Drive to breathe from the central chemoreceptors
variables.why: Carbon dioxide crosses the blood–brain barrier freely, so the brain’s fluid loses it too and its H+ falls. The central chemoreceptors reduce their drive and hold ventilation below what the low oxygen alone would cause.

stages.label: Three weeks later
stages.prompt: After three weeks at the same altitude, compared with the first hours.
stages.start: Low PO2 and alkaline blood persist for days

steps.csfh: Bicarbonate in the cerebrospinal fluid is lowered too
steps.phn: Blood and brain pH move back toward normal
steps.rel: The central brake is released; carotid bodies grow more sensitive
steps.hct: Red blood cell count and hematocrit rise

variables.name: Plasma bicarbonate
variables.why: The kidneys excrete extra bicarbonate in the urine over the first days, removing base from the blood.

variables.name: Blood pH
variables.why: With less bicarbonate, the alkaline blood of the first hours moves back toward a normal pH of about 7.4. Compared with the first hours, it is lower.

variables.name: Ventilation
variables.why: As the pH of the brain’s fluid normalizes, the central chemoreceptors stop braking, and the carotid bodies become more sensitive to low oxygen. Ventilation keeps climbing over days.

variables.name: Arterial PCO2
variables.why: Even more ventilation for the same carbon dioxide production lowers PCO2 further.

variables.name: Arterial PO2
variables.why: More fresh air reaches the alveoli, so alveolar PO2 and with it arterial PO2 rise, though they stay well below sea-level values.

variables.name: 2,3-BPG in red blood cells
variables.why: A lasting low oxygen supply makes red blood cells produce more 2,3-BPG within a day or two, which shifts the dissociation curve right and helps unload oxygen in the tissues.

variables.name: Hematocrit
variables.why: Low oxygen makes the kidneys release more erythropoietin, which speeds red blood cell production. Over weeks, each liter of blood carries more hemoglobin.

scenarios.title: Breathing during a steady jog
scenarios.misconception: you breathe harder in exercise because blood carbon dioxide rises and oxygen falls
scenarios.setup: A healthy person jogs at a moderate, steady pace for 10 minutes. Compare the state a few minutes in with rest.
scenarios.start: Moderate exercise begins

steps.cmd: Motor cortex and limb proprioceptors signal the respiratory centers
steps.met: Working muscle makes more carbon dioxide and uses more oxygen
steps.match: Chemoreceptors fine-tune ventilation to match carbon dioxide production
steps.gas: Arterial PCO2 and PO2 stay near normal
steps.tpo2: PO2 in the working muscle falls
steps.shift: Warmth, carbon dioxide and acid shift the dissociation curve right
steps.unload: More oxygen is unloaded in the working muscle
steps.sym: Sympathetic output to the heart rises

variables.name: Ventilation
variables.why: Signals from the motor cortex to the muscles also reach the respiratory centers, and proprioceptors in the moving limbs add their input, so ventilation rises within a breath or two, before blood chemistry changes.

variables.name: Carbon dioxide production
variables.why: Working muscle runs aerobic respiration faster, making more carbon dioxide and using more oxygen.

variables.name: Arterial PCO2
variables.why: Ventilation rises in step with carbon dioxide production, so the extra is breathed out as fast as it is made. This matched rise, with normal blood gases, is hyperpnea, not hyperventilation.

variables.name: Arterial PO2
variables.why: Alveolar ventilation keeps pace with oxygen use, so alveolar and arterial PO2 stay about the same.

variables.name: PO2 in the working muscle
variables.why: The muscle uses oxygen faster than before, so the PO2 of its tissue fluid falls, sometimes below 20 mm Hg. That steepens the gradient from blood to tissue.

variables.name: Oxygen unloaded from each 100 mL of blood in the muscle
variables.why: A lower tissue PO2 moves blood down the steep part of the dissociation curve, and the right shift lowers saturation further at that PO2. Both release more oxygen.

variables.name: Cardiac output
variables.why: Sympathetic signals speed the heart and strengthen its contraction, so more blood, and more oxygen, reaches the muscles each minute.

scenarios.title: Emphysema
scenarios.misconception: emphysema makes the lungs stiff
scenarios.setup: After 40 years of smoking, a man has lost alveolar walls and their elastic fibers throughout both lungs. Compare his lungs with healthy lungs of the same size.
scenarios.start: Alveolar walls and elastic fibers are destroyed

steps.area: Fewer, larger air spaces: less surface area
steps.diff: Less oxygen diffuses into the blood
steps.po2: Arterial PO2 falls, first during exercise
steps.guy: Small airways lose the outward pull that held them open
steps.coll: Small airways collapse during breath out
steps.trap: Air is trapped: residual volume rises
steps.fev: Air leaves slowly: FEV1 falls much more than FVC

variables.name: Elastic recoil of the lungs
variables.why: Elastic fibers in the alveolar walls supply the recoil that pushes air out in a quiet breath. Destroying them weakens it.

variables.name: Lung compliance
variables.why: With less elastic tissue to stretch, the same pressure change inflates the lungs more. Emphysematous lungs are floppy, not stiff; breathing out is the hard part.

variables.name: Residual volume
variables.why: Elastic fibers attached to the outside of the smallest airways pull them open like guy ropes. Without them, the pressure around the airways squeezes them shut during expiration and traps air behind them.

variables.name: FEV1/FVC ratio
variables.why: Weak recoil and collapsing airways slow the forced breath out, so far less than the usual 80% of the FVC leaves in the first second: an obstructive pattern.

variables.name: Surface area for gas exchange
variables.why: Many small alveoli merge into fewer large spaces, which have much less wall area, and the capillaries in the lost walls are gone too.

variables.name: Arterial PO2 during exercise
variables.why: A smaller surface slows diffusion. In exercise, blood races through the capillaries and leaves before it has fully loaded oxygen.

scenarios.title: High-flow oxygen in severe COPD
scenarios.misconception: oxygen raises PCO2 in COPD mainly by removing a hypoxic drive to breathe
scenarios.setup: A woman with severe COPD has had a high arterial PCO2 for years. In the emergency room she is given high-flow oxygen instead of a controlled amount aimed at a target saturation. Compare an hour later with before the oxygen.
scenarios.start: Alveolar PO2 rises, even in poorly ventilated regions

steps.hpv: Hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction in poorly ventilated regions relaxes
steps.flow: More blood flows past barely ventilated alveoli
steps.less: Less carbon dioxide is removed from that blood
steps.hald: Haldane effect: blood holds less carbon dioxide at a given PCO2

variables.name: Arterial PO2
variables.why: Breathing a higher oxygen fraction raises alveolar PO2 wherever some air arrives, so arterial PO2 rises.

variables.name: Blood flow to poorly ventilated alveoli
variables.why: Low alveolar PO2 had constricted the arterioles there, steering blood away. Extra oxygen reverses that constriction, so blood flows back past alveoli that barely ventilate.

variables.name: Ventilation–perfusion mismatch
variables.why: More blood now passes alveoli with little airflow: low-V/Q units grow.

variables.name: Carbon dioxide the blood can carry at a given PCO2
variables.why: Oxyhemoglobin binds fewer hydrogen ions and less carbamino carbon dioxide than deoxyhemoglobin. That is the Haldane effect, and it shifts carbon dioxide into the dissolved form that sets PCO2.

variables.name: Arterial PCO2
variables.why: Worsening V/Q mismatch plus the Haldane effect raise PCO2; ventilation itself falls only slightly and briefly. For your exam: many EMT and nursing materials say the cause is loss of a “hypoxic drive to breathe.” Know that answer, but never withhold oxygen from a hypoxic patient; give it in controlled amounts, often aiming for 88–92%.

variables.name: Blood pH
variables.why: The extra carbon dioxide forms carbonic acid and releases hydrogen ions, and the kidneys cannot adjust bicarbonate within an hour.

scenarios.title: Left heart failure floods the lungs
scenarios.misconception: fluid in the lungs slows carbon dioxide exchange as much as oxygen exchange
scenarios.setup: A 74-year-old woman’s weakened left ventricle can no longer pump out all the blood it receives, and blood backs up into her lungs. Compare her state with a week ago, when she was well.
scenarios.start: The left ventricle falls behind the blood it receives

steps.back: Blood backs up into the pulmonary veins and capillaries
steps.filt: Filtration outpaces what the lymphatic vessels can carry away
steps.o2: Oxygen diffusion slows far more than carbon dioxide diffusion
steps.stiff: Fluid in the lung tissue stiffens the lungs
steps.rec: Sensory receptors in the alveolar walls detect the fluid

variables.name: Pulmonary capillary hydrostatic pressure
variables.why: Blood the left ventricle cannot move on backs up through the left atrium into the pulmonary veins and capillaries, raising their pressure above the usual 10 mm Hg.

variables.name: Fluid in the lung tissue around the alveoli
variables.why: Higher hydrostatic pressure pushes more fluid out of the capillaries. Once filtration exceeds what the lung’s lymphatic vessels can carry away, fluid builds up.

variables.name: Lung compliance
variables.why: Waterlogged lung tissue resists stretch, so each breath needs a larger pressure change.

variables.name: Arterial PO2
variables.why: Fluid lengthens the diffusion distance. Carbon dioxide is about 20 times more soluble and still crosses readily, but oxygen falls behind, and flooded alveoli later add blood that meets no air.

variables.name: Breathing rate
variables.why: Sensory receptors in the alveolar walls, near the capillaries, respond to the fluid and trigger rapid, shallow breathing with a feeling of breathlessness.

scenarios.title: A deep cut severs a nerve at the wrist
scenarios.misconception: a nerve carries only one kind of signal, so cutting it causes only numbness or only weakness
scenarios.setup: A shard of glass cuts clean through one nerve at the wrist. The nerve carried sensory axons from the skin of the little finger, somatic motor axons to small hand muscles, and autonomic axons to the sweat glands of that patch of skin. Nothing above the wrist is injured.
scenarios.start: One nerve cut at the wrist

steps.noin: Touch signals never reach the CNS
steps.nocmd: Commands never reach the hand muscles
steps.heart: Axons to the heart run elsewhere

variables.name: Feeling in the skin of the little finger
variables.why: Touch is felt only when sensory axons deliver the signal to the CNS. The cut stops every signal from the finger at the wrist, so the finger is numb.

variables.name: Strength of the small hand muscles the nerve supplies
variables.why: Skeletal muscle contracts only when a somatic motor axon brings it a command. The commands still leave the CNS but stop at the cut, so those muscles are weak.

variables.name: Sweating from that patch of skin
variables.why: Sweat glands are autonomic effectors. The autonomic axons that drive them ran in the same nerve, so that patch of skin stays dry.

variables.name: Heart rate
variables.why: The autonomic axons that reach the heart travel in other nerves, nowhere near the wrist, so the cut leaves them working and the heart rate is unchanged.

scenarios.title: An axon in a nerve of the forearm is cut
scenarios.misconception: a cut axon heals by the two cut ends simply growing back together
scenarios.setup: A sensory axon is cut in a nerve of the forearm, and a surgeon sews the nerve ends together. Predict what has happened two weeks later, compared with the day before the injury.
scenarios.start: Axon cut in a nerve

steps.supply: Far part loses its protein supply from the soma
steps.frag: Far part of the axon breaks down
steps.mult: Schwann cells multiply and line up in a tube
steps.soma: Soma switches its protein making to growth
steps.slow: Sprouts regrow only about 1 mm a day
steps.numb: Fingertip still cut off from the CNS

variables.name: Length of intact axon beyond the cut
variables.why: Nearly all of an axon’s proteins are made in the soma and carried out by axonal transport. The part beyond the cut has lost that supply, so within days it breaks down (Wallerian degeneration).

variables.name: Macrophages in the far part of the nerve
variables.why: As the far axon and its myelin fall apart, Schwann cells break down their own myelin and signal macrophages to come in from the blood to clear the debris.

variables.name: Number of Schwann cells in the far part of the nerve
variables.why: Schwann cells can divide. They multiply and line up in a column inside the old connective tissue sheath, building the regeneration tube the new axon will follow.

variables.name: Clumps of Nissl bodies visible in the soma
variables.why: The soma switches its protein making from signaling to growth. Its cell body swells and its clumps of rough ER (Nissl bodies) break up and disperse.

variables.name: Feeling at the fingertip the axon supplied
variables.why: Sprouts grow along the tube at only about a millimeter a day, so after two weeks they are still far from the fingertip. It stays numb for months.

scenarios.title: Myelin is lost from a stretch of axon
scenarios.misconception: losing myelin stops the neuron from making action potentials at all
scenarios.setup: In multiple sclerosis, an immune attack strips the myelin from a few internodes of a myelinated axon in the brain. The nodes before and after the damaged stretch are healthy. An action potential fires at the last healthy node before the bare stretch.
scenarios.start: Myelin lost from a few internodes

steps.leak: Current leaks out across the bare wall
steps.less: Less current reaches the next node
steps.node: Healthy node has its full set of channels

variables.name: Current leaking out through the axon wall between the two healthy nodes
variables.why: Myelin is layers of lipid-rich membrane that insulate the axon. Without it, the bare wall lets current escape instead of carrying it along the inside to the next node.

variables.name: Current reaching the next healthy node
variables.why: Whatever leaks out on the way is lost to the next node, so less current arrives there.

variables.name: Conduction velocity across the damaged stretch
variables.why: With less current arriving, the next node takes longer to reach threshold, or never does. The bare stretch has too few sodium channels to fire along it quickly, so the signal is delayed or blocked.

variables.name: Size of the action potential at the last healthy node before the damage
variables.why: That node still has its dense sodium channels and normal ion gradients, so it fires a full, all-or-none action potential. The problem is getting the current to the next node.

scenarios.title: Pufferfish toxin blocks half the sodium channels
scenarios.theme: a toxin blocks voltage-gated sodium channels
scenarios.misconception: a sodium channel toxin changes the resting potential
scenarios.setup: A small dose of tetrodotoxin, the pufferfish poison, plugs about half of the voltage-gated sodium channels in a motor neuron’s axon. The leak channels, the sodium–potassium pumps and the ion gradients are unchanged. "Increases" for a voltage means the number goes up: −70 mV becoming −60 mV is an increase.
scenarios.start: Half the sodium channels plugged

steps.closed: Sodium channels are closed at rest anyway
steps.rest: Resting potential set by leak and pump
steps.fewer: Fewer sodium channels ready to open
steps.thr: Sodium entry outruns potassium only at a higher voltage
steps.small: Less sodium enters in the rising phase

variables.name: Resting membrane potential
variables.why: The resting potential comes from the leak channels and the pump. Voltage-gated sodium channels are closed at rest, so plugging some of them changes nothing until the membrane depolarizes.

variables.name: Sodium channels available to open
variables.why: A plugged channel cannot pass sodium whatever its gates do, so only about half the usual number can take part.

variables.name: Threshold voltage
variables.why: Threshold is the voltage at which sodium entering first outruns potassium leaving. With fewer channels, the membrane must depolarize further before enough open, so threshold moves up, away from rest.

variables.name: Stimulus strength needed to make the neuron fire
variables.why: The gap from rest to threshold is now larger, so a stimulus that used to be just enough now gives only a graded potential that fades.

variables.name: Height of an action potential that does fire
variables.why: The rising phase is driven by sodium rushing in. With half the channels plugged, less sodium enters before inactivation and the potassium channels cut the rise off, so the spike is smaller, or fails.

scenarios.title: A dentist numbs a tooth with lidocaine
scenarios.misconception: a local anesthetic stops the sensory receptors in the tooth from detecting anything
scenarios.setup: A dentist injects lidocaine around the nerve that carries signals from a lower tooth, a few centimeters from the tooth itself. Lidocaine enters the axons at the injection site and blocks their voltage-gated sodium channels from the inside. Then the drill touches the tooth.
scenarios.start: Lidocaine blocks sodium channels at the injection site

steps.away: Tooth’s sensory endings are beyond the drug
steps.fire: Endings still fire at the tooth
steps.block: Axons at the injection site cannot fire
steps.stop: Action potentials stop at the numbed stretch
steps.brain: No pain signal reaches the brain

variables.name: Action potentials started at the sensory endings in the tooth when drilled
variables.why: The drug sits a few centimeters away, at the injection site. The endings in the tooth still have working sodium channels, so they still respond to the drill and fire.

variables.name: Action potentials passing the injection site toward the brain
variables.why: Each patch of axon must fire its own action potential to pass the signal on. With its sodium channels blocked, the numbed stretch cannot fire, so the signal dies there.

variables.name: Pain felt from the tooth
variables.why: Pain is felt only when the signal reaches the brain. It is stopped at the injection site on the way, so nothing is felt.

variables.name: Resting membrane potential of the axons at the injection site
variables.why: Voltage-gated sodium channels are closed at rest, and the resting potential is set by leak channels and the pump, which the drug does not block.

scenarios.title: A drug blocks the voltage-gated potassium channels
scenarios.misconception: blocking potassium channels stops the action potential from starting
scenarios.setup: A drug blocks the voltage-gated (delayed) potassium channels of an axon. Its potassium leak channels, its sodium channels and its pumps are unchanged. A stimulus brings the axon to threshold.
scenarios.start: Delayed potassium channels blocked

steps.na: Sodium channels open at threshold as usual
steps.nok: Little potassium leaves after the peak
steps.fall: Falling phase slower, relying on inactivation and leak
steps.nodip: No extra potassium outflow after the spike

variables.name: Whether the axon reaches threshold and starts an action potential
variables.why: The start of an action potential depends on voltage-gated sodium channels opening at threshold. They are untouched, so the spike starts normally.

variables.name: Speed of the falling phase
variables.why: The falling phase is fast because the delayed potassium channels let potassium rush out just as the sodium channels inactivate. With them blocked, only the leak channels carry potassium out, so repolarization is slow.

variables.name: Duration of each action potential
variables.why: A slower fall means the membrane stays depolarized longer, so each spike is wider.

variables.name: Depth of the afterhyperpolarization below rest
variables.why: The dip to about −80 mV comes from delayed potassium channels that are slow to close. With them blocked, there is no extra potassium outflow to carry the membrane below rest.

scenarios.title: Blood potassium rises, then stays high
scenarios.misconception: high potassium always makes nerves and muscles more excitable
scenarios.setup: Kidney failure lets the potassium in the extracellular fluid rise (hyperkalemia). Follow a motor neuron’s axon, first after a modest rise, then after potassium has climbed further and stayed high for hours. "Increases" for a voltage means the number goes up: −70 mV becoming −60 mV is an increase.

stages.label: A modest rise
stages.prompt: Just after a modest rise in extracellular potassium, compared with normal.
stages.start: Extracellular potassium rises a little

steps.gap: Smaller gap from rest to threshold

variables.name: Resting membrane potential
variables.why: The resting membrane leaks mostly potassium, so its voltage follows the potassium gradient. A smaller gradient pushes less potassium out, and the resting potential moves a few millivolts toward zero.

variables.name: Depolarization needed to reach threshold
variables.why: Threshold has barely moved, but rest is now closer to it, so a smaller graded potential is enough.

variables.name: Excitability (how easily the neuron fires)
variables.why: With rest closer to threshold, stimuli that used to fade now fire the neuron. Excitability rises at first, although a mild rise often causes no symptoms you would notice.

variables.name: Threshold voltage
variables.why: A small, recent depolarization leaves most sodium channels in the closed, ready state, so threshold is about where it was.

stages.label: Hours later, much higher
stages.prompt: Hours later, with potassium much higher and the membrane held partly depolarized, compared with the modest rise.
stages.start: Membrane held depolarized for hours

steps.inact: More sodium channels drift into the inactivated state

variables.name: Sodium channels stuck in the inactivated state
variables.why: Depolarization swings the inactivation gates shut. A channel resets only when the membrane repolarizes, and a membrane held depolarized never does, so inactivated channels pile up.

variables.name: Threshold voltage
variables.why: Threshold is where sodium entry outruns potassium exit. With fewer ready channels, the membrane must depolarize further before that happens.

variables.name: Size of the action potentials that fire
variables.why: Fewer ready channels let less sodium in during the rising phase, so spikes are smaller, and many fail altogether.

variables.name: Excitability (how easily the neuron fires)
variables.why: Excitability first rose and now falls: a higher threshold and failing spikes mean fewer signals reach the muscles. That is the weakness of severe hyperkalemia; the same failure in the heart makes its rhythm dangerous.

scenarios.title: An SSRI blocks serotonin reuptake
scenarios.theme: reuptake of a transmitter is blocked
scenarios.misconception: blocking reuptake makes the terminal release more neurotransmitter
scenarios.setup: A person takes an SSRI, a drug that blocks the serotonin transporters in the membranes of serotonin-releasing axon terminals. Predict what happens at one of these synapses over the next few hours, after an action potential arrives. Ignore any feedback from serotonin onto the releasing neuron itself.
scenarios.start: Serotonin transporters blocked

steps.ca: Calcium entry and vesicle fusion unchanged
steps.rel: Same amount released per action potential
steps.noup: Serotonin not pumped back into the terminal
steps.bind: It binds receptor proteins again and again

variables.name: Serotonin released per action potential
variables.why: Release depends on calcium entering the terminal and vesicles fusing. The drug acts on removal, not on release, so each action potential releases the usual amount.

variables.name: Serotonin concentration in the synaptic cleft after each release
variables.why: Reuptake is the main way serotonin leaves the cleft. With the transporters blocked, only slow diffusion removes it, so it builds up.

variables.name: How long serotonin stays in the cleft
variables.why: The signal normally ends within milliseconds because transporters pump serotonin back in. Without them, it lingers.

variables.name: Size and duration of the postsynaptic response
variables.why: Serotonin that lingers keeps binding the postsynaptic receptor proteins, so the response is larger and lasts longer. Mood effects take weeks, for reasons still being worked out.

scenarios.title: Calcium is removed from the fluid around a synapse
scenarios.misconception: the action potential itself carries the signal across the synaptic cleft
scenarios.setup: In a lab dish, a researcher replaces the fluid around a chemical synapse with fluid that has no calcium. The presynaptic neuron is then stimulated to fire an action potential.
scenarios.start: No calcium outside the terminal

steps.na: Axon’s sodium and potassium channels unaffected
steps.ap: Action potential still reaches the terminal

variables.name: Action potential arriving at the axon terminal
variables.why: The action potential depends on sodium and potassium channels and gradients, which are unchanged, so it still reaches the terminal.

variables.name: Calcium entering the terminal
variables.why: The depolarization still opens the voltage-gated calcium channels, but calcium can flow in only down its gradient from the fluid outside. With none outside, none enters.

variables.name: Neurotransmitter released into the cleft
variables.why: Calcium binding sensor proteins on the docked vesicles is the trigger for exocytosis. Without calcium the vesicles stay docked.

variables.name: Postsynaptic potential in the next neuron
variables.why: The cleft is far too wide for current to cross. Only neurotransmitter carries the signal across, and none was released.

scenarios.title: A benzodiazepine boosts GABA’s effect
scenarios.misconception: benzodiazepines calm the brain by making neurons release more GABA
scenarios.setup: A person takes a benzodiazepine, a drug that makes GABA’s chloride channels open more readily when GABA binds. Consider a neuron in the brain that receives both excitatory glutamate synapses and inhibitory GABA synapses. The presynaptic neurons fire at their usual rates.
scenarios.start: GABA’s chloride channels open more readily

steps.more: More chloride channels open per release
steps.sum: Sum at the trigger zone stays further below threshold

variables.name: GABA released per action potential
variables.why: The drug acts on the postsynaptic chloride channels, not on release. The presynaptic neurons fire and release as usual.

variables.name: Size of each IPSP
variables.why: Each release of GABA now opens more chloride channels, so more chloride flows in and the membrane is pulled further from threshold.

variables.name: Size of each EPSP from the glutamate synapses
variables.why: The drug does not act on glutamate’s receptor proteins, so each EPSP on its own is the same size. What changes is how much the IPSPs subtract from the sum.

variables.name: Firing rate of the postsynaptic neuron
variables.why: EPSPs and IPSPs add algebraically at the trigger zone. Bigger IPSPs subtract more, so the sum reaches threshold less often. That extra inhibition is the calm and sleepiness the drug causes.

scenarios.title: An insecticide blocks acetylcholinesterase
scenarios.misconception: blocking acetylcholinesterase can only strengthen muscle contraction
scenarios.setup: A farm worker is exposed to an organophosphate insecticide, which blocks acetylcholinesterase at the neuromuscular junctions. Follow a skeletal muscle fiber, first in the early minutes and then with continued exposure.

stages.label: Early minutes
stages.prompt: In the early minutes of exposure, compared with before it.
stages.start: Acetylcholinesterase blocked

steps.rel: Release from the motor neuron unchanged
steps.build: Acetylcholine builds up in the cleft
steps.bind: It keeps binding nicotinic receptor proteins
steps.extra: Extra action potentials in the fiber

variables.name: Acetylcholine released per motor neuron action potential
variables.why: Release depends on calcium entering the motor neuron’s terminal. The insecticide acts on the enzyme in the cleft, not on release.

variables.name: Acetylcholine in the synaptic cleft
variables.why: Acetylcholinesterase normally splits acetylcholine within about a millisecond. With it blocked, acetylcholine stays and piles up with each release.

variables.name: Twitching of the muscle fibers
variables.why: Lingering acetylcholine keeps opening the ionotropic nicotinic channels, so the fiber fires extra action potentials that no command asked for.

stages.label: Continued exposure
stages.prompt: With continued exposure and acetylcholine staying high, compared with the early minutes.
stages.start: Acetylcholine stays high in the cleft

steps.open: Acetylcholine keeps acting on the nicotinic channels
steps.noap: Fiber can no longer fire action potentials

variables.name: Time the muscle fiber membrane spends depolarized
variables.why: Acetylcholine lingers, so at first the nicotinic channels keep letting sodium in and the membrane near the junction stays depolarized. With longer exposure the nicotinic receptor proteins also stop responding to acetylcholine, which adds to the block.

variables.name: Sodium channels in the fiber membrane ready to open
variables.why: Sodium channels inactivate during depolarization and reset only when the membrane repolarizes. A membrane held depolarized keeps them inactivated.

variables.name: Strength of muscle contraction
variables.why: With no ready sodium channels, the fiber cannot fire action potentials, so it cannot be made to contract. The twitching gives way to weakness, and failure of the breathing muscles is what makes these poisons deadly.

scenarios.title: The left side of the cerebellum is damaged
scenarios.misconception: damage to the cerebellum paralyzes the opposite side of the body
scenarios.setup: Loss of blood flow damages the left half of the cerebellum. The cerebral cortex, brainstem and spinal cord are unharmed. The person is asked to reach for a cup with each hand.
scenarios.start: Left cerebellum damaged

variables.name: Grip strength of the left hand
variables.why: Movements start in the motor areas of the frontal lobe, which are unharmed. The cerebellum corrects movements; it does not power them.

variables.name: Accuracy of reaching with the left hand
variables.why: Each side of the cerebellum coordinates the same side of the body. With no comparison of intended and actual movement, the left hand overshoots the cup: ataxia.

variables.name: Accuracy of reaching with the right hand
variables.why: The right side of the cerebellum, which corrects right-side movements, is intact.

scenarios.title: Dopamine neurons of the substantia nigra die
scenarios.misconception: Parkinson’s disease causes weakness because the muscles or motor neurons are damaged
scenarios.setup: In Parkinson’s disease, dopamine neurons of the substantia nigra slowly die. The motor cortex, the muscles and the neurons that drive them are unharmed.
scenarios.start: Substantia nigra neurons die

steps.da: Less dopamine released into the striatum
steps.brake: Globus pallidus keeps inhibiting the thalamus
steps.start: Movements slow and hard to start

variables.name: Dopamine released into the striatum
variables.why: The substantia nigra’s neurons are the source of the dopamine that reaches the striatum. As they die, less is released.

variables.name: Inhibition of the thalamus by the globus pallidus during a planned movement
variables.why: The globus pallidus constantly inhibits the thalamus, and the striatum lifts that brake for a chosen movement. Dopamine makes lifting it easier, so with less dopamine the brake stays on harder.

variables.name: Speed and ease of starting a movement
variables.why: With the brake stuck on, the thalamus passes less drive back to the motor cortex, so movements are slow and hard to begin.

variables.name: Maximum force the muscles can produce
variables.why: The problem is in selecting and starting movements, not in the motor neurons or muscles, so the force they can produce is unchanged.

scenarios.title: A tumor pinches the cerebral aqueduct shut
scenarios.misconception: when CSF cannot drain, the choroid plexus stops making it
scenarios.setup: In an adult, a small tumor presses on the cerebral aqueduct and closes it. The choroid plexuses and the arachnoid granulations are healthy.
scenarios.start: Cerebral aqueduct closed

steps.trap: CSF above the block cannot leave
steps.below: Nothing new reaches the fourth ventricle from above

variables.name: CSF production by the choroid plexuses
variables.why: CSF is secreted by active transport, and production does not slow much when pressure rises. That is exactly why a block makes fluid build up.

variables.name: Size of the lateral ventricles
variables.why: CSF made in the lateral and third ventricles can leave only through the aqueduct. With it closed, fluid builds up above the block and the ventricles swell.

variables.name: Size of the fourth ventricle
variables.why: The fourth ventricle lies below the block. Its own CSF still drains through the median and lateral apertures, so it stays normal. That pattern points to a block in the aqueduct.

variables.name: Pressure inside the skull
variables.why: An adult skull cannot expand, so swelling ventricles push the brain against the bone and pressure rises, causing headache, vomiting and drowsiness.

scenarios.title: Blood clogs the subarachnoid space and granulations
scenarios.misconception: all hydrocephalus comes from a block inside the ventricles
scenarios.setup: After a subarachnoid hemorrhage, blood and debris clog the subarachnoid space and the arachnoid granulations. The ventricles, foramina, aqueduct and apertures are all open.
scenarios.start: Granulations clogged

steps.noret: CSF cannot return to venous blood
steps.back: CSF backs up through the open apertures

variables.name: CSF flowing into the venous blood
variables.why: The arachnoid granulations are the classic route from the subarachnoid space into the venous channels of the dura. Clogged, they pass much less.

variables.name: Size of the fourth ventricle
variables.why: Every passage between the ventricles is open, so the backed-up fluid swells all four ventricles, the fourth included. This is communicating hydrocephalus.

variables.name: CSF production by the choroid plexuses
variables.why: Production is secretion by the choroid plexus cells, and it barely slows as pressure rises, so it carries on at about 500 mL a day.

variables.name: Pressure inside the skull
variables.why: Fluid still enters but cannot leave, and the adult skull cannot expand, so pressure rises.

scenarios.title: Polio destroys ventral horn motor neurons
scenarios.misconception: any damage to the spinal cord causes both numbness and paralysis
scenarios.setup: Polio virus destroys the motor neurons in the ventral horn of several lumbar segments. The dorsal horns, the dorsal roots and the white matter are spared.
scenarios.start: Ventral horn motor neurons destroyed

steps.nocmd: No axons leave through those ventral roots
steps.weak: Leg muscles get no commands: weakness
steps.dr: Dorsal roots and dorsal horns intact
steps.feel: Sensation from the legs still reaches the brain

variables.name: Strength of the leg muscles those segments supply
variables.why: Ventral horn motor neurons are the only route for commands to reach skeletal muscle. With their cell bodies gone, their axons in the ventral root die too, and the muscles get no signal.

variables.name: Bulk of those muscles, over the following months
variables.why: Muscle fibers that lose their nerve supply are no longer used and waste away.

variables.name: Feeling of touch on the skin of the legs
variables.why: Sensation comes in at the back: through the dorsal root, into the dorsal horn and up the white matter. Polio spares those, so touch is felt normally.

scenarios.title: The dorsal roots of three segments are cut
scenarios.misconception: cutting a root at the back of the cord paralyzes the muscles it supplies
scenarios.setup: A surgeon cuts the dorsal roots of three neighboring thoracic segments on the right side, to relieve pain, and leaves the ventral roots intact.
scenarios.start: Right dorsal roots of three segments cut

steps.noin: Sensory axons from those segments cannot enter the cord
steps.numb: That band of skin loses sensation
steps.vr: Ventral roots still carry motor axons out

variables.name: Sensation from the band of skin on the right supplied by the middle one of those segments
variables.why: Sensory axons enter the cord only through the dorsal roots. Each band of skin is also reached by the roots just above and below it, so all three must be cut before the middle band goes numb.

variables.name: Strength of the muscles those segments supply
variables.why: Motor axons leave through the ventral roots, which are intact, so the muscles still receive their commands.

scenarios.title: The hand area of the left primary motor cortex is damaged
scenarios.theme: damage to one functional area of the cortex
scenarios.misconception: damage to one hemisphere weakens the same side of the body
scenarios.setup: Loss of blood flow damages the hand area of the left precentral gyrus. The postcentral gyrus, the language areas and the rest of the cortex are unharmed.
scenarios.start: Left precentral gyrus hand area damaged

steps.cross: Its commands went to the opposite side
steps.lok: Right hemisphere still commands the left hand

variables.name: Strength of the right hand
variables.why: The primary motor cortex sends commands to the motor neurons of the opposite side of the body. The hand area on the left drives the right hand.

variables.name: Strength of the left hand
variables.why: The left hand is driven by the right hemisphere’s motor cortex, which is intact.

variables.name: Feeling of touch on the right hand
variables.why: Touch is received by the primary somatosensory cortex in the postcentral gyrus, behind the central sulcus, which is unharmed. Motor and sensory areas are separate.

scenarios.title: Broca’s area is damaged
scenarios.misconception: aphasia means the person can no longer understand language
scenarios.setup: Loss of blood flow damages Broca’s area in the lower left frontal lobe of a right-handed person. Wernicke’s area and the primary auditory cortex are unharmed.
scenarios.start: Broca’s area damaged

steps.plan: No area to build fluent speech plans

variables.name: Fluency of speech
variables.why: Broca’s area assembles words into fluent, grammatical speech plans. Without it, speech becomes slow, effortful and short on grammar: expressive aphasia.

variables.name: Understanding of spoken sentences
variables.why: Understanding depends on Wernicke’s area in the temporal lobe, which is intact, so comprehension stays mostly good.

variables.name: Ability to repeat a phrase
variables.why: Repeating runs through Broca’s area at the end of the route, so the damaged area blocks it even though the phrase is understood.

scenarios.title: Both hippocampi are removed
scenarios.misconception: memories are stored in the hippocampus, so losing it erases them all
scenarios.setup: Like Henry Molaison in 1953, a patient has the inner parts of both temporal lobes, including most of both hippocampi, removed to stop seizures. Predict the months after surgery.
scenarios.start: Both hippocampi removed

steps.nolink: Nothing links new experiences into one memory
steps.nonew: New declarative memories do not form
steps.cortex: Old memories already stored in the cortex

variables.name: Ability to remember a conversation from ten minutes ago
variables.why: The hippocampus binds the scattered cortical activity of an experience into one memory and consolidates it. Without it, new declarative memories fade within minutes: anterograde amnesia.

variables.name: General memories and facts from childhood
variables.why: Old memories have been consolidated and are stored in the cerebral cortex, so their gist survives without the hippocampus. (Some studies find that vivid detail of old personal events is thinner after hippocampal loss, which is still debated.)

variables.name: Improvement at a new drawing skill practiced over several days
variables.why: Procedural memory is formed by the basal nuclei and cerebellum, not the hippocampus, so skills still improve with practice, even though the patient does not remember practicing.

variables.name: Holding a phone number in mind while dialing it
variables.why: Working memory depends heavily on the prefrontal cortex, which is intact, so a few items can still be held in mind for the moment.

scenarios.title: The corpus callosum is cut
scenarios.misconception: after the corpus callosum is cut, the left hand can no longer feel
scenarios.setup: To stop seizures spreading from one side to the other, surgeons cut a right-handed patient’s corpus callosum. Later, with eyes closed, the patient holds a key in the left hand.
scenarios.start: Key in the left hand, eyes closed

steps.touch: Touch goes to the right postcentral gyrus
steps.pick: Left hand can pick it out of a pile
steps.nolh: Left hemisphere never gets the information

variables.name: Touch information reaching the right hemisphere
variables.why: Touch from the left hand reaches the primary somatosensory cortex of the opposite, right hemisphere by the usual route, which the surgery did not touch.

variables.name: Ability to pick the key out of a pile with the left hand
variables.why: The right hemisphere both feels the key and controls the left hand, so it can find the key again without the left hemisphere.

variables.name: Ability to say the key’s name
variables.why: Speech is produced by the left hemisphere in most right-handed people. The information sits in the right hemisphere, and the corpus callosum that would share it is cut.

scenarios.title: Coffee late in a long day
scenarios.misconception: caffeine removes the adenosine that builds up while you are awake
scenarios.setup: After 15 hours awake, you drink a strong coffee. Caffeine blocks the adenosine receptor proteins on neurons of the arousal systems. Predict the next hour, compared with the hour before.
scenarios.start: Caffeine blocks adenosine receptor proteins

steps.block: Adenosine cannot bind its receptor proteins

variables.name: Adenosine outside the neurons
variables.why: Adenosine comes from active neurons breaking down ATP. Caffeine does not stop that and does not clear it; only sleep does. So adenosine keeps building through the hour, just as it did before the coffee.

variables.name: Inhibition of the arousal systems by adenosine
variables.why: Adenosine inhibits arousal neurons only by binding its receptor proteins. Caffeine occupies them, so the adenosine present has less effect.

variables.name: How sleepy you feel
variables.why: With the brake on the arousal systems eased, you feel less sleepy, although the sleep pressure itself is still there and returns as the caffeine wears off.

scenarios.title: The right L5 dorsal root is cut
scenarios.misconception: cutting one dorsal root leaves its dermatome completely numb and weakens its muscles
scenarios.setup: To relieve severe pain, a surgeon cuts the right L5 dorsal root. The L5 ventral root and the roots above and below are left intact. Compare the right foot with before the operation.
scenarios.start: Right L5 dorsal root cut

steps.blocked: Sensory axons from the L5 dermatome can no longer enter the cord
steps.overlap: Only the overlapping supply from L4 and S1 still reaches that skin
steps.reduced: Sensation over the top of the foot reduced, not lost
steps.ventral: Motor axons leave through the intact ventral root
steps.commands: L5 muscles still receive every command
steps.s1root: The S1 dorsal root is intact
steps.s1skin: The outer edge of the foot reports normally

variables.name: Sensation over the top of the right foot and big toe
variables.why: The L5 dermatome’s sensory axons enter the cord only through the L5 dorsal root. Neighboring dermatomes overlap, so the L4 and S1 roots still supply part of that skin: sensation is reduced rather than lost completely.

variables.name: Strength of ankle dorsiflexion on the right
variables.why: Motor axons leave the cord through the ventral roots, not the dorsal roots. The L5 ventral root was spared, so the muscles that lift the foot still receive their commands.

variables.name: Sensation over the outer edge of the right foot
variables.why: The outer edge of the foot is the S1 dermatome. Its sensory axons enter through the S1 dorsal root, which was not cut.

scenarios.title: A broken humerus injures the radial nerve
scenarios.misconception: a nerve injury in the arm weakens every muscle of the hand
scenarios.setup: A fall breaks the shaft of the right humerus, and the broken edge injures the radial nerve where it spirals around the bone. The median and ulnar nerves are unharmed. Compare the right hand with before the fall.
scenarios.start: Radial nerve injured at mid-humerus

steps.ext: Wrist and finger extensors lose their motor supply
steps.drop: The wrist cannot be lifted: wrist drop
steps.median: The median nerve still supplies most wrist and finger flexors
steps.ulnar: The ulnar nerve still supplies the small muscles inside the hand
steps.spread: The fingers can still spread apart

variables.name: Strength of lifting the right wrist (extension)
variables.why: The radial nerve is the nerve of the back of the arm and forearm and supplies the wrist and finger extensors. Cut off from their motor axons, those muscles cannot contract, so the hand hangs: wrist drop.

variables.name: Strength of curling the right fingers, with the examiner holding the wrist straight
variables.why: Most wrist and finger flexors, on the front of the forearm, are supplied by the median nerve, which the fracture did not touch. (Without that support the drooping wrist makes the grip look weak, although its nerves are intact.)

variables.name: Strength of spreading the right fingers, with the hand resting flat on a table
variables.why: Spreading the fingers uses the small muscles inside the hand, supplied by the ulnar nerve, which runs behind the medial epicondyle, away from the break. (Without that support the drooping wrist makes spreading look weak, although its nerves are intact.)

scenarios.title: The right facial nerve stops working (Bell’s palsy)
scenarios.misconception: the nerve that moves the face also feels it
scenarios.setup: In a woman with Bell’s palsy, the right facial nerve (VII) swells inside its narrow bony canal in the temporal bone, above the point where its taste axons leave it, and stops conducting. The trigeminal nerve and the brain are unharmed. Compare the right side of her face with before.
scenarios.start: Right facial nerve stops conducting

steps.motor: No commands reach the right muscles of facial expression
steps.taste: Taste axons from the front two-thirds of the right tongue are blocked
steps.trig: The trigeminal nerve still carries touch from the face
steps.chew: Trigeminal motor axons still reach the masseter

variables.name: Wrinkling of the right forehead
variables.why: The facial nerve carries the only motor axons to every expression muscle on its side, forehead included. Blocked in its canal, it leaves the whole right half of the face slack, and there is no second route.

variables.name: Strength of closing the right eye
variables.why: The orbicularis oculi, which shuts the lids, is an expression muscle supplied by the facial nerve. Without it the right eye will not close fully.

variables.name: Taste from the front of the right side of the tongue
variables.why: Taste from the front two-thirds of the tongue travels in the facial nerve and leaves it inside the canal, below the swelling here, so those axons are blocked too.

variables.name: Feeling of light touch on the right cheek
variables.why: Touch from the face travels in the trigeminal nerve (the maxillary division for the cheek), not the facial nerve. V feels, VII moves.

variables.name: Strength of clenching the teeth on the right
variables.why: The chewing muscles, such as the masseter, are supplied by the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve, which is working.

scenarios.title: Rising pressure squeezes the right oculomotor nerve
scenarios.misconception: a damaged eye movement nerve leaves the eye unable to move at all
scenarios.setup: After a head injury, rising pressure inside the skull squeezes the right oculomotor nerve (III) until it stops conducting. The trochlear (IV) and abducens (VI) nerves still work. Compare the right eye with before.
scenarios.start: Right oculomotor nerve stops conducting

steps.lidnerve: The muscle that raises the upper lid loses its supply
steps.para: Its parasympathetic axons to the ring of muscle that narrows the pupil are blocked
steps.four: Four of the six eye muscles lose their supply
steps.noin: Nothing turns the eye toward the nose
steps.six: The abducens nerve still drives the muscle that turns the eye out
steps.out: The eye still turns outward, and rests down and out

variables.name: Height of the right upper eyelid
variables.why: The oculomotor nerve supplies the muscle that raises the upper lid. Without its commands the lid droops over the eye.

variables.name: Size of the right pupil
variables.why: Parasympathetic axons riding in the oculomotor nerve drive the ring of muscle that narrows the pupil. With them blocked, the sympathetic side acts unopposed, so the pupil stays wide and ignores light. In a head injury this is an emergency sign.

variables.name: Ability to turn the right eye toward the nose
variables.why: The oculomotor nerve supplies four of the six eye muscles, including the one that turns the eye in. “LR6, SO4, all the rest 3.”

variables.name: Ability to turn the right eye outward
variables.why: The muscle that turns the eye outward is supplied by the abducens nerve (VI), which still works. Pulled only by it and by the trochlear nerve’s muscle, the eye rests turned down and out.

scenarios.title: A firmer press on the fingertip
scenarios.misconception: a stronger stimulus makes bigger action potentials
scenarios.setup: You press on your fingertip lightly, then twice as hard, holding each press for a moment. Compare the firm press with the light one.
scenarios.start: Firmer pressure on the skin

steps.stretch: The membrane of each sensory ending is deformed more
steps.rp: The ending depolarizes more: a larger graded potential
steps.rate: The trigger zone sits further above threshold: faster firing
steps.same: Each action potential stays the same size
steps.higher: Endings with higher thresholds reach threshold

variables.name: Size of the graded depolarization in one sensory ending
variables.why: The depolarization of a sensory ending is graded. More deformation opens more mechanically gated channels, more Na+ flows in, and the ending depolarizes further.

variables.name: Action potentials per second in one sensory neuron
variables.why: A larger graded depolarization holds the trigger zone further above threshold, so the next action potential fires sooner after each refractory period. Strength is coded as frequency.

variables.name: Size of each action potential
variables.why: Action potentials are all-or-none: once threshold is reached, each one is the same size. A stronger stimulus changes how often they fire, never how big they are.

variables.name: Number of sensory neurons firing
variables.why: A stronger press reaches endings farther from the spot and endings with higher thresholds, so more sensory neurons join in. That is the second way strength is coded.

scenarios.title: Disease damages both dorsal columns
scenarios.misconception: damage to one part of the spinal cord removes all feeling below it
scenarios.setup: A disease damages both dorsal columns of the spinal cord in the thoracic region. The spinothalamic tracts, the motor pathways and the peripheral nerves are unharmed. Compare his legs with before.
scenarios.start: Both dorsal columns damaged

steps.blocked: Fine touch, vibration and position signals from both legs cannot climb
steps.vib: Vibration from the feet does not reach the cortex
steps.pos: Toe position does not reach the cortex
steps.st: The spinothalamic tracts still carry pain and temperature
steps.motor: The motor pathways run in other columns and are intact

variables.name: Feeling of a vibrating tuning fork on the big toes
variables.why: Vibration travels in the dorsal column–medial lemniscus pathway. Its first-order axons climb the dorsal columns on their own side, so damage to both columns blocks vibration from both legs.

variables.name: Sense of whether a toe is moved up or down, eyes closed
variables.why: Conscious proprioception also climbs in the dorsal columns, so the brain no longer learns where the toes are.

variables.name: Feeling of a pinprick on the feet
variables.why: Pain travels in the spinothalamic tracts, in the lateral and anterior columns, which the disease spared.

variables.name: Strength of the legs
variables.why: The motor tracts that carry commands to the legs run in other columns of white matter, not the dorsal columns, so strength is normal.

scenarios.title: Pain from the heart felt in the arm
scenarios.misconception: pain felt in the arm means something is wrong with the arm
scenarios.setup: During a heart attack, part of a man’s heart muscle is starved of blood, and its nociceptors fire hard. Nothing is wrong with his arm. Compare with before the attack.
scenarios.start: Heart muscle injured

steps.enter: The heart’s pain axons enter the cord at about T1–T4
steps.conv: They converge on dorsal horn neurons that also receive axons from the skin of the chest and inner arm
steps.climb: Those second-order neurons fire and signal up the spinothalamic tract
steps.assign: The brain assigns the pain to the skin of those dermatomes
steps.quiet: Nociceptors in the arm stay quiet

variables.name: Firing of nociceptors in the heart
variables.why: Injured, oxygen-starved heart muscle releases chemicals that fire its nociceptors.

variables.name: Firing of second-order neurons in the dorsal horn at T1–T4
variables.why: The heart’s pain axons enter at the same segments as axons from the chest wall and inner arm, and converge on the same second-order neurons, which now fire.

variables.name: Pain felt along the inner left arm
variables.why: Those second-order neurons almost always report skin, so the brain places the pain in the matching dermatomes: referred pain.

variables.name: Firing of nociceptors in the skin of the left arm
variables.why: Nothing is damaging the arm. The pain is felt there only because of where the heart’s signals converge in the cord.

scenarios.title: The left half of the spinal cord is cut at T10
scenarios.theme: half the spinal cord is cut at one level
scenarios.misconception: a cord injury on the left causes all its losses on the left
scenarios.setup: A knife wound cuts the left half of the spinal cord at T10. Three weeks later, compare each leg with before the injury.
scenarios.start: Left half of the cord cut at T10

steps.lcst: The left lateral corticospinal tract is cut (it already crossed in the medulla)
steps.noumn: Left leg motor neurons lose their upper motor neuron commands
steps.release: Left cord circuits below the cut lose descending control
steps.ldc: The left dorsal column is cut (it has not crossed yet)
steps.lvib: Vibration and position from the left leg are lost
steps.lst: The left spinothalamic tract is cut: it carries the right leg’s pain
steps.rpain: Pain and temperature from the right leg are lost
steps.rst: The left leg’s pain axons cross to the intact right tract
steps.lpain: The left leg still feels a pinprick
steps.rcst: The right corticospinal tract is intact
steps.rstrong: The right leg keeps its strength

variables.name: Strength of the left leg
variables.why: The lateral corticospinal tract crosses at the pyramidal decussation, so below the medulla the left tract carries commands for the left side. Cut at T10, it leaves the left leg weak.

variables.name: Briskness of the left knee jerk
variables.why: The reflex circuit in the lumbar cord survives, but it has lost the descending control that damps it. After the first floppy phase, the left knee jerk becomes brisk: an upper motor neuron sign.

variables.name: Vibration sense in the left leg
variables.why: Vibration climbs in the dorsal column on the same side and crosses only in the medulla, so the left column carries the left leg’s vibration.

variables.name: Pinprick sensation in the right leg
variables.why: Pain signals from the right leg cross within a segment or two of entry and climb in the left spinothalamic tract, which the knife cut.

variables.name: Pinprick sensation in the left leg
variables.why: The left leg’s pain signals cross near where they enter and climb in the right spinothalamic tract, which is intact.

variables.name: Strength of the right leg
variables.why: The right leg’s commands descend in the right lateral corticospinal tract, on the uninjured side.

scenarios.title: A stroke in the left motor cortex
scenarios.theme: a stroke in the left motor cortex
scenarios.misconception: a stroke weakens the same side of the body and the whole face
scenarios.setup: Loss of blood flow destroys the face and arm areas of the left primary motor cortex. Three weeks later, compare with before the stroke.
scenarios.start: Left face and arm areas of the motor cortex destroyed

steps.umn: Upper motor neurons for the right face and arm are lost
steps.lmnok: Lower motor neurons in the cord survive, released from descending control
steps.brisk: The right biceps tendon jerk becomes brisk
steps.lowerface: The lower face’s facial nucleus gets its input mainly from the opposite hemisphere
steps.droop: The right corner of the mouth droops
steps.bothsides: The forehead’s part of the facial nucleus gets input from both hemispheres
steps.healthy: The lower motor neurons are healthy and do not fire on their own
steps.right: The right hemisphere and its tract are intact

variables.name: Strength of the right arm
variables.why: The corticospinal axons from the left cortex cross at the pyramidal decussation to reach the right side. Damage above the crossing weakens the opposite side.

variables.name: Briskness of the right biceps tendon jerk
variables.why: The reflex circuit in the cervical cord still works but has lost its descending control, so after the early floppy phase the tendon jerk becomes brisk.

variables.name: Movement of the right corner of the mouth
variables.why: The part of the facial nucleus that drives the lower face receives corticobulbar axons mainly from the opposite hemisphere, so losing the left cortex weakens the lower right face.

variables.name: Wrinkling of the right forehead
variables.why: The forehead’s part of the facial nucleus receives corticobulbar axons from both hemispheres, so the right hemisphere still drives it. Forehead sparing marks an upper motor neuron lesion.

variables.name: Visible twitches (fasciculations) in the right arm
variables.why: Fasciculations come from sick lower motor neurons firing on their own. Here the lower motor neurons are healthy; only their upper motor neuron control is gone.

variables.name: Strength of the left arm
variables.why: The left arm is commanded by the right motor cortex, whose axons cross to the left and are untouched.

scenarios.title: Peripheral nerves lose their myelin
scenarios.misconception: most of a reflex’s delay is spent at synapses
scenarios.setup: A disease strips myelin from the large sensory and motor axons of the peripheral nerves, slowing their conduction. The spinal cord and the muscles are healthy. A clinician taps the patellar ligament. Compare with before the illness.
scenarios.start: Myelin lost from peripheral axons

steps.slow: Conduction slows in the spindle sensory axons and the motor axons
steps.longer: More time is spent in the axons
steps.latency: Longer delay from tap to kick
steps.scatter: Signals from the many spindle axons arrive spread out in time
steps.fewer: Fewer motor neurons reach threshold together
steps.ms: The central synapse still adds about 1 ms

variables.name: Conduction velocity in the reflex’s axons
variables.why: Myelin lets the action potential jump from node to node. Without it, current leaks away and conduction slows.

variables.name: Time from tap to kick
variables.why: About four-fifths of the knee jerk’s roughly 23 ms is spent in the axons (time = distance ÷ speed), so slower axons lengthen the delay.

variables.name: Size of the kick
variables.why: Some axons slow more than others, so the burst from the spindles arrives spread out. The motor neurons receive less summed excitation at any moment, fewer reach threshold together, and the reflex weakens or disappears.

variables.name: Time added at the central synapse
variables.why: The disease affects peripheral axons, not the synapse in the ventral horn, which still adds only about a millisecond.

scenarios.title: You step on a tack with your left foot
scenarios.misconception: you must feel the pain before your foot lifts
scenarios.setup: You step on a tack with your left foot. Follow the first fraction of a second, before you feel any pain. Compare with a moment before.
scenarios.start: Tack pierces the left sole

steps.noci: Nociceptors in the left sole fire
steps.inter: Interneurons in several lumbar and sacral segments are excited
steps.lflex: Left flexor motor neurons are excited
steps.lext: Left extensor motor neurons are inhibited
steps.rext: Right extensor motor neurons are excited
steps.rflex: Right flexor motor neurons are inhibited

variables.name: Contraction of the left hip and knee flexors
variables.why: In the withdrawal reflex, interneurons spread the nociceptor signal to the flexor motor neurons of several segments, and the leg bends away from the tack.

variables.name: Contraction of the left quadriceps femoris
variables.why: Inhibitory interneurons silence the extensors of the same limb, so they do not fight the bending.

variables.name: Contraction of the right quadriceps femoris
variables.why: In the crossed-extensor reflex, interneurons that cross the cord excite the extensors of the other leg, which stiffens to take your weight.

variables.name: Contraction of the right hamstrings
variables.why: The same crossing interneurons inhibit the flexors of the supporting leg, so it stays straight.

scenarios.title: A complete spinal cord injury at T6, then two months later
scenarios.misconception: a cut spinal cord leaves the legs floppy for good
scenarios.setup: A diving accident completely cuts the spinal cord at T6, and it never heals. Compare her legs first in the days after the injury, then two months later.

stages.label: The first days
stages.prompt: In the first days after the injury, compared with before it.
stages.start: Cord cut completely at T6

steps.down: Every descending tract to the lower cord is cut
steps.quiet: Circuits below the cut fall silent for days to weeks
steps.nocommand: No commands reach the leg motor neurons
steps.up: Every ascending tract from below is cut
steps.numb: No sensation below the T6 band

variables.name: Muscle tone in the legs
variables.why: Right after a sudden cord injury, the circuits below it go quiet for days to weeks, so the legs are limp: the early floppy phase.

variables.name: Knee jerks
variables.why: In that quiet phase the lumbar reflex arcs, although physically intact, do not respond, so the knee jerks are absent.

variables.name: Voluntary strength of the legs
variables.why: The corticospinal axons for the legs are cut at T6, so no command can reach the lower motor neurons.

variables.name: Pinprick sensation on the legs
variables.why: The spinothalamic tracts carrying pain from the legs are cut, so nothing from below the level reaches the brain.

stages.label: Two months later
stages.prompt: Two months later, compared with those first days. The cord has not healed.
stages.start: Circuits below the cut recover, still cut off from the brain

steps.arcs: Reflex arcs below the cut respond again
steps.brisk: Knee jerks become brisk, sometimes with clonus
steps.stillcut: The descending tracts are still cut
steps.stillup: The ascending tracts are still cut
steps.stillnumb: Still no sensation below the level

variables.name: Muscle tone in the legs
variables.why: The cord’s own circuits recover, but the brainstem motor tracts that normally restrain them are cut, so tone rises above normal: spasticity.

variables.name: Knee jerks
variables.why: The reflex arcs work again with nothing to damp them, so the tendon jerks become brisk: the upper motor neuron picture.

variables.name: Voluntary strength of the legs
variables.why: Recovery of the reflex circuits does not restore the cut corticospinal axons. The legs move by reflex, never on command.

variables.name: Pinprick sensation on the legs
variables.why: The ascending tracts stay cut, so sensation below the level is still absent. A complete injury leaves no sensation in the lowest sacral segments.

scenarios.title: A small stroke in the right side of the pons
scenarios.misconception: weakness of the face and the body always points to the same side of the brain
scenarios.setup: Loss of blood flow damages the right side of the pons, including the right facial nucleus and the corticospinal axons running past it. Compare with before.
scenarios.start: Right side of the pons damaged

steps.nucleus: The right facial nucleus, a lower motor neuron, is destroyed
steps.wholeface: The whole right face is weak, forehead included
steps.cst: Corticospinal axons that have not yet crossed are cut
steps.leftbody: The left arm and leg lose their commands
steps.leftweak: The left arm and leg are weak
steps.release: Left cord circuits lose descending control
steps.rightbody: The right arm and leg’s tract passes in the left pons
steps.rightok: The right arm and leg are normal

variables.name: Wrinkling of the right forehead
variables.why: The facial nucleus is the lower motor neuron for the whole half face. Losing it weakens the forehead too, unlike damage to the cortex, which spares the forehead.

variables.name: Strength of the left arm
variables.why: In the pons the corticospinal axons are still above the pyramidal decussation, so the right side of the pons carries commands for the left body.

variables.name: Briskness of the left knee jerk (weeks later)
variables.why: Cutting the descending axons is upper motor neuron damage, so the left leg’s reflexes become brisk once the early floppy phase passes.

variables.name: Strength of the right arm
variables.why: The commands for the right arm run down the left side of the brainstem, which is undamaged.

scenarios.title: The lens stiffens with age
scenarios.theme: the lens loses flexibility with age
scenarios.misconception: presbyopia happens because the ciliary muscle grows too weak to contract
scenarios.setup: At 52, Dana’s lens has grown stiff. Her eyeball, cornea and ciliary muscle are healthy. Compare her eyes now with her eyes at 25.
scenarios.start: The lens is stiffer

steps.noround: The lens rounds up less when the zonule fibers go slack
steps.less: Less extra bending is added for near objects
steps.farther: The nearest point in focus moves farther away
steps.cm: The ciliary muscle still contracts for near work
steps.parallel: Light from distant objects needs no rounding up
steps.sharp: Distant objects are still in focus

variables.name: Distance of the nearest point she can focus on
variables.why: A near object needs more bending, which comes from the lens rounding up. A stiff lens cannot, so she must hold things farther away to focus them.

variables.name: How much the lens rounds up when she looks at her phone
variables.why: The lens rounds up by its own elasticity when the zonule fibers go slack. With age it keeps adding cells and stiffens, so it barely changes shape.

variables.name: Contraction of the ciliary muscle when she looks at her phone
variables.why: The oculomotor nerve still makes the ciliary muscle contract and the zonule fibers still go slack. The problem is the lens, not the muscle.

variables.name: Sharpness of distant objects
variables.why: Distant objects need the lens at its flattest, with no accommodation, so a stiff lens does not affect far vision.

scenarios.title: A pituitary tumor presses on the optic chiasm
scenarios.misconception: pressure on the optic chiasm blinds one eye
scenarios.setup: A pituitary tumor grows upward and presses on the middle of the optic chiasm. The optic nerves, the optic tracts and the retinas are unharmed. Compare with before.
scenarios.start: The middle of the optic chiasm is squeezed

steps.crossing: The crossing axons from both nasal retinas are blocked
steps.lefttemp: The outer (left) side of the left eye’s field is lost
steps.righttemp: The outer (right) side of the right eye’s field is lost
steps.uncrossed: Uncrossed axons from the temporal retinas pass the edges of the chiasm
steps.inner: The inner half of each eye’s field is still seen
steps.respond: Rods and cones respond normally to light

variables.name: Vision in the outer (left) half of the left eye’s field
variables.why: Light from the outer part of the field lands on the nasal half of the retina, and nasal axons are the ones that cross in the middle of the chiasm, where the tumor presses.

variables.name: Vision in the outer (right) half of the right eye’s field
variables.why: The same crossing fibers carry the right eye’s outer field, so both outer halves are lost: bitemporal hemianopia.

variables.name: Vision in the inner half of each eye’s field
variables.why: The inner field lands on the temporal retina, whose axons stay on their own side at the edges of the chiasm, away from the pressure.

variables.name: Response of the rods and cones to light
variables.why: The damage is behind the eyes. The photoreceptors still respond; their signals are blocked on the way to the brain.

scenarios.title: From a sunny street into a dark cinema
scenarios.misconception: the eyes adjust to the dark within a few seconds
scenarios.setup: You walk from a sunny street into a dark cinema and stay there.

stages.label: The first seconds
stages.prompt: In the first seconds inside, compared with the sunny street.
stages.start: Far less light enters the eyes

steps.dim: Far less light reaches the retinas
steps.drive: Parasympathetic drive to the pupils falls; sympathetic drive rises
steps.bleached: Most rhodopsin is still bleached from the sunlight
steps.norods: Rods cannot yet respond to dim light

variables.name: Pupil diameter
variables.why: In dim light the pupillary light reflex eases off: parasympathetic output to the circular muscle falls and the sympathetic dilator muscle pulls the pupils wider, within a second or so.
