variables.name: Amount of rhodopsin ready to catch light
variables.why: Rebuilding rhodopsin is slow. In the first seconds almost none has been rebuilt, so the amount is as low as it was in the sunlight.

variables.name: Ability to find your seat
variables.why: The light is too dim for cones, and the rods, which could work in dim light, still have too little rhodopsin.

stages.label: After 30 minutes
stages.prompt: After 30 minutes in the dark, compared with those first seconds.
stages.start: Time in the dark

steps.rekink: Retinal gets its kink back in the pigmented epithelium and rejoins opsin
steps.toodim: The light is still too dim for cones
steps.nocolor: Colors are still hard to tell

variables.name: Amount of rhodopsin ready to catch light
variables.why: In the dark, enzymes in the pigmented epithelium put the kink back into retinal, and it rejoins opsin, so rhodopsin builds up over 20 to 30 minutes.

variables.name: Sensitivity of the rods to dim light
variables.why: More rhodopsin means more photons are caught, and with their strong convergence the rods can now signal very faint light: dark adaptation.

variables.name: Ability to find your seat
variables.why: The dark-adapted rods give you night vision, enough to make out the rows.

variables.name: Ability to tell the color of your ticket
variables.why: Rods have only one pigment, so they cannot tell colors apart, and the light is still too dim for the cones. You see shapes in shades of gray.

scenarios.title: A blocked nose at dinner
scenarios.misconception: a cold blocks your sense of taste
scenarios.setup: A bad cold swells the lining of your nose, so air no longer reaches the top of your nose. Your taste buds and olfactory sensory neurons are healthy. You eat a strawberry. Compare with eating one when you are well.
scenarios.start: Air cannot reach the top of the nose

steps.noodor: Odorants cannot reach the olfactory epithelium
steps.unbound: Few odorant receptor proteins are bound
steps.little: The brain gets little smell to combine with taste
steps.reach: Sugars still reach the taste buds

variables.name: Firing of olfactory sensory neurons while you chew
variables.why: Odorants from food normally rise from the mouth up the back of the throat to the olfactory epithelium. Swelling stops them, so few bind their receptor proteins.

variables.name: Strength of the strawberry’s flavor
variables.why: Flavor is taste plus smell, combined by the brain, and most of it is smell. With little smell, the strawberry tastes flat.

variables.name: Ability to tell that it is sweet
variables.why: Sweet is a taste quality, detected by the taste cells of the taste buds, which the blocked nose does not affect.

scenarios.title: Fluid fills the middle ear
scenarios.misconception: any hearing loss means the cochlea is damaged
scenarios.setup: After a head cold, fluid fills six-year-old Aiden’s left middle ear. His cochlea and cochlear nerve are healthy. Compare his left ear with before.
scenarios.start: Fluid fills the left middle ear

steps.damp: The eardrum and ossicles move less
steps.lesspress: Less pressure reaches the oval window
steps.quiet: Sounds through the left ear canal are quieter
steps.bonefork: A fork on the skull shakes the cochlea directly
steps.bypass: Bone conduction bypasses the middle ear
steps.nomask: The left ear no longer hears the room’s background noise
steps.louder: A fork on the forehead sounds louder on the left

variables.name: Vibration of the left eardrum when someone speaks
variables.why: Fluid behind the eardrum weighs it down and resists its movement, so the same sound waves move it less.

variables.name: Loudness of speech heard through the left ear canal
variables.why: The middle ear normally raises the pressure about 20-fold at the oval window. With the chain damped, less of the sound reaches the fluid of the cochlea: a conductive hearing loss.

variables.name: Response of the left cochlea to vibration carried through the skull bone
variables.why: A fork on the bone shakes the whole skull and the cochlea directly, skipping the middle ear. The cochlea is healthy, so it responds normally. The fork may even sound louder on the left, for the same reason as in the Weber test.

variables.name: Loudness in the left ear of a tuning fork placed on the forehead
variables.why: In the Weber test a conductive loss lateralizes to the affected ear: that ear no longer hears the background noise that normally masks the bone-conducted sound, and the blocked route traps the vibration.

scenarios.title: Spinning in an office chair
scenarios.misconception: the semicircular canals report how fast you are turning for as long as you turn
scenarios.setup: You sit upright in an office chair, and a friend spins it steadily with your eyes closed.

stages.label: The first seconds of spinning
stages.prompt: In the first seconds of turning, compared with sitting still.
stages.start: The head starts to turn

steps.turn: The horizontal canals turn with the head
steps.lag: The endolymph lags behind by inertia
steps.bend: The fluid pushes the cupula, bending the stereocilia
steps.fire: Firing of the canal’s sensory neurons rises
steps.utricle: The utricle’s gel is not pulled to one side

variables.name: Bending of the cupula in the horizontal canals
variables.why: The canal turns with your head, but the endolymph lags behind, so it flows through the canal the opposite way and pushes the cupula over.

variables.name: Firing of the sensory neurons of the canal the turn excites
variables.why: Bending the stereocilia toward the tallest ones stretches the tip links and opens channels, so the hair cells release more glutamate and the neurons fire faster.

variables.name: Feeling of turning
variables.why: The vestibular nuclei relay the change in firing through the thalamus to the cortex, and you are aware of the turn even with your eyes closed.

variables.name: Sense of head tilt from the utricle
variables.why: The head stays upright, so gravity does not pull the crystal-weighted gel of the utricle to one side. The maculae report tilt and straight-line movement, not turning.

stages.label: After 30 seconds of steady spinning
stages.prompt: After 30 seconds at the same steady speed, compared with the first seconds.
stages.start: The chair keeps turning at a steady speed

steps.catchup: The endolymph catches up with the canal
steps.rest: Firing returns to its resting rate

variables.name: Bending of the cupula in the horizontal canals
variables.why: After about 20 seconds of steady turning, the fluid moves with the canal, nothing pushes the cupula, and its elasticity returns it upright.

variables.name: Firing of the sensory neurons of the canal the turn excites
variables.why: With the stereocilia straight again, the hair cells return to their resting release, and the neurons to their background rate.

variables.name: Feeling of turning
variables.why: The canals sense changes in turning, not steady turning. With your eyes closed you feel almost still, and when the chair stops, you will feel yourself spin the other way.

variables.name: Actual speed of rotation
variables.why: The chair is still turning just as fast. Only the canals’ signal has faded.

scenarios.title: The right sympathetic chain is damaged in the neck
scenarios.misconception: the sympathetic supply to the head leaves the brain in the cranial nerves
scenarios.setup: A tumor at the top of the right lung damages the right sympathetic chain in the lower neck. Compare the right side of his face with before.
scenarios.start: Right sympathetic chain cut in the lower neck

steps.noclimb: Fibers climbing from T1 to the superior cervical ganglion are cut
steps.dilator: The dilator muscle of the right iris loses its supply
steps.lidmuscle: The small smooth muscle of the right upper lid loses its supply
steps.droop: The right upper lid droops slightly
steps.sweatnerve: Sweat glands on the right of the face lose their supply
steps.dry: The right side of the face stays dry
steps.para: The oculomotor parasympathetic path is intact
steps.narrow: The right pupil still narrows in bright light

variables.name: Size of the right pupil
variables.why: Sympathetic fibers for the head leave the cord at T1 and climb the chain to the superior cervical ganglion. Cut in the neck, the dilator muscle loses its drive, and the parasympathetic sphincter wins.

variables.name: Height of the right upper eyelid
variables.why: A thin sheet of smooth muscle under sympathetic control helps hold the upper lid up. Without it the lid droops a little.

variables.name: Sweating on the right side of the face
variables.why: Sweat glands have only sympathetic fibers. With their chain cut, the right side of the face cannot sweat.

variables.name: Narrowing of the right pupil when a light is shone in
variables.why: Narrowing is driven by parasympathetic fibers in the oculomotor nerve, a completely separate route that the tumor does not touch.

scenarios.title: A beta blocker
scenarios.misconception: a beta blocker blocks all sympathetic effects
scenarios.setup: A man takes metoprolol, a beta blocker that acts mostly on beta-1 receptor proteins. Compare him with before the drug, first at rest and then while he sprints for a bus.
scenarios.start: Beta-1 receptor proteins on the heart are blocked

steps.pace: NE and epinephrine can no longer speed the heart’s pacemaker
steps.rest: At rest, vagal output does most of the work: the rate falls only a little
steps.sprint: The heart rate rises far less during the sprint
steps.calcium: Less calcium enters heart muscle with each beat
steps.beta2: Beta-2 receptor proteins are mostly spared

variables.name: Heart rate at rest
variables.why: Beta-1 receptor proteins let NE and epinephrine bring the heart’s pacemaker tissue to threshold sooner. Blocking them removes that push, but at rest the vagus nerve’s slowing effect dominates, so the rate falls only a little.

variables.name: Heart rate while sprinting
variables.why: Early in exercise the rate rises as vagal output falls, but the climb to high rates depends on NE and epinephrine acting on beta-1 receptor proteins. With those blocked, the heart speeds up much less.

variables.name: Force of each heart contraction
variables.why: Beta-1 activation lets more calcium into heart muscle, strengthening each beat. Blocked, the contractions are weaker.

variables.name: Blood pressure
variables.why: A slower, weaker heart pumps less blood each minute into the same vessels, so pressure falls. That is why beta blockers are used to lower it.

variables.name: Diameter of the small airways
variables.why: Metoprolol acts mostly on beta-1, leaving the airways’ beta-2 receptor proteins free. A drug that blocks beta-2 as well, such as propranolol, can narrow them.

variables.name: Pupil size
variables.why: The dilator muscle of the iris works through alpha-1 receptor proteins, which a beta blocker does not touch.

scenarios.title: Atropine before surgery
scenarios.misconception: atropine blocks every acetylcholine receptor protein, including those on skeletal muscle
scenarios.setup: Before surgery, a patient is given atropine, a muscarinic antagonist. Compare with before the dose.
scenarios.start: Muscarinic receptor proteins are blocked

steps.vagus: Vagal ACh can no longer slow the pacemaker
steps.iris: The circular muscle of the iris cannot respond to ACh
steps.glands: Saliva glands stop responding to ACh
steps.sweatm: The sweat glands’ muscarinic receptor proteins are blocked
steps.nosweat: Sweating falls: the skin is dry and warm
steps.gutm: Gut smooth muscle loses its parasympathetic drive
steps.nic: Nicotinic receptor proteins at neuromuscular junctions are untouched

variables.name: Heart rate
variables.why: At rest, vagal ACh on muscarinic receptor proteins holds the heart well below its own rate. Atropine removes that brake. A dose large enough to block it fully can raise a young adult’s resting rate by 30 beats a minute or more.

variables.name: Pupil size
variables.why: The circular muscle that narrows the pupil is driven by ACh on muscarinic receptor proteins. Blocked, it relaxes, and the sympathetic dilator widens the pupil.

variables.name: Volume of saliva
variables.why: The large volume of watery saliva comes from parasympathetic ACh on muscarinic receptor proteins, which atropine blocks.

variables.name: Sweating
variables.why: Eccrine sweat glands are the oddity: sympathetic fibers drive them with ACh on muscarinic receptor proteins, so atropine blocks sweating too.

variables.name: Movement of the stomach and intestines
variables.why: Parasympathetic ACh on muscarinic receptor proteins speeds the gut. Blocked, gut movement and secretion slow.

variables.name: Strength of skeletal muscle
variables.why: Skeletal muscle responds to ACh through nicotinic receptor proteins at the neuromuscular junction, which atropine does not block.

scenarios.title: An inhaled beta-2 agonist
scenarios.misconception: an inhaled drug acts only on the airways
scenarios.setup: During an attack of airway narrowing, a woman inhales two puffs of albuterol, a beta-2 agonist. Compare the next few minutes with just before the puffs.
scenarios.start: Albuterol reaches the small airways

steps.bind: It activates beta-2 receptor proteins on airway smooth muscle
steps.camp: Cyclic AMP rises and the smooth muscle relaxes
steps.easier: Air moves in and out more easily
steps.absorbed: Some of the drug is absorbed into the blood
steps.muscle: It stimulates beta-2 receptor proteins in skeletal muscle
steps.heart: It also stimulates the heart’s beta receptor proteins a little
steps.noalpha: It has no action on alpha-1 receptor proteins

variables.name: Diameter of the small airways
variables.why: Beta-2 receptor proteins raise cyclic AMP, which in smooth muscle means relaxation. The airway walls are mostly smooth muscle, so they widen.

variables.name: Ease of moving air in and out
variables.why: Wider airways offer less resistance, so the same effort moves more air.

variables.name: Shakiness of the hands
variables.why: Absorbed drug reaches beta-2 receptor proteins in skeletal muscle, which cause a fine tremor: a common side effect.

variables.name: Heart rate
variables.why: Absorbed drug reaches the heart. Its pacemaker tissue carries some beta-2 receptor proteins as well as beta-1, and albuterol is not perfectly selective, so the drug itself nudges the rate up a little. In a severe attack, easing the struggle to breathe can let the rate settle, so the change you see may be small.

variables.name: Pupil size
variables.why: The pupil is widened through alpha-1 receptor proteins on the dilator muscle, which albuterol does not activate.

scenarios.title: A dog lunges from behind a fence
scenarios.misconception: the fright response is carried by nerves alone and ends when the danger does
scenarios.setup: A dog lunges at you from behind a fence. Compare the next minute with a moment before.
scenarios.start: Fear registers in the amygdala

steps.drive: The hypothalamus drives the brainstem and spinal cord
steps.vagus: Vagal output to the heart falls
steps.beta1: Beta-1 receptor proteins speed the pacemaker
steps.dilator: Dilator muscles of the irises contract (alpha-1)
steps.skin: Small arteries in the skin constrict (alpha-1)
steps.palms: Cholinergic sympathetic fibers drive the palms’ sweat glands
steps.adrenal: Preganglionic fibers stimulate the adrenal medulla

variables.name: Heart rate
variables.why: Vagal output falls and sympathetic output rises together, and NE and epinephrine on beta-1 receptor proteins bring the heart’s pacemaker tissue to threshold sooner.

variables.name: Pupil size
variables.why: Sympathetic fibers from the superior cervical ganglion contract the radial dilator muscle through alpha-1 receptor proteins.

variables.name: Blood flow to the skin
variables.why: Vasomotor nerves constrict small arteries in the skin through alpha-1 receptor proteins, so you go pale.

variables.name: Sweating on the palms
variables.why: Sympathetic fibers to eccrine sweat glands release ACh onto muscarinic receptor proteins, so fear makes your palms sweat.

variables.name: Glucose released into the blood by the liver
variables.why: Epinephrine from the adrenal medulla reaches the liver through the blood and, on beta-2 receptor proteins, makes liver cells break glycogen down into glucose.

variables.name: Diameter of the small airways
variables.why: Few sympathetic varicosities reach the airways’ beta-2 receptor proteins, so the widening comes mainly from circulating epinephrine.

variables.name: Movement of the stomach and intestines
variables.why: Sympathetic activity slows gut movement and secretion through alpha and beta receptor proteins, while parasympathetic drive to the gut falls.

scenarios.title: A transplanted heart without its nerves
scenarios.misconception: the heart needs its nerves to beat
scenarios.setup: A woman has a heart transplant. The autonomic nerves to the new heart were cut and have not regrown. Compare her new heart with a heart whose nerves are intact.
scenarios.start: The heart’s autonomic nerves are cut

steps.novagal: No vagal tone reaches the pacemaker
steps.ownrate: The pacemaker beats at its own rate
steps.faster: Resting rate about 90 to 110 a minute
steps.atropine: Atropine has no vagal ACh to block
steps.epi: The rate rises only as epinephrine arrives in the blood, over minutes
steps.slowrise: A slow rise at the start of exercise
steps.intrinsic: The heart’s pacemaker fires on its own

variables.name: Resting heart rate
variables.why: Normally vagal tone holds the heart 20 to 40 beats a minute below its own rate. With the vagus cut, the pacemaker runs at its intrinsic rate, around 100.

variables.name: Rise in heart rate after a dose of atropine
variables.why: Atropine speeds a normal heart by blocking vagal ACh. With no vagal fibers, there is nothing for it to block.

variables.name: Speed of the heart rate rise in the first seconds of exercise
variables.why: A normal heart speeds up within seconds as vagal output falls and sympathetic output rises. The transplanted heart must wait for epinephrine from the adrenal medulla to arrive in the blood.

variables.name: Ability of the heart to keep beating
variables.why: Autonomic nerves only adjust the rate. The heart’s own pacemaker starts each beat by itself, which is why cutting its nerves does not stop it.

scenarios.title: The first dose of an alpha-1 blocker
scenarios.misconception: blocking alpha-1 receptor proteins shuts down the entire blood pressure reflex
scenarios.setup: A man takes his first dose of prazosin, an alpha-1 antagonist, and then stands up. Follow the next minute.

stages.label: As the drug takes hold
stages.prompt: As the drug takes effect, before any reflex response, compared with before the dose.
stages.start: Alpha-1 receptor proteins on vessel smooth muscle are blocked

steps.notone: Sympathetic tone can no longer keep small arteries partly constricted
steps.lessstretch: The walls of the large arteries are stretched less

variables.name: Diameter of small arteries in the skin
variables.why: Sympathetic tone normally keeps these vessels partly constricted through alpha-1 receptor proteins. Blocking them removes the tone, and the vessels widen.

variables.name: Blood pressure
variables.why: Wider vessels offer less resistance, so pressure in the large arteries falls, especially on standing.

variables.name: Firing of stretch-sensitive sensory receptors in the large arteries
variables.why: These sensory receptors fire in proportion to how far the artery wall is stretched, and lower pressure stretches it less.

stages.label: Seconds later, with the reflex running
stages.prompt: Seconds later, once the blood pressure reflex has responded, compared with the moment the pressure fell.
stages.start: Fewer signals reach the medulla oblongata

steps.medulla: The medulla oblongata cuts vagal output and raises sympathetic output
steps.vagal: Vagal output to the heart falls
steps.beta1: Beta-1 receptor proteins on the heart still work
steps.partial: Blood pressure recovers part of the way
steps.blocked: Alpha-1 receptor proteins are still blocked

variables.name: Vagal output to the heart
variables.why: Less input from the stretch-sensitive sensory receptors tells the medulla oblongata the pressure is low, and it turns vagal tone down.

variables.name: Heart rate
variables.why: Less vagal tone and more sympathetic output act on the heart through muscarinic and beta-1 receptor proteins, which prazosin does not block, so the heart speeds up.

variables.name: Blood pressure
variables.why: A faster, stronger heart pushes pressure back up, but only part of the way, so he may still feel dizzy on standing after that first dose.

variables.name: Diameter of small arteries in the skin
variables.why: The medulla sends more sympathetic output to the vessels, but NE cannot act on blocked alpha-1 receptor proteins, so the vessels stay wide.

scenarios.title: Losing plasma water on a hot day
scenarios.misconception: a higher hematocrit always means more red blood cells
scenarios.setup: A runner sweats out 2 L of water on a hot afternoon and drinks nothing. She loses no blood. Predict her blood at the end of the run, compared with before it.
scenarios.start: Water leaves the plasma as sweat

steps.hct: Red cells make up a larger share of each sample: hematocrit rises
steps.visc: More cells in each milliliter: blood is more viscous

variables.name: Plasma volume
variables.why: Sweat is drawn from the interstitial fluid, which is refilled from the plasma, so the plasma loses water.

variables.name: Total volume of red cells in her body
variables.why: No blood left her body and the red cells do not leave the vessels in sweat, so she has the same red cells as before.

variables.name: Hematocrit
variables.why: The hematocrit is a ratio: red cell volume divided by blood volume. The same red cells now sit in less plasma, so they make up a larger share of each sample. This is a relative rise, not a gain in cells.

variables.name: Blood viscosity
variables.why: Most of blood’s viscosity comes from its red cells. More cells per milliliter make the blood thicker, so it meets more resistance to flow.

scenarios.title: The liver makes too little albumin
scenarios.misconception: plasma proteins leak out of the blood with the water
scenarios.setup: Years of liver damage have cut the liver’s albumin output in half. Predict the state of her blood and tissues, compared with when her liver was healthy.
scenarios.start: The liver makes less albumin

steps.pull: Less solute held back in the plasma: its osmotic pull falls
steps.out: Less water is held in the blood; more leaves for the tissues
steps.wbc: Gamma globulins come from white blood cells, not the liver

variables.name: Plasma albumin concentration
variables.why: The liver makes albumin. With half the output, the plasma concentration falls.

variables.name: Osmotic pull of the plasma on water
variables.why: Albumin cannot cross the capillary wall, so it is a solute the barrier holds back. It supplies most of the plasma’s osmotic pull because it is the most abundant plasma protein. Less albumin, less pull.

variables.name: Water moving from the blood into the tissues
variables.why: Water follows solute. With less albumin holding water in the blood, more of it stays out in the tissues.

variables.name: Swelling of her tissues
variables.why: Extra water collects between the cells of the tissues, which swell, most visibly in the legs and abdomen.

variables.name: Gamma globulins in her plasma
variables.why: Gamma globulins are made by white blood cells, not the liver, so liver damage does not directly cut their supply.

scenarios.title: Six weeks in a mountain town
scenarios.theme: living at high altitude, red cell count over weeks
scenarios.misconception: the bone marrow senses low oxygen and speeds up on its own
scenarios.setup: A student moves from sea level to a town at 3,800 m and stays. Predict her blood after six weeks, compared with her first day in the town.
scenarios.start: Each breath brings in less oxygen

steps.load: Blood leaves the lungs carrying less oxygen
steps.kidney: Less oxygen reaches the kidney tissue
steps.epo: Kidney cells release more EPO, peaking in the first one to two days
steps.marrow: More erythroid precursors survive, divide and mature
steps.rbc: Red cell count and hemoglobin climb over the weeks
steps.carry: Each liter of blood carries more oxygen
steps.air: The thin air at 3,800 m has not changed

variables.name: Red blood cell count
variables.why: The sensors are kidney cells, not the marrow. Less oxygen reaching them raises EPO within hours. EPO lets more erythroid precursors survive and mature, and new red cells keep arriving for weeks.

variables.name: Hemoglobin concentration (g/dL)
variables.why: Every new red cell is filled with hemoglobin, so more red cells in each deciliter means more hemoglobin in each deciliter.

variables.name: Hematocrit
variables.why: More red cells make up a larger share of each spun sample, so the red column in the tube is taller.

variables.name: Oxygen carried by each liter of arterial blood
variables.why: Each hemoglobin carries up to four oxygen molecules. More hemoglobin per liter carries more oxygen, even though each breath still brings in thin air. That is the response that eases the stimulus: negative feedback.

variables.name: Blood viscosity
variables.why: Red cells supply most of blood’s viscosity, so a higher hematocrit makes the blood thicker. This is the cost of the adjustment.

variables.name: Oxygen in each breath of air
variables.why: She is still at 3,800 m. The adjustment happens in her blood, not in the air, which holds as little oxygen as on her first day.

scenarios.title: Arriving at altitude: EPO first, red cells later
scenarios.misconception: EPO stays at its peak for as long as you stay at altitude
scenarios.setup: A climber flies from sea level to a research station at 4,300 m and stays for six weeks. Follow her EPO and red cells.

stages.label: After two days
stages.prompt: Two days after arrival, compared with sea level.
stages.start: Each breath brings in less oxygen

steps.load: Blood leaves the lungs carrying less oxygen
steps.kidney: Less oxygen reaches the kidney tissue
steps.gene: In the kidney cells, the factor that switches on the EPO gene survives
steps.epo: EPO in the blood climbs to its peak
steps.lag: Precursors need 3–5 days to release reticulocytes
steps.mass: No new red cells have reached the blood yet

variables.name: Oxygen reaching the kidney tissue
variables.why: Thinner air loads less oxygen into the blood in the lungs, so less of it is delivered to every tissue, the kidneys included.

variables.name: EPO in the blood
variables.why: In low oxygen, a transcription factor that is normally destroyed within minutes survives and switches on the EPO gene. EPO rises within hours and peaks at about one to two days.

variables.name: Total number of red cells in her body
variables.why: EPO acts on precursors in the marrow, and it takes 3–5 days before extra reticulocytes pour out. Two days in, the red cells in her blood are still the ones she arrived with.

stages.label: Six weeks later
stages.prompt: Six weeks after arrival, compared with day two. She is still at 4,300 m.
stages.start: Weeks of faster red cell production

steps.retic: Reticulocytes keep pouring out and maturing
steps.more: Total red cells and hemoglobin rise
steps.carry: Each liter of blood carries more oxygen
steps.kidney: More oxygen reaches the kidney tissue again

variables.name: Total number of red cells in her body
variables.why: Each day since day three or so, the marrow has released more new red cells than old ones were destroyed, so the total has climbed.

variables.name: Oxygen carried by each liter of arterial blood
variables.why: More hemoglobin in each liter means more iron sites to bind oxygen, so each liter carries more even though the air is just as thin.

variables.name: Oxygen reaching the kidney tissue
variables.why: Blood that carries more oxygen delivers more of it to the kidneys. The stimulus that started the loop has shrunk.

variables.name: EPO in the blood
variables.why: As oxygen delivery to the kidney cells recovers, they release less EPO, so it eases back from its early peak toward its sea-level value. The response has reduced the stimulus: negative feedback.

variables.name: Blood viscosity
variables.why: More red cells in each milliliter make the blood thicker.

scenarios.title: A sudden bleed: the hematocrit over days
scenarios.misconception: the hematocrit falls the moment blood is lost
scenarios.setup: A cyclist loses about 1 L of blood from a deep cut in her thigh before the bleeding is stopped. She gets no transfusion and no fluid through a drip.

stages.label: Right after the bleed
stages.prompt: Just after the bleeding stops, compared with before the injury.
stages.start: About 1 L of whole blood is lost

steps.whole: Cells and plasma leave together, in their usual proportion
steps.ratio: The share of red cells in what is left is unchanged
steps.total: Fewer red cells in her body in total

variables.name: Blood volume
variables.why: A liter of whole blood has left the vessels, about a fifth of her blood.

variables.name: Hematocrit
variables.why: The hematocrit is a ratio. Whole blood carries cells and plasma out in their usual proportion, so the blood left behind has the same share of red cells.

variables.name: Hemoglobin concentration (g/dL)
variables.why: Each deciliter of the blood that remains holds the same number of red cells as before, so it holds the same hemoglobin.

variables.name: Total number of red cells in her body
variables.why: The red cells in the lost liter are gone. The ratio hides this loss for now.

stages.label: Four days later
stages.prompt: Four days later, compared with just after the bleed.
stages.start: Fluid moves in and the marrow responds

steps.fluid: Fluid moves into the blood from the tissues
steps.dilute: The remaining red cells are spread through more plasma
steps.kidney: Less oxygen reaches the kidney tissue
steps.retic: The marrow releases reticulocytes from day 3–5

variables.name: Blood volume
variables.why: Over the hours after a bleed, fluid moves from the tissues into the blood, refilling the vessels.

variables.name: Hematocrit
variables.why: The new fluid is plasma without cells. The same reduced number of red cells now sits in a refilled volume, so their share falls: about 36% if 1 L of 5 L was lost at a starting value of 45%.

variables.name: EPO in the blood
variables.why: Diluted blood carries less oxygen per liter, so less reaches the kidney cells, and they release more EPO. EPO peaked a day or two after the bleed and is now easing back, but on day four it is still above its level just after the bleed.

variables.name: Reticulocyte count
variables.why: EPO speeds the maturation of erythroid precursors, and after 3–5 days extra reticulocytes appear. A healthy marrow facing blood loss speeds up, which is why the count rises in hemorrhagic anemia.

scenarios.title: Failing kidneys and the red cell count
scenarios.theme: chronic kidney disease and red cell count
scenarios.misconception: anemia makes you breathe faster at rest because your blood oxygen sensors fire
scenarios.setup: A 60-year-old’s kidneys have been failing slowly for years. Her marrow is healthy and her iron, vitamin B12 and folate are normal. Predict her state compared with before her kidneys failed.
scenarios.start: Kidney tissue is scarred and lost

steps.cells: Fewer EPO-making cells in the kidney tissue
steps.epo: EPO stays low even when oxygen delivery falls
steps.marrow: Erythroid precursors get too little EPO signal
steps.rbc: Red cell count and hemoglobin fall: anemia
steps.build: Iron, B12 and folate are available, so each cell is built normally
steps.deliver: Less oxygen delivered to working muscles
steps.acid: On exertion, muscles lean on glycolysis sooner and release acid
steps.breathe: The acid drives faster breathing on exertion
steps.dissolved: Dissolved oxygen in arterial blood stays normal, so the oxygen sensors are not triggered
steps.pale: Less red pigment in the skin’s vessels

variables.name: EPO in the blood
variables.why: The cells that sense oxygen and release EPO sit in the kidney tissue. When that tissue is lost, EPO stays low even though oxygen delivery has fallen: the loop cannot respond.

variables.name: Reticulocyte count
variables.why: Without enough EPO, fewer erythroid precursors survive and mature, so the marrow releases fewer reticulocytes. The low count shows the problem is making cells, not losing them.

variables.name: Hemoglobin concentration
variables.why: Red cells still wear out after about 120 days, but fewer replace them, so red cells and hemoglobin fall. This is the anemia of kidney failure, treated with injected EPO.

variables.name: Size of each red cell
variables.why: The marrow has what it needs to build each cell: iron for heme and B12 and folate for DNA. It simply gets too little signal to make enough of them, so the cells are normal in size.

variables.name: Breathing rate during a brisk walk
variables.why: Less hemoglobin delivers less oxygen to working muscle. The muscle leans on glycolysis sooner and releases acid, and the acid drives faster breathing.

variables.name: Breathing rate at rest
variables.why: Your blood’s oxygen sensors respond to the pressure of dissolved oxygen, which stays normal in anemia because the lungs load the blood normally. At rest there is little acid from muscle, so breathing does not speed up.

variables.name: Paleness of her skin and nail beds
variables.why: Hemoglobin is the red pigment of blood. With less of it in the skin’s vessels, skin, lips and nail beds look pale.

scenarios.title: Two years of heavy periods
scenarios.misconception: iron-deficiency anemia is a marrow that has stopped making cells
scenarios.setup: A 30-year-old has had heavy periods for two years, losing a little more iron each month than she absorbs from food. Her iron stores are now empty. Predict her blood, compared with two years ago.
scenarios.start: Iron lost each month exceeds iron absorbed

steps.leak: Less ferritin leaks into the plasma
steps.heme: Too little iron to make heme
steps.small: Erythroblasts keep dividing but cannot fill with hemoglobin: small, pale cells
steps.retic: Without iron the marrow cannot speed up: reticulocytes stay low

variables.name: Plasma ferritin
variables.why: Ferritin is the iron store inside cells, and a little leaks into plasma in proportion to the store. A low plasma ferritin is the sign that the stores are empty.

variables.name: Size of each new red cell
variables.why: Without enough iron, erythroblasts keep dividing but cannot fill their cytoplasm with hemoglobin, so the cells come out small and pale.

variables.name: Hemoglobin concentration
variables.why: Each new cell holds less hemoglobin, so each deciliter of blood holds less.

variables.name: Reticulocyte count, compared with a healthy marrow facing the same blood loss
variables.why: A marrow with plenty of iron would speed up after blood loss. Without iron, it cannot build extra cells, so the reticulocyte count stays low.

scenarios.title: Red cells destroyed early
scenarios.misconception: all jaundice turns the urine dark
scenarios.setup: An inherited defect makes a man’s red cells fragile, and macrophages destroy them after about 15 days instead of 120. His marrow and liver are healthy. Predict his blood and urine, compared with a healthy person.
scenarios.start: Red cells are destroyed eight times faster

steps.heme: Much more heme is broken down each day
steps.bili: More unconjugated bilirubin enters the plasma than the liver can handle
steps.insol: Unconjugated bilirubin rides on albumin and cannot enter urine
steps.fewer: Red cells are lost faster than they are made
steps.epo: Less oxygen reaches the kidneys: EPO rises
steps.retic: The healthy marrow speeds up: reticulocytes rise

variables.name: Unconjugated bilirubin in the plasma
variables.why: Every destroyed red cell’s heme becomes bilirubin. When cells are destroyed faster than the liver can conjugate their bilirubin, unconjugated bilirubin builds up: jaundice from before the liver.

variables.name: Yellowness of the whites of his eyes
variables.why: Bilirubin building up in the blood stains the tissues yellow, and it shows first in the sclera.

variables.name: Bilirubin in his urine
variables.why: Only conjugated bilirubin dissolves in water and can spill into urine. The extra bilirubin here is unconjugated and travels bound to albumin, so the urine is normally colored.

variables.name: Hemoglobin concentration
variables.why: A healthy marrow can speed up several times over, but an eightfold faster loss is more than it can fully match, so red cells and hemoglobin settle lower: a hemolytic anemia.

variables.name: Reticulocyte count
variables.why: A healthy marrow facing early destruction gets more EPO and responds, so reticulocytes rise. That is what separates losing or destroying cells from failing to make them.

scenarios.title: A gallstone blocks the flow of bile
scenarios.misconception: jaundice always means red cells are being destroyed
scenarios.setup: A gallstone lodges in the duct that carries bile to the intestine and blocks it completely. Her red cells and liver cells are healthy. Predict the state after a week, compared with before.
scenarios.start: Bile cannot drain into the intestine

steps.back: Conjugated bilirubin backs up into the blood
steps.urine: Water-soluble conjugated bilirubin spills into urine
steps.sterco: No stercobilin forms: pale, clay-colored feces
steps.rbc: Red cells still last about 120 days

variables.name: Conjugated bilirubin in the plasma
variables.why: The liver still takes up and conjugates bilirubin, but cannot get it out in bile. The conjugated form backs up into the blood: jaundice from after the liver.

variables.name: Yellowness of the whites of her eyes
variables.why: Bilirubin building up in the blood stains the tissues yellow, first in the sclera.

variables.name: Darkness of her urine
variables.why: Conjugated bilirubin dissolves in water, so the kidneys can excrete it, and it darkens the urine.

variables.name: Brown color of her feces
variables.why: Intestinal bacteria make brown stercobilin from bilirubin that arrives in bile. With none arriving, no stercobilin forms and the feces are pale.

variables.name: Rate at which her red cells are destroyed
variables.why: The block is in the drainage of bile, after the liver. Nothing has changed the lifespan of her red cells.

scenarios.title: A sickle cell crisis
scenarios.misconception: sickled cells cause harm only by being too few
scenarios.setup: A teenager with sickle cell disease has a stomach bug, becomes dehydrated and spends a cold night outdoors. Predict the next day, compared with his usual state.
scenarios.start: Dehydration crowds HbS together, and cold slows blood through chilled small vessels, where HbS gives up its oxygen

steps.patch: Deoxygenated HbS shows a sticky patch on its surface
steps.fibers: HbS molecules line up into long, stiff fibers
steps.sickle: Red cells bend into rigid sickles
steps.flow: Tissue downstream is starved of oxygen
steps.bili: More heme broken down: bilirubin rises

variables.name: Share of his red cells that are sickled
variables.why: When HbS gives up oxygen, the valine in place of glutamic acid forms a sticky patch. The molecules stick together into stiff fibers that bend the cell into a sickle. Crowding the HbS, as dehydration does, speeds this up.

variables.name: Blood flow through his small vessels
variables.why: A rigid sickle cannot fold to pass single file through a capillary, so sickled cells jam the small vessels.

variables.name: Pain
variables.why: Tissue beyond the jammed vessels is starved of oxygen, which causes the severe pain of a crisis.

variables.name: Bilirubin in his plasma
variables.why: Sickled cells are destroyed early. Every destroyed cell’s heme becomes bilirubin, so bilirubin rises and jaundice can follow.

scenarios.title: A bacterial infection
scenarios.misconception: a lower lymphocyte percentage always means fewer lymphocytes
scenarios.setup: A man develops a bacterial infection in a cut on his leg and a fever. Predict his blood count, compared with a week ago when he was well.
scenarios.start: Bacteria multiply in the tissue

steps.signal: Chemical signals from the infected tissue reach the marrow
steps.release: The marrow releases more neutrophils, some before their nucleus has lobed
steps.share: Neutrophils take a larger share of the count
steps.lymph: Lymphocytes are not driven up by a bacterial infection

variables.name: Total white blood cell count
variables.why: Neutrophils are the largest share of white cells, so a big rise in them raises the total above 11,000 per µL: leukocytosis.

variables.name: Absolute neutrophil count
variables.why: Neutrophils are the first white cells to arrive at a bacterial infection. The marrow releases its reserve and speeds production.

variables.name: Band cells in the blood
variables.why: In a serious bacterial infection the marrow releases neutrophils early, before the nucleus has finished lobing. These young band cells rise on the count.

variables.name: Lymphocytes as a percentage of white cells
variables.why: A percentage is a share. When neutrophils rise a lot, every other type becomes a smaller share, even if its own number is unchanged.

variables.name: Absolute lymphocyte count
variables.why: Lymphocytes rise mainly in viral infections. Multiply the lower percentage by the higher total and the absolute count comes out about the same, which is why you always check absolute counts.

scenarios.title: Ten days after chemotherapy
scenarios.misconception: chemotherapy lowers every blood cell at the same rate
scenarios.setup: A woman receives chemotherapy that kills dividing cells, including those in her marrow. Predict her blood ten days later, compared with before treatment.
scenarios.start: Dividing marrow cells are killed

steps.stop: Few new blood cells are made for a while
steps.short: Neutrophils circulate for less than a day and are not replaced
steps.plt: Platelets live 7–10 days and are not replaced
steps.bleed: Small vessels leak: bruises and petechiae
steps.retic: Reticulocytes last about a day in the blood and are not replaced

variables.name: Absolute neutrophil count
variables.why: Neutrophils survive only a day or two, so without new production their count falls within days, often below 500 per µL.

variables.name: Risk of a serious bacterial infection
variables.why: Neutrophils are the first defense against bacteria. With too few, bacteria that would normally be engulfed can spread.

variables.name: Platelet count
variables.why: Platelets are removed after 7–10 days. By day ten most of those in the blood before treatment are gone, and few new ones replace them.

variables.name: Easy bruising and pinpoint skin bleeds
variables.why: Too few platelets cannot seal the tiny breaks that happen every day in small vessels, so single capillaries bleed into the skin as petechiae.

variables.name: Reticulocyte count
variables.why: Each reticulocyte matures within a day or two in the blood. With few new ones released, the count falls quickly, even though the red cells themselves last much longer.

scenarios.title: A newborn without vitamin K
scenarios.misconception: vitamin K deficiency stops platelets from working
scenarios.setup: A baby is born at home, is breastfed only, and is not given the vitamin K injection at birth. At three weeks she oozes blood from a heel-prick site and bruises easily. Compare her blood with that of a baby who had the injection.
scenarios.start: Very little vitamin K in the baby

steps.low: Little vitamin K reached her before birth, and breast milk holds little
steps.liver: Her liver makes II, VII, IX and X without their extra acid groups
steps.calcium: These factors cannot bind calcium or attach to phospholipid surfaces
steps.work: Too little working II, VII, IX and X
steps.thrombin: Less thrombin made at an injury
steps.pt: The extrinsic and common pathways run slowly: PT is long
steps.aptt: The intrinsic pathway needs IX and X too: aPTT is long
steps.plt: Making platelets does not need vitamin K
steps.fib: Fibrinogen does not need vitamin K

variables.name: Working factor VII in her plasma
variables.why: The liver needs vitamin K to add the extra acid groups that let II, VII, IX and X bind calcium. Without them, the proteins are made but do not work.

variables.name: Thrombin made at a small cut
variables.why: Factors that cannot attach to cell and platelet surfaces cannot build the burst of thrombin, so less fibrin forms.

variables.name: Prothrombin time (PT)
variables.why: The PT tests the extrinsic and common pathways, which use VII, X and II. With those factors not working, the sample takes longer to clot.

variables.name: aPTT
variables.why: The aPTT tests the intrinsic and common pathways, which use IX, X and II. It lengthens too, though usually less than the PT.

variables.name: Platelet count
variables.why: Vitamin K is needed to finish clotting factors in the liver, not to make platelets. Her platelet plugs form normally; the fibrin that should reinforce them is what is missing.

variables.name: Fibrinogen level
variables.why: Fibrinogen (factor I) is not one of the vitamin K–dependent factors, so its level is normal.

scenarios.title: A week on warfarin
scenarios.misconception: anticoagulants dissolve clots that have already formed
scenarios.setup: A 70-year-old with a clot in a deep leg vein starts warfarin tablets. Predict his state after a week on a steady dose, compared with before the first tablet.
scenarios.start: Warfarin blocks the liver enzyme that recycles vitamin K

steps.k: Too little active vitamin K in the liver
steps.made: II, VII, IX and X are made in a non-working form
steps.used: Working factors already in the blood are used up over 3–5 days
steps.thr: Less thrombin is made, so the clot stops growing
steps.lysis: Fibrinolysis runs at its usual pace

variables.name: INR
variables.why: Warfarin is monitored with the PT, reported as the INR, because the PT tests VII, X and II. A usual target is 2–3.

variables.name: Working factors II, VII, IX and X
variables.why: The liver keeps making the proteins, but without recycled vitamin K they lack the calcium-binding groups. Working factors fall over 3–5 days as the old ones are used up, which is why warfarin is slow to act.

variables.name: Growth of the clot in his leg vein
variables.why: Less thrombin means less new fibrin, so the clot stops growing and new clots are less likely.

variables.name: Platelet count
variables.why: Warfarin acts on clotting factors made in the liver. It does not touch the marrow’s megakaryocytes.

variables.name: Rate at which the existing clot is broken down
variables.why: Warfarin does not dissolve a clot. Plasmin made on the clot breaks it down at its usual pace while warfarin stops it from growing.

scenarios.title: Daily low-dose aspirin
scenarios.misconception: aspirin works by lowering the platelet count
scenarios.setup: A man takes a low-dose aspirin tablet every day for two weeks. Predict his hemostasis, compared with before he started.
scenarios.start: Aspirin permanently blocks cyclooxygenase in platelets

steps.time: A small cut bleeds for longer

variables.name: Thromboxane A2 made by his platelets
variables.why: Cyclooxygenase is the platelet enzyme that makes thromboxane A2. A platelet has no nucleus and can make almost no new enzyme, so the block lasts for the platelet’s life.

variables.name: Platelet aggregation at a cut
variables.why: Thromboxane A2 is one of the chemicals by which activated platelets activate passing ones. With less of it, the positive feedback that builds the plug is weaker.

variables.name: Time a small cut takes to stop bleeding
variables.why: A weaker, slower plug seals small breaks less quickly, so small cuts ooze longer.

variables.name: Platelet count
variables.why: Aspirin changes what platelets do, not how many there are.

variables.name: Prothrombin time (PT)
variables.why: The PT adds tissue factor and phospholipid to plasma. It does not depend on platelets, and aspirin does not change the clotting factors.

scenarios.title: A knock to the knee in hemophilia A
scenarios.misconception: in hemophilia the platelet plug cannot form
scenarios.setup: A 9-year-old boy with hemophilia A (no working factor VIII) bumps his knee hard on a table. Compare what happens in the injured knee with what would happen in a boy with normal clotting.
scenarios.start: Small vessels inside the knee joint tear

steps.plug: Platelets stick to exposed collagen and form a plug as usual
steps.tf: Tissue factor with VIIa makes a first trickle of thrombin as usual
steps.stop: The tissue factor–VIIa pair is switched off within seconds
steps.noviii: Without VIIIa, IXa cannot activate X fast on the platelet surface
steps.burst: Little thrombin burst: too little fibrin
steps.bleed: The soft plug gives way: bleeding into the joint

variables.name: Platelet plug formation
variables.why: Platelet adhesion and aggregation do not need factor VIII, so the plug forms. Platelet problems cause skin and mucous membrane bleeding; his problem comes later.

variables.name: The first trickle of thrombin on tissue factor cells
variables.why: Initiation uses tissue factor, VIIa, X and V, none of which he lacks, so clotting starts normally.

variables.name: The burst of thrombin on the platelet surface
variables.why: Once the tissue factor–VIIa pair is switched off, X is activated mainly by IXa with VIIIa on the platelet surface. Without VIII there is no burst, which is exactly what the cell-based model explains.

variables.name: Bleeding into the knee joint over the next hours
variables.why: Without enough fibrin to reinforce it, the soft plug gives way. Deep bleeding into joints and muscles, often starting again hours later, is the pattern of a clotting factor problem.

variables.name: aPTT
variables.why: In the lab model, VIII is part of the intrinsic pathway, which the aPTT tests.

variables.name: PT
variables.why: The PT tests the extrinsic and common pathways (VII, X, V, II, I), which do not use VIII.

scenarios.title: A type A patient receives type B blood
scenarios.theme: a type A patient receives type B blood
scenarios.misconception: a transfusion reaction is the donor blood clotting
scenarios.setup: Because of a labeling error, a type A positive patient is given a unit of type B positive red cells. Predict the next few hours, compared with just before the transfusion.
scenarios.start: Red cells carrying B antigen enter plasma that holds anti-B

steps.bind: Her anti-B binds the B antigens on the donor cells within seconds
steps.agg: Antibodies bridge donor cells into clumps
steps.lyse: Bound antibodies switch on plasma proteins that punch holes: donor cells burst
steps.free: Hemoglobin is released into the plasma
steps.urine: Free hemoglobin spills into the urine
steps.bili: Its heme is converted to bilirubin
steps.signal: The antibody attack releases chemical signals

variables.name: Agglutination of the donor red cells
variables.why: Everyone with type A blood has anti-B in their plasma from infancy, without any earlier transfusion. Each antibody has several binding sites and links B antigens on neighboring cells.

variables.name: Donor red cells surviving in her blood
variables.why: After agglutination, the bound antibodies switch on other plasma proteins that punch holes in the red cell membranes, and the donor cells burst inside her vessels.

variables.name: Red-brown color of her urine
variables.why: Hemoglobin released from burst cells is small enough to spill into the urine, turning it red or dark brown.

variables.name: Plasma bilirubin
variables.why: The heme from the released hemoglobin is broken down to bilirubin, faster than the liver can handle, so jaundice can follow.

variables.name: Body temperature
variables.why: The antibody attack releases chemical signals that cause fever and chills.

variables.name: Blood pressure
variables.why: The same signals cause a fall in blood pressure that can lead to shock, which is why the transfusion is stopped at once.

scenarios.title: An Rh-negative mother’s second Rh-positive baby
scenarios.misconception: the first Rh-positive baby is the one at risk
scenarios.setup: An Rh-negative woman was not given anti-D immune globulin after her first baby, who was Rh positive. She is now late in a second pregnancy with another Rh-positive fetus. Compare this pregnancy with one in which she had been given the injection.
scenarios.start: At the first birth, fetal Rh-positive cells entered her blood

steps.made: Her immune system made its own anti-D over the following weeks
steps.cross: Her anti-D is the kind that crosses to the fetus
steps.bind: Anti-D binds the fetus’s Rh-positive red cells
steps.blasts: Fetal marrow and liver pour out still-nucleated erythroblasts
steps.bili: After birth, bilirubin climbs faster than the baby’s liver can clear it
steps.own: Her own red cells carry no D antigen

variables.name: Anti-D in the mother’s plasma
variables.why: An Rh-negative person makes anti-D only after exposure to Rh-positive cells. The first birth exposed her, and without the injection to clear those cells, she was sensitized.

variables.name: Fetal red cell count
variables.why: Her anti-D crosses to the fetus, binds its Rh-positive cells and they are destroyed faster than the fetus can replace them.

variables.name: Nucleated erythroblasts in the fetus’s blood
variables.why: Anemia drives the fetal marrow and liver so hard that immature, still-nucleated cells are released: the reason for the old name erythroblastosis fetalis.

variables.name: The baby’s bilirubin in the days after birth
variables.why: Before birth the mother’s liver clears the bilirubin. After birth the baby’s immature liver cannot keep up with the destroyed cells, so bilirubin climbs fast.

variables.name: The mother’s own red cell count
variables.why: Anti-D binds only cells that carry the D antigen. Her own cells are Rh negative, so they are untouched.

scenarios.title: A drug knocks a steroid off its carrier proteins
scenarios.misconception: the total level of a hormone is what sets its effect
scenarios.setup: A steroid hormone circulates mostly bound to carrier proteins in the plasma. A new drug binds the same carrier proteins and pushes some of the hormone off. Compare the first hour on the drug with just before, before the gland or the liver has had time to adjust.
scenarios.start: The drug takes over binding sites on the carrier proteins

steps.off: Hormone is pushed off the carrier proteins
steps.free: More hormone is free in the plasma
steps.same: No hormone is added or removed yet
steps.total: Total hormone is unchanged for now
steps.bind: More free hormone reaches target cells and binds their receptor proteins

variables.name: Hormone bound to carrier proteins
variables.why: The drug occupies binding sites, so some hormone that was riding on the carrier proteins is released and less remains bound.

variables.name: Free hormone in the plasma
variables.why: Every hormone molecule pushed off a carrier protein becomes free hormone. Because the free share is small to start with, even a few percent more makes a large relative rise.

variables.name: Total hormone in the plasma (bound plus free)
variables.why: The drug only moves hormone from the bound form to the free form. Nothing has been secreted or cleared yet, so the total stays the same at first.

variables.name: Hormone effect on target cells
variables.why: Only free hormone can leave the capillaries and bind receptor proteins, so the extra free hormone acts on the targets. Over the following hours, faster clearance and negative feedback bring the free level back toward normal.

scenarios.title: Theophylline blocks phosphodiesterase in airway muscle
scenarios.misconception: a drug must bind the receptor protein to change a hormone signal
scenarios.setup: Epinephrine is relaxing airway smooth muscle through the cAMP pathway. A patient then takes theophylline, which blocks phosphodiesterase in that muscle. Compare the muscle cells a few minutes later with before the drug, with the same level of epinephrine.
scenarios.start: Theophylline blocks phosphodiesterase

steps.pde: cAMP is broken down to AMP more slowly
steps.camp: cAMP builds up in the cell
steps.pka: More protein kinase A is switched on
steps.outside: The drug acts inside the cell, after the receptor protein
steps.bindng: Epinephrine binds its receptor protein as before

variables.name: cAMP in the smooth muscle cells
variables.why: Adenylyl cyclase keeps making cAMP from ATP, but phosphodiesterase, which breaks it down, is blocked. Making continues while removal slows, so cAMP rises.

variables.name: Active protein kinase A
variables.why: cAMP is what switches on protein kinase A, so more cAMP means more of the kinase is active.

variables.name: Diameter of the airways
variables.why: More kinase activity phosphorylates more of the proteins that relax the muscle, so the airway walls relax and the airways widen. That is why the drug was used for narrowed airways.

variables.name: Epinephrine bound to its receptor proteins
variables.why: The drug acts on the enzyme that ends the signal inside the cell. The hormone level and its binding to the receptor protein are unchanged.

scenarios.title: The pituitary stalk is cut
scenarios.misconception: cutting the link to the hypothalamus lowers every pituitary hormone
scenarios.setup: A head injury tears the infundibulum, cutting both the hypophyseal portal veins and the axons that run down to the posterior pituitary. The pituitary gland itself is unharmed. Compare a day or two later with before the injury.
scenarios.start: The infundibulum is torn

steps.portal: Portal veins no longer carry hypothalamic hormones down
steps.rel: Releasing hormones (TRH, CRH, GHRH) stop reaching the anterior pituitary
steps.dop: Dopamine stops reaching the anterior pituitary
steps.prl: Prolactin cells are released from their brake
steps.axons: Axons to the posterior pituitary are cut

variables.name: TSH
variables.why: TSH release is driven by TRH arriving through the portal veins. With the veins cut, the drive is lost and TSH falls.

variables.name: ACTH
variables.why: ACTH depends on CRH delivered through the portal system, so it falls for the same reason.

variables.name: Prolactin
variables.why: Prolactin is held back more than it is pushed: dopamine from the hypothalamus inhibits it. Cutting the portal veins removes that brake, so prolactin rises while the other anterior hormones fall.

variables.name: Urine volume
variables.why: ADH is made in hypothalamic cell bodies and released from axon terminals in the posterior lobe. With the axons cut, little ADH reaches the blood, the kidney cells keep few aquaporins, and a large volume of dilute urine flows out.

scenarios.title: A bag of salted chips
scenarios.misconception: ADH responds mainly to blood volume
scenarios.setup: You eat a large bag of salted chips and drink nothing. The salt is absorbed into your blood. Compare half an hour later with before the snack.
scenarios.start: Absorbed salt raises plasma osmolarity

steps.shrink: Water leaves the osmoreceptors, which shrink
steps.adh: More ADH is released from the posterior pituitary
steps.keep: More water returns from the urine to the blood

variables.name: Osmoreceptor firing
variables.why: Water follows solute out of the osmoreceptors, they shrink, channels that open as the membrane slackens let ions in, and the cells depolarize and fire faster.

variables.name: ADH in the blood
variables.why: The osmoreceptors excite the neurons that make ADH, so their axon terminals in the posterior pituitary release more of it. A rise in osmolarity is ADH’s main and most sensitive trigger.

variables.name: Thirst
variables.why: The same osmoreceptors excite the thirst center in the hypothalamus, so you want to drink.

variables.name: Urine volume
variables.why: ADH, through cAMP, moves aquaporins into the membranes of the last stretch of the kidney’s tubules. More water returns to the blood, so you pass a small volume of concentrated urine.

scenarios.title: A growth hormone–secreting tumor in an adult
scenarios.misconception: too much growth hormone makes an adult taller
scenarios.setup: A 42-year-old man has a benign pituitary tumor that makes far too much growth hormone. His epiphyseal plates closed years ago. Compare him after several years of the tumor with before it began.
scenarios.start: The tumor releases too much GH

steps.liver: The liver and other tissues release more IGF-1
steps.closed: The epiphyseal plates have already closed
steps.thick: Bones of the hands, feet, jaw and face thicken
steps.fb: GH and IGF-1 feed back on the hypothalamus
steps.glu: Muscle and fat take up less glucose and the liver releases more

variables.name: IGF-1
variables.why: GH makes the liver, and many tissues on their own, release IGF-1, which carries most of GH’s growth effects.

variables.name: Height
variables.why: Height grows only while the epiphyseal plates are open. In an adult they have closed, so extra GH cannot lengthen the long bones. This is acromegaly, not gigantism.

variables.name: Size of the jaw and hands
variables.why: Bones can still thicken, and soft tissues still grow, so the jaw juts, the hands and feet widen, and his ring and shoe sizes go up.

variables.name: GHRH from the hypothalamus
variables.why: High GH and IGF-1 feed back to cut GHRH and raise somatostatin release. The tumor ignores the brake, so GH stays high while GHRH falls.

variables.name: Glucose in the blood
variables.why: GH makes muscle and fat take up less glucose and the liver release more, so the glucose level runs high.

scenarios.title: The thyroid gland is removed
scenarios.misconception: losing the thyroid gland’s calcitonin makes blood calcium rise
scenarios.setup: A surgeon removes a patient’s whole thyroid gland but leaves all four parathyroid glands intact and working. For this question, no replacement hormone is given. Compare two months later with before the surgery.
scenarios.start: No thyroid gland is left

steps.t3: Tissues have no T4 to convert, so T3 falls
steps.tsh: The anterior pituitary releases more TSH
steps.pumps: Cells make fewer pumps and mitochondria
steps.heat: Less oxygen used; less heat made
steps.beta: Heart cells make fewer beta-1 receptor proteins
steps.ccell: Calcitonin is lost, a minor effect in adults
steps.pth: The parathyroid glands still sense calcium and release PTH
steps.ca: Blood calcium is held in range

variables.name: T4 in the blood
variables.why: All T4 comes from the follicular cells, so with the gland gone, T4 falls. With a half-life of about a week, it falls over several weeks, not at once.

variables.name: TSH
variables.why: Thyroid hormones normally hold TSH down. As they fall, the brake comes off both the hypothalamus and the anterior pituitary, and TSH rises high: low final hormone with high tropic hormone.

variables.name: Heat production (feels cold)
variables.why: T3 makes cells build sodium–potassium pumps and mitochondria. Without it they use less ATP and oxygen, make less heat, and the person feels cold.

variables.name: Resting heart rate
variables.why: Thyroid hormones keep heart cells stocked with beta-1 receptor proteins, the permissive effect on epinephrine. With fewer of them, the heart beats more slowly.

variables.name: Blood calcium
variables.why: The parafollicular cells go with the gland, so calcitonin is lost. In adults that hardly matters: PTH and calcitriol are the main regulators, and people without a thyroid gland keep normal calcium as long as their parathyroid glands work.

scenarios.title: Too little iodine in the diet
scenarios.misconception: a goiter means the thyroid gland is overactive
scenarios.setup: A woman lives inland, far from the sea, where the soil is poor in iodine and salt is not iodized. She has eaten very little iodine for years. Compare her now with someone of the same age who gets about 150 micrograms a day.
scenarios.start: Too little iodine reaches the follicular cells

steps.noI: Too few iodines can be attached to thyroglobulin
steps.tsh: The anterior pituitary releases more TSH
steps.grow: TSH drives follicular cells to grow and make thyroglobulin
steps.rate: Cells use less oxygen and fuel

variables.name: T4 in the blood
variables.why: Each T4 molecule needs four iodines attached to tyrosines in thyroglobulin. Without enough iodine the follicular cells cannot finish the hormone, however hard they work.

variables.name: TSH
variables.why: Low thyroid hormone releases the brake on the anterior pituitary, so TSH rises.

variables.name: Size of the thyroid gland
variables.why: TSH makes follicular cells grow and make thyroglobulin. The gland swells even though it cannot make enough hormone, so this goiter comes with too little hormone, not too much.

variables.name: Oxygen use by her cells at rest
variables.why: With less thyroid hormone, cells make fewer sodium–potassium pumps and mitochondria, so they use less ATP and oxygen: she is hypothyroid.

scenarios.title: The parathyroid glands are bruised in neck surgery
scenarios.misconception: low calcium makes nerves and muscles less excitable
scenarios.setup: During thyroid surgery, all four parathyroid glands are bruised and stop releasing hormone for a while. Compare the next evening with before the operation.
scenarios.start: The chief cells stop releasing PTH

steps.less: Bone releases less calcium, the kidneys keep less, and the intestine absorbs less
steps.na: Voltage-gated sodium channels open more easily

variables.name: Blood calcium
variables.why: PTH is the main hormone that raises blood calcium. Without it, bone releases less calcium, the kidneys keep less, and with less calcitriol the intestine absorbs less, so calcium falls.

variables.name: Blood phosphate
variables.why: PTH normally makes the kidneys lose phosphate in the urine. Without it, they keep more, and phosphate rises.

variables.name: Calcitriol
variables.why: PTH switches on the kidney enzyme that makes calcitriol, so with PTH low, less calcitriol is made and the intestine absorbs less calcium.

variables.name: Excitability of nerves and muscles
variables.why: Low extracellular calcium lets voltage-gated sodium channels open more easily. Nerves fire on their own: tingling around the mouth, cramps and tetany.

scenarios.title: Graves disease
scenarios.misconception: high thyroid hormone always comes with high TSH
scenarios.setup: A woman’s immune system makes a protein that binds the TSH receptor protein on her follicular cells and switches it on, as TSH does. Compare her after a few months with before the disease began.
scenarios.start: An immune protein switches on the TSH receptor proteins

steps.fb: High thyroid hormone brakes the pituitary
steps.beta: Heart cells make more beta-1 receptor proteins
steps.burn: Cells burn more fuel and make more heat
steps.wt: She loses weight despite eating more

variables.name: T4 in the blood
variables.why: The immune protein acts like TSH on every step, from iodide trapping to release, but feedback cannot turn it off.

variables.name: TSH
variables.why: The pituitary sees high thyroid hormone and cuts TSH release. That does not help, because the gland is being driven by the immune protein, not by TSH.

variables.name: Size of the thyroid gland
variables.why: Switching on the TSH receptor protein also makes the follicular cells grow, so Graves disease often causes a goiter.

variables.name: Resting heart rate
variables.why: Thyroid hormones raise the number of beta-1 receptor proteins on heart cells, so the heart responds more to sympathetic signals and races at rest.

variables.name: Body weight
variables.why: Every cell uses more oxygen and fuel and makes more heat, so she loses weight despite a big appetite.

scenarios.title: Untreated type 1 diabetes
scenarios.misconception: without insulin, cells have plenty of glucose because the blood is full of it
scenarios.setup: A 12-year-old’s immune system has destroyed nearly all her beta cells over the past few months, and she has not yet been diagnosed or given insulin. Compare her now with before her beta cells were lost.
scenarios.start: Almost no insulin is released

steps.glut: Muscle and fat take in little glucose, and the liver keeps releasing it
steps.sat: Kidney carriers can take back only so much glucose
steps.osm: Glucose holds water in the kidney fluid by osmosis
steps.fat: Nothing blocks fat breakdown, and glucagon runs high
steps.alpha: Alpha cells lose the beta cells’ brake: glucagon high
steps.acid: The liver pours out acids made from fat
steps.breathe: Deep, rapid breathing blows off carbon dioxide
steps.lose: Calories are lost as glucose, and fat and muscle are broken down

variables.name: Blood glucose
variables.why: With almost no insulin, muscle and fat let little glucose in, and the liver keeps making and releasing glucose. Nothing else lowers it, so blood glucose climbs.

variables.name: Glucagon
variables.why: Insulin from neighboring beta cells normally damps the alpha cells. With the beta cells gone, the brake is lost and glucagon runs high even though glucose is already high.

variables.name: Urine volume
variables.why: Once blood glucose passes about 180 mg/dL, the kidney’s carriers are saturated and glucose stays in the urine. It holds water with it by osmosis, so urine volume rises.

variables.name: Thirst
variables.why: Losing so much water raises the concentration of the plasma and lowers blood volume, and both drive thirst.

variables.name: Body weight
variables.why: Calories leave in the urine as glucose, and cells short of glucose break down fat and muscle, so she loses weight despite eating.

variables.name: Blood pH
variables.why: With no insulin to block fat breakdown and glucagon high, the liver turns fatty acids into acids faster than tissues can burn them, and they lower the blood pH.

variables.name: Depth and rate of breathing
variables.why: Acid in the blood drives breathing harder. Deep, rapid breaths blow off carbon dioxide, which partly offsets the fall in pH.

scenarios.title: Too much insulin before a skipped meal
scenarios.misconception: the brain can switch to fat when blood glucose falls
scenarios.setup: A man with type 1 diabetes injects his usual mealtime insulin, then skips the meal. An hour later his blood glucose is 50 mg/dL. Compare now with before the injection.
scenarios.start: Injected insulin acts with no meal to match it

steps.in: Muscle and fat take glucose in; the liver stops releasing it
steps.med: The adrenal medulla releases more epinephrine
steps.hr: The heart beats faster and harder
steps.sweat: Sympathetic cholinergic fibers drive the sweat glands
steps.brain: Neurons, with almost no stored glycogen, run short of glucose

variables.name: Epinephrine
variables.why: The adrenal medulla responds at about 65 to 70 mg/dL, raising glucose release from the liver. In type 1 diabetes the alpha cells’ glucagon response to a low usually fades within the first few years, so epinephrine becomes the main defense.

variables.name: Heart rate
variables.why: Sympathetic activation and circulating epinephrine speed the heart. A pounding heart is one of the warning signs of a low.

variables.name: Sweating
variables.why: Sweat glands are driven by sympathetic cholinergic fibers, so sweating comes with the other warning signs.

variables.name: Clarity of thinking
variables.why: Neurons store almost no glycogen and cannot burn fatty acids, so they depend on glucose from the blood minute by minute. As it falls, thinking becomes slow and confused.

scenarios.title: Months of steroid tablets, then stopping suddenly
scenarios.theme: long-term steroid therapy, then stopping suddenly
scenarios.misconception: the adrenal glands restart as soon as the steroid drug is stopped
scenarios.setup: A woman takes a high dose of prednisone, a synthetic glucocorticoid, every day for six months for inflammatory lung disease. Then she runs out and stops it all at once.

stages.label: After months on the drug
stages.prompt: After six months of daily prednisone, compared with before she started it.
stages.start: Prednisone acts like cortisol on the hypothalamus and pituitary

steps.shrink: Without ACTH, the zona fasciculata shrinks
steps.gluc: The drug drives gluconeogenesis and insulin resistance
steps.ang: Angiotensin II and potassium still drive the zona glomerulosa

variables.name: ACTH
variables.why: The drug acts on the hypothalamus and anterior pituitary just as cortisol does, so CRH and ACTH release are held down.

variables.name: Cortisol made by her own adrenal glands
variables.why: ACTH keeps the zona fasciculata large and working. With ACTH suppressed for months, the zone shrinks and makes little cortisol.

variables.name: Blood glucose
variables.why: The drug does what cortisol does in excess: it switches on gluconeogenesis and makes muscle and fat respond less to insulin, so glucose rises.

variables.name: Aldosterone
variables.why: Aldosterone’s main drivers are angiotensin II and plasma potassium, not ACTH, so the zona glomerulosa keeps working.

stages.label: The first days after stopping
stages.prompt: In the first few days after stopping, compared with while she was still taking the drug.
stages.start: The drug is gone from her blood

steps.gone: No glucocorticoid comes from the drug
steps.slow: The hypothalamus and pituitary take weeks to restart
steps.small: The shrunken zona fasciculata cannot make much cortisol
steps.total: Total glucocorticoid falls far below normal
steps.bp: Vessels respond weakly to sympathetic signals: blood pressure falls
steps.ang: Angiotensin II and potassium still drive the zona glomerulosa

variables.name: ACTH
variables.why: The brake has lifted, but the suppressed hypothalamus and pituitary need weeks to months to recover, so ACTH stays low at first instead of jumping up.

variables.name: Total glucocorticoid activity (drug plus her own cortisol)
variables.why: The drug has gone, ACTH is still low, and the shrunken zona fasciculata cannot make up the gap. There is little glucocorticoid from either source.

variables.name: Blood glucose
variables.why: Without cortisol driving gluconeogenesis, the liver makes less glucose, and glucose can fall low, especially under stress.

variables.name: Blood pressure
variables.why: Cortisol keeps vascular smooth muscle able to respond to norepinephrine and epinephrine. Without it, vessels respond weakly and pressure falls. That is how an adrenal crisis begins, and why these drugs are tapered.

variables.name: Aldosterone
variables.why: The zona glomerulosa was never under ACTH’s main control, so it keeps making aldosterone.

scenarios.title: A pituitary tumor secreting ACTH
scenarios.misconception: high cortisol always means low ACTH
scenarios.setup: A benign tumor of the anterior pituitary releases ACTH on its own and responds only weakly to feedback (Cushing disease). Compare the patient after a year with before the tumor.
scenarios.start: The tumor releases too much ACTH

steps.fb: Cortisol feeds back on the hypothalamus
steps.gng: Gluconeogenesis rises and muscle and fat resist insulin

variables.name: Cortisol
variables.why: ACTH binds receptor proteins on zona fasciculata cells and makes them make and release cortisol, so excess ACTH means excess cortisol.

variables.name: CRH
variables.why: The hypothalamus still obeys feedback: high cortisol cuts CRH. The tumor ignores the brake, so ACTH and cortisol both stay high while CRH falls.

variables.name: Size of the adrenal cortexes
variables.why: Over weeks, ACTH keeps the zona fasciculata and zona reticularis large; too much of it makes them grow.

variables.name: Blood glucose
variables.why: Cortisol switches on gluconeogenesis and makes muscle and fat respond less to insulin, so glucose runs high, often to the point of diabetes.

variables.name: Strength of the thigh and shoulder muscles
variables.why: Cortisol breaks down muscle protein to supply amino acids for gluconeogenesis, so the large muscles of the thighs and shoulders waste and weaken.

scenarios.title: Addison disease
scenarios.misconception: adrenal insufficiency affects only cortisol
scenarios.setup: A man’s immune system slowly destroys his adrenal cortexes. All three zones fail. Compare him after this has developed with before.
scenarios.start: The adrenal cortexes are destroyed

steps.fb: Negative feedback on the pituitary is lost
steps.mel: ACTH and a related hormone stimulate melanocytes
steps.na: The kidneys lose sodium and water
steps.perm: Without cortisol, vessels respond weakly to sympathetic signals

variables.name: ACTH
variables.why: The pituitary is healthy. With cortisol low, feedback no longer holds it back, so ACTH rises very high: low final hormone with high tropic hormone points to the target gland.

variables.name: Skin color (darkness)
variables.why: ACTH is cut from a larger precursor that also yields a melanocyte-stimulating hormone, and at high levels ACTH itself stimulates melanocytes, so skin creases and gums darken.

variables.name: Plasma potassium
variables.why: Aldosterone normally makes the kidney secrete potassium. Without it, potassium stays in the blood.

variables.name: Vessel constriction in response to sympathetic signals
variables.why: Cortisol keeps vessel smooth muscle responsive to norepinephrine. Without it, the same sympathetic signals constrict the vessels less, which adds to the fall in blood pressure.

variables.name: Blood pressure
variables.why: Two losses add up: without aldosterone the kidneys lose sodium and water, so blood volume falls, and at the same time, without cortisol, the vessels constrict weakly when sympathetic nerves signal them.

variables.name: Blood glucose
variables.why: Cortisol drives gluconeogenesis. Without it, the liver makes less glucose, and glucose runs low, especially between meals.

scenarios.title: An ACE inhibitor for raised blood pressure
scenarios.misconception: blocking ACE lowers renin
scenarios.setup: A man with raised blood pressure starts a drug that blocks angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE). Compare him a few weeks later with before the drug.
scenarios.start: ACE is blocked

steps.ang2: Less angiotensin I is converted to angiotensin II
steps.ald: The zona glomerulosa releases less aldosterone
steps.na: The kidney keeps less sodium, and less water follows
steps.fb: Angiotensin II and lower pressure both act back on the renin cells

variables.name: Angiotensin II
variables.why: ACE, on the inner lining of blood vessels and most plentiful in the lungs, is the enzyme that makes angiotensin II from angiotensin I. Blocking it cuts angiotensin II.

variables.name: Aldosterone
variables.why: Angiotensin II is one of the two main signals for aldosterone release, so less of it means less aldosterone.

variables.name: Plasma potassium
variables.why: Aldosterone makes the kidney secrete potassium. With less aldosterone, a little more potassium stays in the blood, which is why potassium is checked on these drugs.

variables.name: Blood volume
variables.why: Aldosterone makes the kidney reabsorb sodium, and water follows by osmosis. With less aldosterone, a little more sodium and water leave in the urine, so volume falls slightly and pressure with it.

variables.name: Renin
