variables.why: The drug acts after renin. With less angiotensin II and lower pressure in the kidney’s small arteries, the renin-releasing cells release more renin. It has little effect, because the next step is blocked.

scenarios.title: A year of anabolic steroids, then stopping
scenarios.misconception: a man’s own testosterone comes back as soon as he stops taking anabolic steroids
scenarios.setup: A 25-year-old man injects high doses of an anabolic steroid for a year while he trains, then stops. Follow his muscles and his own hormones.

stages.label: Months on the drug
stages.prompt: After several months on the drug, compared with before he started.
stages.start: A high level of a synthetic androgen circulates in his blood

steps.bind: The drug binds androgen receptor proteins in skeletal muscle fibers
steps.brake: The high androgen level brakes the hypothalamus and anterior pituitary
steps.lh: GnRH, LH and FSH release fall
steps.own: Without LH, his testes make little testosterone of their own
steps.shrink: Without LH and FSH, his testes shrink

variables.name: Muscle mass
variables.why: At high doses the drug binds androgen receptor proteins in skeletal muscle, speeds protein synthesis, and the fibers grow thicker (hypertrophy).

variables.name: LH in his blood
variables.why: Androgens exert negative feedback on the hypothalamus and anterior pituitary. The drug keeps that brake on hard, so GnRH, LH and FSH fall.

variables.name: Testosterone made by his own testes
variables.why: LH is the signal that drives the testes to make testosterone. With LH suppressed, his own production falls, even though the drug floods his blood with androgen.

variables.name: Size of his testes
variables.why: LH and FSH keep the testes working and full-sized. With both suppressed for months, the testes shrink and sperm production falls.

stages.label: Two months after stopping
stages.prompt: Two months after his last dose, compared with while he was on the drug.
stages.start: The drug clears from his blood while his own LH is still suppressed

steps.total: Total androgen in his blood falls low
steps.loss: Muscle fibers make protein more slowly and shrink
steps.lift: The feedback brake on his hypothalamus and pituitary lifts
steps.climb: GnRH and LH begin to climb, but slowly

variables.name: Total androgen in his blood (the drug plus his own testosterone)
variables.why: The drug is gone, and his own axis has not caught up: after a year of suppression, LH recovers slowly, so his testes still make little testosterone. For weeks to months he has less androgen than before he ever started.

variables.name: Muscle mass
variables.why: With little androgen binding the receptor proteins in his muscle fibers, protein synthesis slows and the fibers shrink, so much of the drug-built muscle is lost.

variables.name: Negative feedback holding back his hypothalamus and pituitary
variables.why: With so little androgen in his blood, the brake on GnRH and LH lifts. His axis starts to climb back, but it can take months to reach its old level: negative feedback restores the set point slowly.

scenarios.title: Two liters of saline in an hour
scenarios.misconception: the heart plays no part in hormone control of salt and water
scenarios.setup: A patient is given two liters of saline through a drip over one hour. Compare the end of the hour with before the drip.
scenarios.start: Blood volume rises

steps.ret: More blood returns to the heart
steps.str: The walls of the upper chambers are stretched
steps.anp: Stretched muscle cells there release ANP
steps.filt: The kidneys filter more and reabsorb less sodium
steps.na: More sodium and water leave in the urine

variables.name: ANP in the blood
variables.why: The extra volume returns to the heart and stretches its upper chambers, and their stretched muscle cells release ANP.

variables.name: Sodium excreted in the urine
variables.why: ANP makes the kidneys filter more fluid and reabsorb less sodium, so sodium, and water with it, leaves in the urine.

variables.name: Aldosterone
variables.why: ANP cuts renin release, and so angiotensin II, and aldosterone release falls with it. The signals that make the kidneys keep salt are removed.

variables.name: Diameter of small arteries
variables.why: ANP relaxes vascular smooth muscle: vasodilation. All its effects lower volume and pressure, and as stretch eases, ANP falls again.

scenarios.title: Bright light in the middle of the night
scenarios.misconception: melatonin is controlled by the image the eyes see
scenarios.setup: At 2 a.m. a sleeper is woken and turns on a bright, blue-rich light. Compare five minutes later with just before the light went on.
scenarios.start: Bright light reaches the retina

steps.symp: The pathway down to the superior cervical ganglion shuts down

variables.name: Norepinephrine released onto pinealocytes
variables.why: At night, sympathetic fibers from the superior cervical ganglion release norepinephrine onto the pineal gland. Light, through the suprachiasmatic nucleus, shuts that pathway down.

variables.name: Melatonin in the blood
variables.why: Without norepinephrine, pinealocytes stop making and releasing melatonin within minutes. The same light signal also resets the suprachiasmatic nucleus itself, which is why light at night, including from screens, pushes the body clock later.

scenarios.title: The spleen is removed
scenarios.misconception: the spleen is just a large lymph node that filters lymph
scenarios.setup: A car crash tears a 30-year-old woman’s spleen beyond repair, and surgeons remove it. Predict the changes over the following months, compared with before the injury.
scenarios.start: The spleen is removed

steps.reserve: The platelets the spleen held in reserve are no longer held back
steps.plt: They circulate: the platelet count rises
steps.nored: No red pulp to squeeze-test blood cells
steps.oldrbc: Old and misshapen red cells stay in the blood longer
steps.liver: Liver macrophages take over some of the filtering, but not all
steps.caps: Sugar-coated bacteria in the blood are cleared less well
steps.sepsis: Risk of an overwhelming bloodstream infection rises for life
steps.nodes: Lymph still flows through the lymph nodes

variables.name: Platelet count
variables.why: The spleen normally holds about a third of your platelets in reserve. Without it, those platelets stay in the circulating blood, so the count rises.

variables.name: Old and misshapen red cells in the blood
variables.why: In the red pulp, stiff old red cells get stuck in the narrow slits of the venous sinuses and are engulfed. Without that squeeze test they stay in circulation longer, until macrophages elsewhere remove them.

variables.name: Risk of an overwhelming bloodstream infection
variables.why: Red pulp macrophages are the main way to clear bacteria wrapped in a slippery sugar coat, which are hard to engulf anywhere else. The liver takes over only part of the job, so the risk stays higher for life. That is why she gets extra vaccines and should seek care at the first sign of a fever.

variables.name: Filtering of lymph by lymph nodes
variables.why: The spleen has no afferent lymphatic vessels: it filters blood, not lymph. Lymph goes on passing through the lymph nodes, whose macrophages and lymphocytes clear it as before.

scenarios.title: Lymph nodes of the armpit are removed
scenarios.misconception: lymphedema is caused by capillaries filtering too much fluid
scenarios.setup: During breast cancer surgery, the lymph nodes of a woman’s left armpit are removed and the area is treated with radiation. Months later her left arm begins to swell. Compare her left arm with her right.
scenarios.start: Nodes and lymphatic vessels of the left armpit are lost

steps.block: Lymph from the left arm has too few routes back to the blood
steps.same: Blood capillaries in the arm are unchanged
steps.filt: Capillary blood pressure stays at its usual level
steps.stay: Filtered fluid stays in the tissue
steps.isf: Interstitial fluid volume rises: the arm swells
steps.prot: Leaked plasma protein is not carried away
steps.protup: Protein in the interstitial fluid rises
steps.cells: Stagnant fluid draws in lymphocytes, whose signals drive fibroblasts
steps.firm: Collagen and fat build up: the arm turns firm and stops pitting

variables.name: Blood pressure in the arm’s capillaries
variables.why: Nothing in the blood capillaries has changed: capillary pressure and plasma protein are normal, so the forces pushing fluid out are the same as in her right arm. Lymphedema is a failure of drainage, not of filtration.

variables.name: Interstitial fluid volume in the arm
variables.why: Fluid keeps filtering out of the capillaries, but with the drainage route cut, less of it returns to the blood. The difference collects in the tissue.

variables.name: Protein in the interstitial fluid
variables.why: Only the lymphatic route can return leaked plasma protein to the blood. With it blocked, protein builds up in the tissue, which is why lymphedema fluid is protein-rich.

variables.name: Firmness of the tissue over months
variables.why: The stagnant, protein-rich fluid keeps drawing lymphocytes into the tissue. Their chemical signals drive fibroblasts to lay down collagen, and fat builds up, so the swelling turns firm and stops pitting under a thumb.

variables.name: Risk of skin infection in the arm
variables.why: Bacteria that get into the skin are carried to lymph nodes less well, and the stagnant fluid gives them a place to grow.

scenarios.title: A fever starts, then breaks
scenarios.misconception: a fever means the body has lost control of its temperature
scenarios.setup: Macrophages fighting an infected cut release interleukin-1 and other pyrogens. Prostaglandin E2 in the hypothalamus raises the set point from 36.6 to 39 °C. Follow the fever from its start to its end.

stages.label: Minutes after the set point rises
stages.prompt: Compared with just before the set point rose.
stages.start: The set point jumps to 39 °C

steps.below: Body temperature, still 36.6 °C, is now below the set point
steps.skin: Less warm blood flows through the skin
steps.shiver: Motor signals make skeletal muscles shiver
steps.heat: Less heat lost and more heat made

variables.name: Blood flow through the skin
variables.why: The hypothalamus responds exactly as it would to cold: sympathetic signals constrict the skin arterioles, so the skin turns pale and the hands feel cold, and less heat leaves at the surface.

variables.name: Shivering
variables.why: Your temperature is below the new target, so the hypothalamus signals skeletal muscles to shiver, releasing heat. The control system is working normally, just toward a higher set point.

variables.name: Body temperature
variables.why: Heat is kept in and made faster than it is lost, so temperature rises until it meets the new set point. Then the chills stop.

variables.name: Feeling cold
variables.why: You feel chilled and reach for a blanket even though your temperature is normal or rising, because it is still below what the hypothalamus is now aiming for.

stages.label: When the pyrogens are cleared
stages.prompt: Later, often after a day or more, the infection is under control and the pyrogens are cleared while body temperature is 39 °C. Compared with the plateau just before.
stages.start: The set point falls back to 36.6 °C

steps.above: Body temperature, 39 °C, is now above the set point
steps.dil: Skin arterioles dilate: flushed, warm skin
steps.loss: Heat is lost faster than it is made

variables.name: Blood flow through the skin
variables.why: With temperature above the set point, the hypothalamus runs its heat-loss responses: the skin arterioles dilate and warm blood flows near the surface.

variables.name: Sweating
variables.why: Sweat glands are signaled to release sweat, which carries heat away as it evaporates. This is the drenching sweat that ends a fever.

variables.name: Body temperature
variables.why: Heat now leaves faster than it is made, so temperature falls until it meets the normal set point again. The same negative feedback loop that raised it now lowers it.

scenarios.title: Bacteria enter a fingertip
scenarios.misconception: the redness and swelling are damage done by the bacteria
scenarios.setup: A splinter carries bacteria into your fingertip. Predict the changes at the site and in your blood over the next day, compared with before the splinter.
scenarios.start: Bacteria enter the tissue

steps.alarm: Mast cells release histamine; macrophages release cytokines
steps.flow: More blood flows in: redness and heat
steps.leak: Capillary and venule walls pull apart and leak
steps.swell: Plasma pours into the tissue: swelling
steps.prot: Plasma proteins, including complement, enter the tissue
steps.sticky: Cytokines make the venule walls sticky
steps.out: Neutrophils roll, stick, squeeze out and follow chemotaxis
steps.marrow: Cytokines in the blood make the marrow release neutrophils
steps.wbc: The blood white cell count rises

variables.name: Blood flow to the fingertip
variables.why: Histamine and prostaglandins relax the arterioles at the site, so more blood flows in. That is the redness and heat.

variables.name: Interstitial fluid at the site
variables.why: The same messengers make capillary and venule endothelial cells pull apart, so plasma leaks out faster than it can drain away: swelling.

variables.name: Complement proteins in the tissue
variables.why: Complement circulates in the plasma. When the vessels leak, it pours into the tissue with the plasma, where it can coat the bacteria.

variables.name: Neutrophils at the site
variables.why: Cytokines switch on adhesion proteins on the venule wall. Neutrophils roll, stick, squeeze out between endothelial cells and crawl up the gradient of attractants to the bacteria.

variables.name: White cell count in the blood
variables.why: Cytokines that reach the blood make the bone marrow release its reserve of neutrophils, so the count rises in a bacterial infection.

scenarios.title: A first dose of a new vaccine
scenarios.misconception: lymphocytes shape their antigen receptor proteins to fit a new antigen
scenarios.setup: A child gets her first dose of a vaccine containing an antigen her immune system has never met. Predict the changes one to two weeks later, compared with before the dose.
scenarios.start: The new antigen reaches a lymph node

steps.select: The rare naïve lymphocytes that already fit an epitope are selected
steps.divide: They divide every 6 to 8 hours for several days
steps.clone: Each forms a clone of identical cells
steps.mem: Some clone members become long-lived memory cells
steps.made: Antigen receptor proteins were built at random before the antigen arrived
steps.shape: No lymphocyte changes its receptor protein to fit the antigen

variables.name: Lymphocytes that fit the vaccine antigen
variables.why: Only about 1 in 100,000 to 1 in a million naïve lymphocytes fits any one epitope. The antigen selects those cells, and they multiply into clones of tens of thousands or more.

variables.name: Size of the lymph node draining the injection site
variables.why: Clonal expansion happens in the lymph node, and more lymphocytes are held back from leaving, so the node swells.

variables.name: Memory cells for this antigen
variables.why: A smaller part of each clone becomes long-lived memory cells. Their larger numbers are what make a later exposure faster and stronger.

variables.name: Shape of any one lymphocyte’s antigen receptor protein
variables.why: Each lymphocyte joined the gene pieces for its receptor protein at random while it matured. The antigen does not reshape any receptor protein; it selects the cells whose receptor proteins already fit.

scenarios.title: A baby is born without a thymus
scenarios.misconception: every lymphocyte matures in the thymus
scenarios.setup: A baby girl is born without a thymus; her bone marrow is normal. Compare her at four months with a healthy baby.
scenarios.start: No thymus

steps.nowhere: Thymocytes from the marrow have nowhere to mature
steps.fewt: Few mature T cells reach the body
steps.blood: T cells in the blood are scarce
steps.para: The paracortex of her lymph nodes is nearly empty
steps.infect: Virus-infected cells are not found and removed: infections linger
steps.innate: Neutrophils, macrophages and NK cells are made and work as usual
steps.bmat: B cells still mature in the marrow

variables.name: T cells in the blood
variables.why: T cells leave the marrow as thymocytes and mature only in the thymus. Without it, almost none become mature T cells.

variables.name: Lymphocytes in the paracortex of lymph nodes
variables.why: The deep cortex of a lymph node is where T cells gather. With few T cells, it is nearly empty.

variables.name: Viral and fungal infections that will not clear
variables.why: T cells are what find and kill infected cells and coordinate the rest of the response. Without them, viral and fungal infections persist.

variables.name: Neutrophil count
variables.why: Neutrophils are made in the bone marrow and belong to innate immunity. They need no thymus, so their numbers and function are normal.

variables.name: B cells in the blood
variables.why: B cells finish maturing in the bone marrow, not the thymus, so their numbers are normal.

scenarios.title: A transplant patient takes tacrolimus
scenarios.misconception: anti-rejection drugs act only on the transplanted organ
scenarios.setup: After a kidney transplant, a man takes tacrolimus, which stops activated T cells from making IL-2. Predict the changes, compared with the same man without the drug.
scenarios.start: Activated T cells cannot make IL-2

steps.nosignal: No IL-2 growth signal after activation
steps.noexp: Clonal expansion of T cells is blocked
steps.fewer: Few effector T cells form against donor HLA
steps.every: The block hits every T cell response, not only the graft
steps.hla: The drug does not act on the donor’s cells
steps.same: Donor HLA on the kidney is unchanged

variables.name: Clonal expansion of activated T cells
variables.why: An activated T cell drives its own division by making IL-2 and the receptor protein for it. Without IL-2, it cannot expand into a clone.

variables.name: Risk of acute rejection
variables.why: Acute rejection is carried out by the recipient’s helper and cytotoxic T cells reacting to donor HLA. Without clonal expansion, too few effector cells form to destroy the graft.

variables.name: Risk of infections
variables.why: The drug cannot tell a T cell reacting to the graft from one reacting to a virus. All T cell responses are damped, so recipients get more infections and some virus-driven cancers.

variables.name: HLA proteins on the donor kidney’s cells
variables.why: The drug acts on the recipient’s T cells. The graft still carries the donor’s HLA, which is why the drug must be taken for life.

scenarios.title: A virus switches off MHC class I
scenarios.misconception: a cell that hides from cytotoxic T cells is safe from all immune killing
scenarios.setup: A virus makes the cells it infects stop putting MHC class I on their surface. Predict the immune response, compared with an infection by a similar virus that does not do this.
scenarios.start: Infected cells show little MHC class I

steps.nopep: Viral peptides are not displayed on the cell surface
steps.blind: Cytotoxic T cells cannot recognize the infected cells
steps.ctl: Killing by cytotoxic T cells falls
steps.missing: The self-identity signal NK cells check for is missing
steps.nk: NK cells detect the loss and are no longer held back
steps.free: Free virus between cells still carries its surface proteins
steps.ab: Antibody binding of free virus is unaffected

variables.name: Killing of infected cells by cytotoxic T cells
variables.why: A cytotoxic T cell sees only a peptide held in MHC class I, using its T cell receptor protein and CD8. With no MHC class I, there is nothing for it to recognize.

variables.name: Killing of infected cells by NK cells
variables.why: NK cells are held back by MHC class I on healthy cells. A cell that has lost it tips the balance toward "kill me", so NK cells attack it.

variables.name: Antibody binding to free virus particles
variables.why: Antibody binds whole antigens on the virus’s surface, with no MHC involved. Hiding MHC class I inside infected cells does not change the free virus.

scenarios.title: A tetanus booster ten years later
scenarios.theme: second exposure to the same antigen
scenarios.misconception: a booster simply repeats the first response
scenarios.setup: A woman had her first tetanus vaccination as a child. Ten years after her last dose she gets a booster. Compare her antibody response to this booster with her response to her very first dose.
scenarios.start: Memory B cells meet tetanus toxoid again

steps.mem: Memory B cells far outnumber the original naïve B cells
steps.fast: They switch on faster, with less stimulation
steps.lag: Antibody appears in about 1 to 3 days instead of 5 to 10
steps.peak: The peak is often 10 to 100 times higher
steps.switched: Memory B cells already make switched antibody
steps.igg: Mostly IgG from the start, not IgM first
steps.matured: Their antibody has been through affinity maturation
steps.fit: The antibody binds the toxin more tightly
steps.marrow: More long-lived plasma cells settle in the marrow
steps.last: Antibody stays high for months or years

variables.name: Time before antibody appears in the blood
variables.why: The first time, the few naïve B cells that fit had to be found, activated and expanded, which took 5 to 10 days. Memory B cells are more numerous and quicker to switch on, so antibody appears within 1 to 3 days.

variables.name: Peak antibody level
variables.why: Far more memory cells respond, and they produce far more plasma cells, so the peak is often 10 to 100 times higher than in the primary response.

variables.name: Share of the antibody that is IgG
variables.why: A primary response makes IgM first, then IgG. Memory B cells have already switched class, so the secondary response is mostly IgG from the start.

variables.name: How tightly the antibody binds the toxin
variables.why: Memory B cells come from germinal centers, where cells with better-fitting antibody were selected. The booster recalls those cells, and they improve further.

variables.name: How long antibody stays high
variables.why: After a primary response antibody falls within weeks. After a secondary response more plasma cells move to the bone marrow and keep releasing antibody, so the level stays high for months or years.

scenarios.title: Borrowed antibody for a dirty wound
scenarios.misconception: passive immunity leaves lasting protection
scenarios.setup: A man who was never vaccinated against tetanus gets a deep, dirty wound. He is given tetanus immune globulin: antibody against tetanus toxin collected from other people. Predict the changes over the next day, compared with before the injection.
scenarios.start: Ready-made antitoxin antibody is injected

steps.blood: Antitoxin reaches his blood and tissue fluid within hours
steps.level: Antitoxin in his blood rises within hours, with no wait for his own B cells
steps.neut: Antibody covers the part of the toxin that binds nerve endings
steps.less: Less toxin reaches his nerve endings
steps.noag: No antigen has selected any of his own B cells

variables.name: Antitoxin antibody in his blood
variables.why: Passive immunity needs no lag: the antibody was made by someone else, so it starts working as soon as it is absorbed from the injection site. That takes hours, not the week or more his own B cells would need.

variables.name: Tetanus toxin reaching his nerve endings
variables.why: This is neutralization. Antibody bound to the toxin blocks the part that attaches to nerve endings, so it cannot act.

variables.name: His memory B cells against tetanus toxin
variables.why: Borrowed antibody does not activate his own B cells, so no memory cells form. The antibody is cleared over weeks, which is why he is also given the vaccine to start active immunity.

scenarios.title: Ten years of untreated HIV
scenarios.misconception: HIV only weakens the response to HIV itself
scenarios.setup: A man has had untreated HIV infection for ten years. Predict the changes, compared with the year after his first, acute illness ended.
scenarios.start: HIV keeps infecting and killing CD4 cells

steps.loss: Helper T cells are lost faster than they are replaced
steps.cd4: The CD4 count falls toward or below 200 per microliter
steps.nobhelp: B cells get little helper T cell help
steps.ab: Weak antibody response to a new protein antigen
steps.noctlhelp: Cytotoxic T cells get little IL-2 and licensing
steps.ctl: Weak cytotoxic response to a new virus
steps.opp: Opportunistic infections such as Pneumocystis appear
steps.noskin: HIV does not infect the epidermis

variables.name: CD4 count
variables.why: Infected helper T cells are killed by the virus and by cytotoxic T cells, and uninfected ones die in the constant immune activation. The count falls slowly, year after year.

variables.name: Antibody response to a new protein vaccine
variables.why: Most protein antigens are T cell-dependent: a B cell needs a helper T cell’s contact and cytokines to expand, switch class and make memory. With few helper T cells, the response is weak.

variables.name: Cytotoxic T cell response to a newly caught virus
variables.why: Helper T cells supply IL-2 and license dendritic cells to activate cytotoxic T cells. Without that help, cytotoxic responses are weak too.

variables.name: Opportunistic infections
variables.why: With both arms of adaptive immunity failing, microbes that rarely trouble healthy people cause disease. A CD4 count below 200 or one of these defining illnesses marks AIDS.

variables.name: Barrier function of intact skin
variables.why: HIV infects cells that carry CD4. The keratinized layers of the skin are not among them, so this first line of defense still works.

scenarios.title: The first months of HIV infection
scenarios.misconception: antibodies are what bring HIV down after the first weeks
scenarios.setup: A woman is infected with HIV and is not yet diagnosed or treated. Follow her blood through the first months.

stages.label: About two weeks after infection
stages.prompt: About two weeks after infection, compared with before it.
stages.start: HIV enters CD4 cells and copies itself

steps.explode: The virus multiplies explosively with no adaptive response yet
steps.lag: B cells have not yet expanded and released antibody
steps.test: An antibody test is still negative: the window period

variables.name: HIV in the blood
variables.why: In the first weeks nothing specific is yet acting against the virus, so it multiplies explosively, often with a flu-like illness. She is highly infectious.

variables.name: CD4 count
variables.why: HIV binds CD4 and kills the helper T cells it infects, so the count dips.

variables.name: Antibody against HIV in the blood
variables.why: A primary antibody response needs time for clonal selection and expansion. Before seroconversion an antibody test can be negative even though she is infected.

stages.label: Three months later
stages.prompt: Three months after infection, compared with the peak of the acute phase.
stages.start: Cytotoxic T cells against HIV have expanded

steps.ctl: CD8 cytotoxic T cells kill infected cells showing HIV peptides
steps.viral: HIV in the blood falls to a lower, steady level
steps.recover: Fewer helper T cells are being killed
steps.bcells: B cells have expanded and plasma cells release antibody
steps.escape: The virus mutates around the antibodies

variables.name: HIV in the blood
variables.why: The fall comes mainly from CD8 cytotoxic T cells killing infected cells before they release new virus. It never reaches zero: the virus hides silently in some memory T cells.

variables.name: CD4 count
variables.why: With less virus, fewer helper T cells are killed, so the count rebounds partway. It then falls slowly for years without treatment.

variables.name: Antibody against HIV in the blood
variables.why: Antibody appears within a few weeks to 3 months, which is why the test turns positive. It does little to control HIV, because the error-prone copying lets the virus change the parts antibodies bind.

scenarios.title: Anaphylaxis after eating peanut
scenarios.misconception: anaphylaxis is just a large skin reaction
scenarios.setup: A man sensitized to peanut eats a cookie that contains it. Within minutes, mast cells and basophils throughout his body degranulate. Predict the changes, compared with just before.
scenarios.start: Peanut protein cross-links IgE on mast cells everywhere

steps.release: Histamine and leukotrienes are released throughout the body
steps.map: MAP = CO × TPR falls: distributive shock
steps.baro: Baroreceptors fire less; sympathetic output rises
steps.smooth: Smooth muscle of the small airways contracts

variables.name: Total peripheral resistance
variables.why: Histamine and leukotrienes relax the smooth muscle of arterioles everywhere at once. Wider arterioles mean lower resistance.

variables.name: Plasma volume
variables.why: The same mediators make capillaries and venules leaky, and plasma pours into the tissues. In a severe reaction a large share can leave the vessels within minutes.

variables.name: Venous return
variables.why: Blood pools in the widened veins and plasma leaks away, so less blood returns to the heart.

variables.name: Mean arterial pressure
variables.why: Both terms of MAP = CO × TPR fall: TPR from vasodilation and cardiac output from low venous return. This is distributive shock with a hypovolemic part from the leak.

variables.name: Heart rate
variables.why: The fall in MAP reduces baroreceptor firing, so the brainstem raises sympathetic output and lowers parasympathetic output, and the heart speeds up.

variables.name: Diameter of the small airways
variables.why: Histamine and leukotrienes contract airway smooth muscle and thicken mucus, so the airways narrow and he wheezes. This reaches past the immune system to breathing.

scenarios.title: Epinephrine for anaphylaxis
scenarios.misconception: an antihistamine is the treatment for anaphylaxis
scenarios.setup: Minutes into the same man’s anaphylaxis, 0.3 mg of epinephrine from an auto-injector is given into his outer thigh muscle. Predict the changes over the next several minutes, compared with just before the injection.
scenarios.start: Epinephrine binds adrenergic receptor proteins

steps.a1: Alpha-1: smooth muscle of arterioles and veins contracts
steps.b1: Beta-1: heart rate and contractility rise
steps.camp: Beta-2 raises cyclic AMP in mast cells

variables.name: Total peripheral resistance
variables.why: Through alpha-1 receptor proteins, epinephrine contracts the smooth muscle of arterioles, reversing the vasodilation.

variables.name: Cardiac output
variables.why: Veins constrict and return more blood, and through beta-1 receptor proteins the heart beats faster and more forcefully.

variables.name: Mean arterial pressure
variables.why: Both terms of MAP = CO × TPR rise. An antihistamine cannot do this: it blocks only histamine, not leukotrienes, and acts slowly.

variables.name: Plasma leak into the tissues
variables.why: Constricted vessels leak less, so the swollen lips, tongue and throat shrink.

variables.name: Diameter of the small airways
variables.why: Through beta-2 receptor proteins, airway smooth muscle relaxes and the airways widen.

variables.name: Further mediator release by mast cells
variables.why: Beta-2 stimulation raises cyclic AMP inside mast cells, which reduces further release of histamine and leukotrienes.

scenarios.title: Myasthenia gravis and a sustained upward gaze
scenarios.misconception: myasthenia gravis damages the nerves to the muscles
scenarios.setup: A woman with myasthenia gravis looks up at the ceiling and holds her gaze for a minute. Compare the last few seconds with the same test in a healthy person.
scenarios.start: IgG binds acetylcholine receptor proteins at the end plate

steps.loss: Receptor proteins are taken in and destroyed; complement damages the folds
steps.few: Fewer acetylcholine receptor proteins at the end plate
steps.epp: Each release of acetylcholine gives a smaller end plate potential
steps.rep: With repeated firing, each impulse releases a little less acetylcholine
steps.thr: More end plate potentials fall below threshold
steps.weak: Fewer fibers contract: the eyelid droops
steps.nerve: The axon terminals are not attacked
steps.ach: Acetylcholine release per impulse matches a healthy person’s

variables.name: Acetylcholine receptor proteins at each end plate
variables.why: Antibody cross-links the receptor proteins so the muscle cell takes them in and breaks them down faster, and complement damages the end plate.

variables.name: Size of each end plate potential
variables.why: The same amount of acetylcholine finds fewer receptor proteins to open, so less current flows in.

variables.name: Strength of the eyelid-raising muscle
variables.why: Normally the end plate potential is far above threshold. Hers starts closer to it, so as release falls with repeated firing, more fibers fail to reach threshold and the eyelid droops. The weakness is fatigable.

variables.name: Acetylcholine released per nerve impulse
variables.why: The antibodies target the receptor proteins on the muscle side. The axon terminal releases acetylcholine normally; only its effect is smaller.

scenarios.title: A hard sprint just after lunch
scenarios.misconception: the brain runs the gut, so the gut simply stops when the nerves from the brain change their output
scenarios.setup: Twenty minutes after lunch, a student sprints hard for two minutes to catch a bus that is pulling away. Compare her gut during the sprint with just before it.
scenarios.start: Sympathetic activity rises sharply

steps.ens: Sympathetic fibers inhibit the enteric neurons
steps.sec: The glands of the gut wall secrete less
steps.flow: Blood flow to the gut falls, and more goes to the working muscles

variables.name: Motility of the stomach and intestine
variables.why: Sympathetic fibers do not stop the enteric nervous system; they turn it down. With the enteric neurons inhibited, fewer slow waves reach threshold and the contractions weaken.

variables.name: Secretion by the gut’s glands
variables.why: Secretion is run by the submucosal plexus. Sympathetic input inhibits it, the reverse of the rest-and-digest pattern.

variables.name: Tone of the gut sphincters
variables.why: Norepinephrine acts on alpha-1 receptor proteins on sphincter smooth muscle and contracts it, so contents are held back while motility is low.

variables.name: Blood flow to the gut
variables.why: Sympathetic fibers narrow the gut’s arterioles. Their resistance rises, so flow to the gut falls and more of the cardiac output reaches skeletal muscle.

scenarios.title: The diaphragm no longer pinches the lower esophagus
scenarios.misconception: heartburn is a problem of the heart
scenarios.setup: In a hiatal hernia, the top of the stomach slides up through the opening in the diaphragm, so the diaphragm no longer wraps around the lower esophageal sphincter. Compare with before the hernia.
scenarios.start: The diaphragm’s pinch around the sphincter is lost

steps.pressure: Pressure in the sphincter zone falls
steps.reflux: Stomach contents flow back up more easily
steps.burn: Acid irritates the squamous lining of the esophagus
steps.swallow: Swallowing still relaxes the sphincter through nitric oxide

variables.name: Pressure in the lower esophageal sphincter zone
variables.why: The closing pressure comes from two sources: the thickened smooth muscle and the diaphragm pinching it. Losing the diaphragm’s part lowers the total.

variables.name: Reflux of stomach contents into the esophagus
variables.why: Reflux happens whenever pressure in the stomach beats the pressure in the sphincter zone. With the zone weaker, that happens more often.

variables.name: Heartburn
variables.why: Stratified squamous epithelium resists rough food but has little protection against acid, so more reflux means more burning pain behind the sternum. It has nothing to do with the heart.

variables.name: Relaxation of the sphincter when you swallow
variables.why: Opening is still run by vagal fibers and enteric inhibitory neurons releasing nitric oxide, so the bolus still passes normally.

scenarios.title: A brainstem stroke delays the swallowing reflex
scenarios.misconception: if a person can still move the tongue, swallowing must be safe
scenarios.setup: A small stroke damages the swallowing center in the medulla oblongata. The cortex and the nerves to the tongue are unharmed, and sensation in her larynx and her cough reflex are intact. Compare her swallows of water with before the stroke.
scenarios.start: The swallowing center fires late and weakly

steps.tongue: The tongue still pushes the bolus back on command
steps.seal: The vocal folds and epiglottis close the airway late
steps.slip: Water slips into the larynx before the airway is sealed
steps.cough: Sensory receptors in the larynx trigger coughing
steps.lung: Aspirated liquid carries mouth bacteria into the lungs

variables.name: The tongue’s push in the voluntary phase
variables.why: The voluntary phase is started by you and carried out by the tongue muscles, which are unharmed. The damage is in the reflex that should follow.

variables.name: Liquid entering the larynx
variables.why: Thin liquid reaches the pharynx fast. If the reflex that closes the vocal folds and tips the epiglottis fires late, some of it runs into the open larynx first: aspiration.

variables.name: Coughing while drinking
variables.why: Liquid in the larynx stimulates its sensory receptors, which trigger the cough reflex to expel it.

variables.name: Risk of pneumonia
variables.why: Repeated aspiration carries mouth bacteria into the lower airways, and if the cough cannot clear them, pneumonia can follow.

scenarios.title: Chewing food without swallowing it
scenarios.misconception: the stomach only starts secreting once food lands in it
scenarios.setup: In a physiology experiment, a volunteer smells, chews and tastes a meal but spits it out instead of swallowing (sham feeding). Nothing reaches his stomach. Compare his stomach with before the meal was served.
scenarios.start: Sight, smell, taste and chewing act on the brain

steps.vagus: The hypothalamus and medulla oblongata send signals down the vagus nerves
steps.ach: Vagal and enteric neurons release acetylcholine onto parietal and chief cells
steps.g: Vagal signals stimulate the G cells

variables.name: Vagal output to the stomach
variables.why: This is the cephalic phase: signals about food reach the hypothalamus and medulla oblongata, which increase vagal output before any food arrives.

variables.name: Acid secreted by the stomach
variables.why: Acetylcholine acts on the parietal cells’ muscarinic receptor proteins and switches acid secretion on. The cephalic phase supplies roughly a third of a meal’s acid.

variables.name: Gastrin in the blood
variables.why: Vagal signals also stimulate the G cells of the antrum, so gastrin rises even though no protein has reached them.

scenarios.title: Taking a proton pump inhibitor
scenarios.misconception: a drug that blocks acid also switches off the hormone that drives acid
scenarios.setup: A man with a peptic ulcer takes omeprazole, a proton pump inhibitor, every morning for eight weeks. Compare his stomach and blood an hour after a meal with the same time after a meal before he started.
scenarios.start: Omeprazole blocks the H+/K+ proton pumps of the parietal cells

steps.pump: Parietal cells pump far less H+ into the gland lumen
steps.acid: Less hydrochloric acid reaches the stomach contents
steps.ph: The pH of the stomach contents stays higher
steps.dcell: D cells in the antrum release less somatostatin
steps.gastrin: The brake on the G cells lifts, so they release more gastrin
steps.pepsin: Less pepsinogen is converted to pepsin
steps.tide: Less bicarbonate is left behind to enter the blood

variables.name: Acid secreted after a meal
variables.why: The proton pump is the last step of acid secretion. Blocking it cuts acid whatever mix of acetylcholine, gastrin and histamine is arriving.

variables.name: pH of the stomach contents
variables.why: Fewer hydrogen ions reach the lumen, and food buffers those that do, so the pH stays higher. That is what lets the ulcer heal.

variables.name: Gastrin in the blood
variables.why: Acid normally switches off its own stimulus: low pH in the antrum makes D cells release somatostatin, which restrains the G cells. With the pH held higher, that brake weakens and gastrin rises. The parietal cells cannot answer it, because the pump is blocked.

variables.name: Pepsin activity in the stomach
variables.why: Pepsinogen activates only in acid below about pH 5, and pepsin works best near pH 2. With less acid, less pepsin is made and it works poorly.

variables.name: The alkaline tide after a meal
variables.why: Every H+ pumped into the stomach leaves a bicarbonate ion that goes to the blood. Fewer pumped hydrogen ions mean less bicarbonate added.

scenarios.title: The immune system destroys the parietal cells
scenarios.misconception: pernicious anemia comes from eating too little vitamin B12
scenarios.setup: Over many years, a woman’s immune system destroys the parietal cells of her stomach. Her diet contains plenty of vitamin B12. Compare her, years into the disease, with before it began.
scenarios.start: Parietal cells are destroyed

steps.acid: Almost no hydrochloric acid is secreted
steps.ph: The stomach contents stay close to neutral
steps.dcell: D cells sense no acid, so somatostatin stays low
steps.b12: Almost none of the vitamin B12 in food is absorbed
steps.store: The liver’s B12 store runs out over the years
steps.rbc: Developing red blood cells cannot divide normally
steps.count: Fewer red blood cells are made: pernicious anemia

variables.name: Acid secreted by the stomach
variables.why: Only parietal cells make hydrochloric acid. With them gone, the stomach secretes almost none.

variables.name: Gastrin in the blood
variables.why: Acid is gastrin’s brake: low pH in the antrum releases somatostatin, which restrains the G cells. The G cells sit in the antrum and survive, and with no acid the brake never engages, so gastrin climbs very high.

variables.name: Vitamin B12 absorbed from food
variables.why: Parietal cells also make intrinsic factor. Only B12 bound to intrinsic factor can be taken up in the intestine, so almost none is absorbed however much she eats.

variables.name: Red blood cell count
variables.why: Developing red blood cells need B12 to divide normally. Once the liver’s store is used up, which takes years, fewer red blood cells are made. The fix is B12 by injection or in very large oral doses, not more B12 in food.

scenarios.title: A day of repeated vomiting
scenarios.misconception: losing stomach acid makes the blood acidic
scenarios.setup: A child with a stomach virus vomits stomach contents every hour for a day and keeps no fluid down. Compare her blood at the end of the day with before she fell ill.
scenarios.start: Stomach contents are lost through the mouth

steps.hcl: H+ and Cl− secreted by the parietal cells are lost
steps.tide: Each H+ secreted left a bicarbonate ion in the blood
steps.alk: The extra bicarbonate makes the blood alkaline (alkalosis)
steps.k: Potassium is lost in the vomit and in the urine
steps.water: Water from drinks and secretions is lost

variables.name: Blood pH
variables.why: For every hydrogen ion a parietal cell secretes, a bicarbonate ion enters the blood. Normally that is balanced when the acid reaches the intestine; vomited acid never gets there, so bicarbonate piles up and the blood becomes alkaline.

variables.name: Chloride in the blood
variables.why: Chloride follows H+ into the stomach to make hydrochloric acid. Vomiting throws that chloride away, and the parietal cells keep taking more from the blood to replace it.

variables.name: Potassium in the blood
variables.why: Some potassium is lost in the vomit, and more is lost in the urine, so blood potassium falls (hypokalemia).

variables.name: Blood volume
variables.why: Water is lost in the vomit and none is kept down to replace it, so plasma volume falls.

variables.name: Heart rate
variables.why: Lower blood volume lowers venous return and blood pressure. Baroreceptors fire less, and the baroreflex raises sympathetic drive to the heart.

scenarios.title: Months of daily ibuprofen
scenarios.misconception: ulcers come from too much acid, stress or spicy food
scenarios.setup: A man with back pain takes high doses of ibuprofen, an NSAID, every day for months. Compare the lining of his stomach with before.
scenarios.start: Ibuprofen blocks prostaglandin production in the gastric mucosa

steps.pg: Prostaglandins in the gastric mucosa fall
steps.mucus: Surface cells secrete less mucus and bicarbonate
steps.flow: Blood flow in the mucosa falls
steps.ulcer: Acid and pepsin can erode the lining

variables.name: Bicarbonate secreted into the mucus layer
variables.why: Mucosal prostaglandins drive the surface cells to secrete mucus and bicarbonate. Without them, less bicarbonate reaches the gel that keeps the cell surface near pH 7.

variables.name: Blood flow in the gastric mucosa
variables.why: Prostaglandins keep the mucosa’s vessels open. Less flow carries away less of any acid that gets in.

variables.name: Risk of a peptic ulcer
variables.why: An ulcer forms when the barrier weakens, usually not because acid secretion rises. With thinner mucus, less bicarbonate and less blood flow, acid and pepsin reach the cells and erode them.

scenarios.title: A disease flattens the villi
scenarios.misconception: eating more always makes up for poor absorption
scenarios.setup: In untreated celiac disease, an immune reaction to gluten in wheat flattens the villi of a man’s small intestine. He eats a normal amount of food. Compare with a healthy intestine.
scenarios.start: The villi are flattened

steps.area: The absorptive surface shrinks to a fraction of normal
steps.abs: Fewer nutrients are absorbed from each meal
steps.weight: He loses weight and develops deficiencies
steps.cells: Brush border enzymes are lost with the damaged villus cells
steps.lact: Lactase, the least abundant, falls first

variables.name: Absorptive surface of the small intestine
variables.why: Villi multiply the surface several times over. Flatten them and much of that multiplication is lost, even if the circular folds remain.

variables.name: Nutrients absorbed from each meal
variables.why: The rate of absorption rises and falls with the area of the surface it crosses, so less area means less absorbed per meal.

variables.name: Body weight
variables.why: Enough food is eaten, but less of it crosses into the blood, so he loses weight and becomes short of iron and other nutrients.

variables.name: Lactase activity
variables.why: Brush border enzymes are built into the absorptive cells, so they go when the villi are damaged. Lactase is the least abundant and is usually the first to fall. It recovers when the lining heals.

scenarios.title: A gallstone blocks the common bile duct
scenarios.theme: a gallstone blocks the common bile duct
scenarios.misconception: without bile, no fat can be digested at all
scenarios.setup: A gallstone lodges in a woman’s common bile duct above the point where the pancreatic duct joins it. No bile reaches her duodenum, but pancreatic juice still does. Compare her over the next week with before.
scenarios.start: No bile reaches the duodenum

steps.salts: No bile salts reach the fat in the duodenum
steps.drops: Fat stays in large droplets with little surface
steps.slow: Lipase works on a smaller fat surface, and the fatty acids it frees have no bile salts to ferry them to the lining
steps.fecal: Much of the fat, digested or not, passes into the feces
steps.back: Bile backs up behind the stone into the liver
steps.urine: Water-soluble conjugated bilirubin passes into the urine
steps.gut: No bilirubin reaches the gut, so no brown stercobilin is made
steps.panc: Pancreatic juice still reaches the duodenum

variables.name: Fat in the feces
variables.why: Bile salts do not digest fat. They keep it in tiny droplets with a large surface, and they carry the digested products to the absorptive cells (you will see how in Chemical digestion and absorption). Without them, fat is digested more slowly and much of what is digested is not absorbed, so fat appears in the feces.

variables.name: Bilirubin in the blood
variables.why: Hepatocytes keep conjugating bilirubin and secreting it into bile. With the exit blocked, it backs up into the blood: obstructive jaundice.

variables.name: Darkness of the urine
variables.why: Conjugated bilirubin is water-soluble, so once it is in the blood it passes into the urine and darkens it.

variables.name: Brown color of the feces
variables.why: Feces are brown because bacteria in the intestine turn bilirubin into stercobilin. No bilirubin reaches the gut, so the feces turn pale.

variables.name: Protein digestion
variables.why: Protein is digested by pepsin and by trypsin and the other pancreatic enzymes, which still arrive. Bile has no digestive enzymes.

scenarios.title: The pancreatic duct is blocked
scenarios.misconception: blocking the pancreas’s duct also stops insulin reaching the blood
scenarios.setup: A tumor in the head of the pancreas squeezes the main pancreatic duct shut. The common bile duct is still open. Compare the next few days with before the blockage.
scenarios.start: Pancreatic juice cannot reach the duodenum

steps.lip: Almost no pancreatic lipase reaches the fat
steps.fat: Fat passes undigested into pale, greasy feces
steps.prot: No trypsin, chymotrypsin or elastase reaches the lumen
steps.protd: Protein digestion in the small intestine falls
steps.bicarb: No bicarbonate-rich juice neutralizes the acid chyme
steps.bile: Bile still flows into the duodenum
steps.emul: Bile salts still emulsify the fat
steps.islet: The islets release insulin into their capillaries, not the duct

variables.name: Fat in the feces
variables.why: Pancreatic lipase does most fat digestion. Gastric lipase does only a small share, so most fat leaves undigested.

variables.name: Protein digestion
variables.why: Pepsin does only a minority of protein digestion. Most is done by the pancreatic enzymes, and they can no longer reach the lumen.

variables.name: pH of the duodenal contents
variables.why: Bicarbonate from the pancreatic duct cells normally neutralizes acid chyme. Without it, the duodenum stays acidic, relying only on its alkaline mucus.

variables.name: Secretin in the blood
variables.why: Secretin is released by acid and switched off when the acid is neutralized. Its effect cannot reach the duodenum, so the stimulus persists and secretin stays high.

variables.name: Emulsification of fat
variables.why: Emulsification is done by bile salts, and the bile duct is open. The fat is emulsified but barely digested.

variables.name: Insulin reaching the blood
variables.why: The islets are endocrine: they release insulin into capillaries, not into the duct, so a blocked duct does not stop it.

scenarios.title: Fatty chyme reaches the duodenum
scenarios.misconception: the liver makes more bile on the spot to handle a fatty meal
scenarios.setup: You eat a large cheeseburger and fries. Compare what happens while fatty chyme is entering the duodenum with the fasting hours before the meal.
scenarios.start: Fat and protein fragments reach the duodenum

steps.cck: Enteroendocrine cells release CCK into the blood
steps.gb: The smooth muscle of the gallbladder contracts
steps.bile: Stored, concentrated bile flows into the duodenum

variables.name: CCK in the blood
variables.why: Fat and protein fragments in the duodenum stimulate its enteroendocrine cells to release cholecystokinin.

variables.name: Bile entering the duodenum
variables.why: CCK contracts the gallbladder and relaxes the hepatopancreatic sphincter at the same time, so the bile stored between meals is squeezed out.

variables.name: Volume of bile in the gallbladder
variables.why: Between meals the gallbladder fills with bile; now it contracts and empties.

variables.name: Pancreatic enzyme secretion
variables.why: CCK acts on the acinar cells, which release their stored enzymes by exocytosis.

variables.name: Rate of gastric emptying
variables.why: CCK weakens the antrum’s waves and tightens the pylorus, so the stomach holds a fatty meal longer while the intestine digests what it already has.

scenarios.title: Acid chyme arrives in the duodenum
scenarios.misconception: the stomach decides by itself how fast to empty and how much acid to make
scenarios.setup: A squirt of chyme at pH 2 passes the pylorus into the duodenum. Compare the next few minutes with just before it arrived.
scenarios.start: Acid lowers the pH in the duodenum

steps.duct: Pancreatic duct cells secrete bicarbonate-rich fluid
steps.vol: A large volume of watery pancreatic juice flows
steps.hblood: Duct cells send H+ into the blood leaving the pancreas
steps.stom: Secretin slows acid secretion and gastric emptying

variables.name: Secretin in the blood
variables.why: Acid is secretin’s stimulus. Enteroendocrine cells in the duodenal lining sense it and release secretin into the blood.

variables.name: Volume of pancreatic juice
variables.why: Secretin targets the duct cells, which add a large volume of watery, bicarbonate-rich fluid. The bicarbonate neutralizes the acid that triggered the secretin.

variables.name: pH of the blood leaving the pancreas
variables.why: Making bicarbonate is the mirror image of making acid: the duct cells put bicarbonate into the duct and hydrogen ions into the blood, so blood leaving the pancreas is slightly more acidic.

variables.name: Acid secretion by the stomach
variables.why: Secretin slows acid secretion and gastric emptying, so the stomach sends less acid until the duodenum has neutralized what it has.

scenarios.title: Years of cirrhosis
scenarios.misconception: cirrhosis only affects the liver
scenarios.setup: A man has had cirrhosis for years. Bands of scar divide his liver into nodules, and many hepatocytes have been lost. Compare him with a person with a healthy liver.
scenarios.start: Scar replaces normal lobules, and fewer hepatocytes work

steps.portal: Pressure in the hepatic portal vein rises
steps.veins: Blood backs up into veins at the lower esophagus
steps.leak: Fluid leaks from congested vessels into the peritoneal cavity
steps.bili: Less bilirubin is taken up and secreted into bile
steps.jaund: Bilirubin builds up in the blood

variables.name: Pressure in the hepatic portal vein
variables.why: All the portal blood must cross the sinusoids. Scar squeezes them, so resistance rises and pressure builds in the portal vein behind them.

variables.name: Swelling of the veins at the lower esophagus
variables.why: Blood that cannot get through the liver backs up into veins that link the portal system to the systemic veins. They swell and can burst and bleed heavily.

variables.name: Fluid in the peritoneal cavity
variables.why: Raised pressure in the congested vessels pushes fluid out of them into the peritoneal cavity: ascites. Low albumin makes it worse.

variables.name: Plasma albumin
variables.why: Albumin is made by hepatocytes. With fewer of them working, less is made.

variables.name: Time for blood to clot
variables.why: Hepatocytes make most clotting factors. With fewer factors, the cascade runs slowly and the patient bruises and bleeds easily.

variables.name: Bilirubin in the blood
variables.why: Hepatocytes clear bilirubin from the blood and secrete it into bile. With fewer working, bilirubin accumulates and the skin turns yellow.

scenarios.title: Two weeks of opioid pain medicine
scenarios.misconception: constipation means the colon is absorbing too little
scenarios.setup: After knee surgery, a woman takes an opioid pain medicine for two weeks. Compare her colon and stools with before the surgery.
scenarios.start: The opioid inhibits the enteric neurons

steps.mot: Propulsive contractions and mass movements weaken
steps.time: Feces spend longer in the colon
steps.water: The colon absorbs more water from them
steps.fewer: Fewer mass movements push feces into the rectum

variables.name: Propulsive movement in the colon
variables.why: The enteric nervous system runs the colon’s contractions. Opioids inhibit its neurons, so the waves that push contents along, including mass movements, weaken. Squeezing that only mixes the contents in place does not fall, and may even rise.

variables.name: Time contents spend in the colon
variables.why: With weaker propulsive contractions, contents move more slowly from the cecum to the rectum.

variables.name: Water absorbed from the feces
variables.why: The colon keeps absorbing sodium, and water follows, for as long as the contents stay. More time means more water taken out.

variables.name: Water content of the stool
variables.why: With more water removed, stools are harder and drier, which slows them further: constipation feeds itself.

variables.name: Bowel movements per week
variables.why: Mass movements are what fill the rectum and trigger the defecation reflex. Fewer of them means fewer bowel movements.

scenarios.title: A course of broad-spectrum antibiotics
scenarios.misconception: gut bacteria are only germs, so killing them can only help
scenarios.setup: A man takes a broad-spectrum antibiotic for ten days. Compare his colon near the end of the course with before it.
scenarios.start: Many of the normal colon bacteria are killed

steps.scfa: Fewer short-chain fatty acids, such as butyrate, are made
steps.fuel: The colon’s epithelial cells get less of their main fuel
steps.gas: Less gas is made from fiber
steps.space: Space and nutrients open up for resistant microbes

variables.name: Short-chain fatty acids made in the colon
variables.why: You have no enzymes for most fiber; colon bacteria ferment it into acetate, propionate and butyrate. Fewer bacteria, less fermentation.

variables.name: Butyrate available to the colon’s epithelial cells
variables.why: Butyrate made by bacteria is the main fuel of the colon’s own lining cells, so they get less of it.

variables.name: Gas made from fiber
variables.why: Hydrogen, carbon dioxide and methane are products of fermentation, so less fermentation makes less gas.

variables.name: Risk of Clostridioides difficile overgrowth
variables.why: A settled community crowds out invaders. With it thinned out, a resistant species can overgrow and release toxins that inflame the colon and cause severe diarrhea.

scenarios.title: A milkshake with too little lactase
scenarios.misconception: lactose intolerance is an allergy to milk
scenarios.setup: A 25-year-old whose lactase production fell after childhood drinks a large milkshake, about 50 g of lactose, on an empty stomach. Compare the next few hours with a friend who still makes plenty of lactase and drinks the same milkshake.
scenarios.start: Little lactase at the brush border

steps.undig: Most of the lactose stays undigested in the lumen
steps.mono: Less glucose and galactose are released for SGLT1 to absorb
steps.osm: Undigested lactose holds water in the lumen by osmosis
steps.colon: Lactose and extra water reach the colon
steps.breath: Some of the hydrogen made is absorbed and breathed out
steps.stool: The extra water and solutes cause osmotic diarrhea
steps.immune: No antibody or immune cell reacts to the milk

variables.name: Rise in blood glucose after the milkshake
variables.why: Only monosaccharides can be absorbed. Undigested lactose releases no glucose or galactose for SGLT1, so her blood glucose rises less than her friend’s.

variables.name: Hydrogen in her exhaled breath
variables.why: Colon bacteria ferment the lactose into hydrogen, carbon dioxide and fatty acids. Some hydrogen enters the blood and is breathed out, which is what the hydrogen breath test measures.

variables.name: Water in the stool
variables.why: Unabsorbed lactose holds water in the lumen, and fermentation adds more solute in the colon. The colon cannot absorb all of it: osmotic diarrhea.

variables.name: Antibody response to the milk
variables.why: Lactose intolerance is a shortage of an enzyme, not an immune reaction. A milk allergy is the immune response to milk proteins, and it is a different condition.

scenarios.title: The last part of the ileum is removed
scenarios.misconception: any length of small intestine can do any job of absorption
scenarios.setup: After years of inflammatory bowel disease, a woman has the last 150 cm of her ileum removed. The rest of her small intestine and her colon are healthy, and she takes no vitamin supplements. Compare her a year later with before surgery.
scenarios.start: The terminal ileum and its carriers are gone

steps.if: No cells are left with receptor proteins for the B12–intrinsic factor complex
steps.b12: Almost no vitamin B12 is absorbed
steps.salts: Bile salts are not reabsorbed and are lost in the feces
steps.mic: Fewer micelles carry lipids to the brush border
steps.fat: Fat absorption falls, and fat appears in the feces
steps.vitk: Vitamin K, which travels with fat, is poorly absorbed
steps.clot: The liver makes fewer active clotting factors

variables.name: Vitamin B12 absorbed each day
variables.why: The receptor proteins that take up B12 bound to intrinsic factor are found only in the terminal ileum. No other part of the intestine can take over.

variables.name: Bile salts lost in the feces
variables.why: About 95% of bile salts are normally reabsorbed by carriers in the last part of the ileum. With those carriers gone, most are lost each time they are secreted.

variables.name: Fat in the feces
variables.why: The liver cannot make new bile salts fast enough to replace a pool lost with every meal. Fewer bile salts mean less emulsification and fewer micelles, so less fat is absorbed.

variables.name: Time for blood to clot
variables.why: Vitamin K dissolves in fat and is absorbed with it. Without enough vitamin K, the liver cannot finish making factors II, VII, IX and X, so clotting slows.

scenarios.title: Cholera, then oral rehydration
scenarios.misconception: drinking is useless in cholera because the gut is secreting, not absorbing
scenarios.setup: A woman catches cholera. The toxin of Vibrio cholerae reaches the cells of her intestinal glands. First she goes untreated for several hours; then she is given an oral rehydration solution of salt and glucose.

stages.label: The first hours, untreated
stages.prompt: Six hours into the illness, with no treatment, compared with before she fell ill.
stages.start: The toxin locks the chloride channels of the intestinal glands open

steps.na: Sodium and water follow the chloride
steps.stool: More fluid arrives than the villi and colon can absorb
steps.k: Potassium, secreted by the colon, is lost in the stool
steps.hco3: Bicarbonate is lost in the stool

variables.name: Volume of watery stool
variables.why: Chloride secretion drags sodium and water into the lumen faster than the intestine can take them back, so liters of watery stool pour out.

variables.name: Blood volume
variables.why: The water in the stool comes from the extracellular fluid, so plasma volume falls. More than 10 liters a day can be lost.

variables.name: Heart rate
variables.why: Lower volume lowers venous return and blood pressure, baroreceptors fire less, and sympathetic drive speeds the heart.

variables.name: Blood potassium
variables.why: Stool water carries potassium, which the colon secretes, so blood potassium falls.

variables.name: Blood pH
variables.why: Stool water also carries bicarbonate. Losing base leaves the blood more acidic.

stages.label: Two hours of oral rehydration
stages.prompt: After two hours of drinking the salt and glucose solution, with the toxin still active, compared with the untreated hours.
stages.start: Glucose and sodium from the solution reach the brush border

steps.sglt: SGLT1, untouched by the toxin, carries sodium and glucose into the absorptive cells
steps.water: Water follows them into the body by osmosis
steps.hr: The baroreflex lets the heart slow
steps.tox: The toxin still holds the chloride channels open

variables.name: Sodium absorbed through SGLT1
variables.why: Each glucose that SGLT1 carries brings two sodium ions with it. The toxin does not affect SGLT1, so glucose in the solution drives sodium in.

variables.name: Blood volume
variables.why: Sodium and glucose moving from the lumen into the body pull water after them by osmosis, faster than the toxin drives it out.

variables.name: Heart rate
variables.why: As volume and blood pressure recover, baroreceptors fire more and sympathetic drive to the heart eases.

variables.name: Chloride secreted into the lumen
variables.why: The solution does not undo the toxin; the chloride channels stay open. It works by opening a second route that brings sodium and water back, not by stopping the loss.

scenarios.title: Cyanide blocks complex IV
scenarios.theme: cyanide blocks the electron transport chain
scenarios.misconception: cyanide kills by stopping oxygen from reaching the cells
scenarios.setup: A man is pulled from a burning building after breathing smoke that contains hydrogen cyanide. Cyanide binds the iron in complex IV of the electron transport chain in his cells. His lungs and blood still work. Predict the changes over the next few minutes.
scenarios.start: Cyanide binds complex IV

steps.c4: Complex IV cannot pass electrons to oxygen
steps.back: Electrons back up along the whole chain
steps.pump: H+ pumping stops, and the gradient runs down
steps.ven: Blood leaves the tissues still carrying much of its oxygen
steps.nad: NADH cannot be oxidized, so NAD+ runs out in the matrix
steps.lac: Pyruvate is turned into lactate to regenerate NAD+
steps.ph: Lactate and H+ build up in the blood
steps.lung: Lungs and hemoglobin load oxygen normally
steps.art: Oxygen delivered to the tissues is unchanged

variables.name: ATP made by ATP synthase
variables.why: Without electron flow, complexes I and III stop pumping H+. The gradient runs down, and with no H+ flowing back through ATP synthase, it makes no ATP.

variables.name: Oxygen used by the cells
variables.why: Oxygen is used only at complex IV, where it accepts electrons and becomes water. With complex IV blocked, oxygen is no longer taken up.

variables.name: Oxygen left in the venous blood
variables.why: Blood delivers oxygen as usual but the tissues take little out, so venous blood keeps much of its oxygen and looks unusually red.

variables.name: Oxygen carried to the tissues in arterial blood
variables.why: Cyanide acts inside the mitochondria, not in the lungs or on hemoglobin, so the blood arrives as well loaded as before. The problem is use, not delivery.

variables.name: Rate of the citric acid cycle
variables.why: The cycle needs NAD+ and FAD, and only the electron transport chain turns NADH and FADH2 back into them. With the chain stopped, the cycle stops within seconds.

variables.name: Rate of glycolysis
variables.why: As ATP falls, AMP builds up and speeds phosphofructokinase, so glucose is broken down faster, giving 2 ATP per glucose without the mitochondria.

variables.name: Blood lactate
variables.why: Pyruvate cannot enter the stalled mitochondria. Turning it into lactate regenerates the NAD+ that glycolysis needs to keep running, and lactate spills into the blood.

variables.name: Blood pH
variables.why: Lactate is made with H+ as fast glycolysis runs, and the H+ builds up in the blood faster than it can be buffered and removed.

scenarios.title: A drug makes the inner mitochondrial membrane leak H+
scenarios.misconception: burning more fuel always means making more ATP
scenarios.setup: A bodybuilder takes dinitrophenol, an industrial chemical once sold as a weight-loss drug. It carries H+ back across the inner mitochondrial membrane without passing through ATP synthase. Predict the changes in his cells and body over the next hours.
scenarios.start: H+ leaks back into the matrix

steps.leak: H+ returns to the matrix without passing through ATP synthase
steps.fast: The electron transport chain speeds up to rebuild it
steps.fuel: More fuel is broken down to supply NADH
steps.less: Less of the H+ flow passes through ATP synthase
steps.per: Less ATP is made from each glucose
steps.heat: The energy of the electrons leaves as heat

variables.name: Size of the H+ gradient across the inner membrane
variables.why: The drug gives H+ a second way back into the matrix, so the gradient runs down even though the chain keeps pumping.

variables.name: Oxygen use by the cells
variables.why: Electron flow is held back by the gradient. With the gradient lower, electrons flow faster down the chain to oxygen, so more oxygen is used.

variables.name: Fuel broken down per hour
variables.why: A faster chain turns NADH and FADH2 back into NAD+ and FAD faster, so glycolysis and the citric acid cycle can run faster and burn more fuel.

variables.name: ATP made per glucose broken down
variables.why: H+ that leaks back does not turn ATP synthase, so each glucose, which still pumps the same H+, yields fewer ATP.

variables.name: Heat produced by the cells
variables.why: The energy released as electrons pass to oxygen is no longer captured as ATP, so it is released as heat.

variables.name: Body temperature
variables.why: Heat is made faster than it can be lost. Users of this drug died from body temperatures that rose out of control.

scenarios.title: A liver without glucose-6-phosphatase
scenarios.misconception: a liver full of glycogen can always keep blood glucose up
scenarios.setup: A toddler was born without glucose-6-phosphatase (glycogen storage disease type I). Compare her with a healthy toddler four hours after the same meal.
scenarios.start: No glucose-6-phosphatase in the liver

steps.noenz: The liver cannot remove the phosphate from glucose-6-phosphate
steps.trap: Glucose-6-phosphate stays trapped in liver cells
steps.norel: No free glucose is released into the blood
steps.bg: Blood glucose falls a few hours after a meal
steps.pile: Glycogen keeps piling up in the liver
steps.push: Trapped glucose-6-phosphate is pushed down glycolysis
steps.mnorm: Muscle breaks down its own glycogen normally

variables.name: Glucose released by the liver
variables.why: Glucose from glycogen or gluconeogenesis ends as glucose-6-phosphate, which is charged and cannot use the glucose carriers. Without the enzyme, no free glucose leaves.

variables.name: Blood glucose four hours after a meal
variables.why: Once the meal has been absorbed, the liver is the only supply of blood glucose. With that supply cut off, glucose falls sharply between meals.

variables.name: Glycogen stored in the liver
variables.why: The liver can still build glycogen and break it down to glucose-6-phosphate, but the glucose has nowhere to go, so glycogen accumulates.

variables.name: Size of the liver
variables.why: The extra stored glycogen swells the liver cells, so the liver enlarges.

variables.name: Blood lactate
variables.why: The trapped glucose-6-phosphate is broken down by glycolysis instead, and much of the pyruvate is turned into lactate, which leaves the liver.

variables.name: Muscle use of its own glycogen during play
variables.why: Muscle has no glucose-6-phosphatase in anyone. Its glycogen is broken to glucose-6-phosphate that enters glycolysis in the same muscle, so the missing enzyme does not affect it.

scenarios.title: Type 1 diabetes: two days without insulin
scenarios.misconception: the liver can turn the extra fatty acids into glucose
scenarios.setup: A 20-year-old with type 1 diabetes loses her insulin supplies on a trip and takes none for two days. Compare her now with when she was taking insulin.
scenarios.start: Insulin almost absent

steps.brake: Nothing brakes lipolysis in fat cells
steps.fa: Fatty acids pour into the blood
steps.liv: The liver takes up fatty acids and runs beta oxidation at a high rate
steps.acoa: Acetyl CoA piles up in liver mitochondria
steps.kb: Ketone bodies are made faster than other tissues can burn them
steps.h: Their H+ is released into the blood
steps.bic: Bicarbonate is used up buffering the H+
steps.breathe: Low pH stimulates deep, rapid breathing
steps.ace: Some acetoacetate breaks down to acetone
steps.oneway: Acetyl CoA cannot be turned back into pyruvate
steps.nogl: No glucose is made from the fatty acids

variables.name: Lipolysis in adipose tissue
variables.why: Insulin brakes lipolysis even at low levels. With it almost gone, and epinephrine and glucagon unopposed, stored triglyceride is broken down fast.

variables.name: Fatty acids in the blood
variables.why: Fat cells release the fatty acids from lipolysis into the blood, where they travel on albumin.

variables.name: Ketone bodies made by the liver
variables.why: Beta oxidation makes acetyl CoA faster than the citric acid cycle can take it, and the liver is drawing oxaloacetate off for gluconeogenesis. The extra acetyl CoA is made into ketone bodies.

variables.name: Glucose the liver makes from fatty acids
variables.why: Fatty acids are broken down to acetyl CoA, and the step from pyruvate to acetyl CoA cannot run backward. However much fat is burned, none of it becomes glucose; only glycerol can.

variables.name: Blood bicarbonate
variables.why: Acetoacetic and beta-hydroxybutyric acid give up their H+ at body pH. Bicarbonate combines with that H+ and is used up.

variables.name: Blood pH
variables.why: Once bicarbonate is used up, the H+ is no longer mopped up, and pH falls below 7.35: ketoacidosis.

variables.name: Depth and rate of breathing
variables.why: Chemoreceptors sense the rise in H+ and drive the brainstem to deepen and speed breathing.

variables.name: Arterial PCO2
variables.why: Deep, rapid breathing blows off CO2 faster than it is made, so PCO2 falls, which partly offsets the acid.

variables.name: Acetone on the breath
variables.why: With acetoacetate so high, more of it loses CO2 on its own to form acetone, which is volatile and gives the breath a fruity smell.

scenarios.title: Starting a statin
scenarios.misconception: statins lower blood cholesterol by blocking its absorption from food
scenarios.setup: A 55-year-old with high LDL starts a daily statin, a drug that blocks HMG CoA reductase. Compare him after two months with before the drug.
scenarios.start: The statin blocks HMG CoA reductase

steps.rec: Liver cells make more LDL receptor proteins
steps.up: More LDL is pulled out of the blood

variables.name: Cholesterol made by liver cells
variables.why: HMG CoA reductase catalyzes the control step of cholesterol synthesis from acetyl CoA. Blocking it cuts the cells’ own production.

variables.name: LDL receptor proteins on liver cells
variables.why: A cell short of cholesterol makes more LDL receptor proteins, just as a cell with plenty makes fewer.

variables.name: LDL taken up by the liver
variables.why: More receptor proteins bind more LDL particles and bring them into the cells by endocytosis.

variables.name: Blood LDL
variables.why: LDL is removed from the blood faster than it is made from VLDL, so its level falls, often by a third to a half.

variables.name: Rate of plaque growth in artery walls
variables.why: LDL is a direct cause of atherosclerosis: less LDL entering artery walls means slower plaque growth, which is why statins prevent heart attacks and strokes.

scenarios.title: A failing liver and ammonia
scenarios.misconception: liver failure raises blood urea
scenarios.setup: A 60-year-old has advanced cirrhosis: too few liver cells still work. He eats a normal amount of protein. Compare him with a healthy adult on the same diet.
scenarios.start: Too few working liver cells

steps.cyc: The urea cycle cannot keep up with the ammonia from amino acids
steps.nh3: Ammonia builds up in the blood
steps.neuro: Neurotransmission is disturbed and astrocytes swell
steps.conf: Confusion and a flapping tremor of the hands

variables.name: Urea made each day
variables.why: Only liver cells run the urea cycle. With too few working, less ammonia is turned into urea.

variables.name: Blood urea
variables.why: Blood urea reflects the balance of urea made by the liver and removed by the kidneys. The kidneys still work, but less urea is being made, so the level is often low.

variables.name: Urea excreted in the urine
variables.why: The kidneys can excrete only the urea that reaches them, and less is being made.

variables.name: Blood ammonia
variables.why: Deamination of amino acids still releases ammonia, but it is not cleared into urea, so it builds up in the blood.

variables.name: Confusion
variables.why: Ammonia disturbs neurotransmission and swells astrocytes even at small rises, so brain function suffers: confusion, a flapping tremor and, eventually, coma.

scenarios.title: A large meal after an afternoon without food
scenarios.misconception: after a meal the liver keeps making and releasing new glucose
scenarios.setup: You have eaten nothing since lunch, and at 7 pm you eat a large plate of pasta with meat sauce. Compare one hour after the meal with just before it.
scenarios.start: Glucose and amino acids are absorbed

steps.abs: Glucose and amino acids enter the portal blood
steps.liv: The liver takes up glucose and builds glycogen
steps.gng: Gluconeogenesis slows; the glucose it still makes goes into glycogen
steps.glut: Insulin moves GLUT4 carriers into muscle membranes
steps.ffa: Fat cells release fewer fatty acids
steps.brain: Brain glucose uptake does not depend on insulin
steps.bn: The brain keeps burning glucose at the same rate

variables.name: Blood insulin
variables.why: Rising glucose and amino acids, and gut hormones released as food arrives, make beta cells release insulin.

variables.name: Blood glucagon
variables.why: Rising glucose, and insulin from nearby beta cells, hold back glucagon release.

variables.name: Glucose released by the liver
variables.why: With insulin up and glucagon down, glycogen breakdown stops and the liver stops exporting glucose; the gut now supplies the blood.

variables.name: Glycogen in the liver
variables.why: Glucose from the portal blood reaches the liver first, and insulin and high glucose switch glycogen synthase on.

variables.name: Gluconeogenesis in the liver
variables.why: Insulin switches gluconeogenesis off and glucagon no longer drives it. It slows rather than stopping, and much of the glucose it still makes is stored as glycogen instead of leaving.

variables.name: Glucose uptake by skeletal muscle
variables.why: Insulin moves GLUT4 carriers into the muscle cell membrane, so glucose floods in to be burned or stored as glycogen.

variables.name: Fatty acids released from fat cells
variables.why: Insulin switches lipolysis off within minutes, so fat cells store fat instead of releasing it.

variables.name: Glucose used by the brain
variables.why: Brain glucose uptake does not depend on insulin, and the brain burns glucose at a steady rate whether you have eaten or not.

scenarios.title: Three days without food
scenarios.misconception: ketone bodies in a fast make the blood acidic
scenarios.setup: A hiker is lost in the mountains with water but no food. Compare her on day 3 with the morning after her last meal, when she had fasted only overnight.
scenarios.start: No food for three days
